Good morning, everybody. Welcome to the last day of Senate estimates for the week. I declare open this hearing of the Education and Employment Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present, and I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today. The committee has fixed Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with corporate and enabling services of the Department of Education.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings.

I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. I now welcome Senator the Hon. Dr Jess Walsh, the Minister for Early Childhood Education and the Minister for Youth, who is representing the Minister for Education. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement today?
Good morning, Chair. No, I don't.
I welcome Mr Tony Cook PSM, Secretary of the Department of Education. Mr Cook, do you wish to make an opening statement?
Just a very short statement, if that's okay, Chair.
Please proceed.

Before we begin, I'd like to acknowledge the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines MP. On behalf of the Department of Education, I express our support for Dr Haines as she recovers in hospital following the recent deeply distressing event. Violence against anyone in any form is totally unacceptable. Our thoughts are with Dr Haines's family, her electorate staff and the broader Indi community. We recognise that an event of this nature can have a profound impact on many people, and our thoughts are with all those affected. We wish Dr Haines strength and comfort as she continues to recovery.

I'd also like, on behalf of the department, to welcome Senator Scarr, a fellow Queenslander, to the committee. It's great to have you here, Senator Scarr.
I'm changing my questions!

I hoped that would happen; that's why I said that! As per normal practice, our graduates will also rotate through towards the back. Finally, I'd like to wish my mum happy birthday. It's her birthday today. I won't say how old she is; otherwise, I'll never be in the committee again.
What is your mother's name, Mr Cook?
Marie Cook—she's in Dalby.
Happy birthday, Marie, from the Education and Employment Legislation Committee.
I wish her a happy birthday.
I'm going through Dalby on Friday. If you've got a present that you want me to deliver—
I'll be there next Friday, so—
let me know!
we can catch up!
We'll take that one offline. That sounds like a good idea.
Thanks, Chair.

To your graduates listening, we're very much looking forward to having them in here today. I said last time that I started my career as a graduate in the Public Service. It's a fantastic thing to do. We're really looking forward to their attendance today, and, hopefully, we don't scare them off a lifetime of public service. We'll get underway with corporate and enabling services, and I'll go to the opposition. Senator O'Sullivan.

Thank you, Secretary, for those remarks in relation to Dr Helen Haines. Can I ask about the departmental expenses. I see they rose from $416 million in 2024-25 to $437.9 million in 2025-26—an increase of approximately five per cent, which, as we know, is above inflation. What's driving that increase in spending?
I might get my COO to help me with that.

In part, the increase in expenditure has been due to new measures that were provided throughout the year. I think last time at estimates we gave you a table of some measures. We've had two things happening. We've had some measures coming on and some going off. I think we spoke last time around some of the child safety measures where the department was given additional resourcing. In line with that additional resourcing, we've had additional expenditure. That's the primary reason, but I might see if the CFO has anything he would like to add to that.
You said that's the main. Have you got a breakdown of how much for that particular measure as a percentage, maybe, or an impact?
Was that 2024-25 into 2026?
I'm comparing 2024-25 to 2025-26.

The largest component was a measure in relation to safety and quality in early childcare settings. It provided for the department 86½ ASL. It brought in additional funding across the forwards of about $80 million. Within the year, that staffing increase alone was about $12½ million—$12.3 million, if memory serves. That is that increase in revenue across those financial years.

You've got 27 performance measures. I understand that six of them were not met and two of them don't have assessable results. Does that mean that, in the last year, you haven't met roughly a quarter of your targets? Does that concern you, Secretary?

As you would imagine, a number of these targets relate to work that we do with states and territories. I'm having a quick look over at the targets which are numbered. Mr Markovic might be able to help me with what they actually are. I imagine some of these are probably in relation to literacy and numeracy performance of schools. Obviously, if we don't meet targets, that does concern me—of course it does—but part of our work is working closely with states and territories in relation to the funding that we provide to states and territories—and, then, their meeting targets which, effectively, we set. But, as you know, we don't run schools and employ teachers and things like that. Part of the work that we've done is around the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement, as you know—we can go into that in the next outcome—and focusing very much on reforms that will enable us to meet those targets. But my preference as a secretary of course is that—we would like to meet all targets that we set.

I want to ask about some specific performance measures that are of concern to me. They appear to be going backwards. I'll run through them and then ask my question. The first one is: the proportion of people attaining a year 12 certificate or equivalent is not on track and has gone backwards. The proportion of 25- to 34-year-olds obtaining a tertiary qualification is not growing. The proportion of domestic undergraduates who rate teaching quality positively is going backwards. The proportion of employers who are satisfied with the skills of graduates is going backwards. And finally, the proportion of HELP debt not expected to be repaid is growing. So that's a pretty dire picture for the department but, more importantly, it paints a dire picture for our education system as a whole, particularly in higher education. Why is the department's annual report so at odds with what I would say is the upbeat tone of the minister's description of the higher education system?
That might be opinion, but I'm very happy to talk about the things you've just raised. You're right, almost all of them are in the higher education space.
And we'll go into detail on those.

Yes, sure. For some of them, of course, again, it's funding that we provide to those providers. We have some influence then as to how that funding is used and how those providers best support their students to enable them to be satisfied with their courses, to enable employers to be satisfied with the skills of graduates. It's work that we're continuing to do, and that's why the minister's very focused on things like regulations in terms of universities, focusing on teaching and learning. ATEC will be here a little later tonight to talk about some of the work they're doing, including some of the focus they might have on teaching and learning.

The proportion of HELP debt not expected to be repaid on new debt: as you know, the government made a significant action in relation to reducing 20 per cent of HELP debt over the last year or so. That's basically the actuary information that they provide to us in terms of what they expect that would be. That's updated every year. It's stayed around about 13 per cent. I think it's 13-point-something per cent at the moment, so there hasn't been a significant difference, I don't think, in terms of what the data has been over the last couple of years, but we continue to work with universities in terms of the quality of the work that we're doing. ATEC has a big role around that now. They're looking at that in terms of compacts. They can talk about compacts later tonight. Some of their focus will be around things like teaching and learning, what they can do to ensure that graduates are able to assess their program as being more positive than what their what they're saying at the moment. They're some of the reforms the government is putting in to address some of these issues that you've raised, particularly around higher ed.

Is the reason for HELP debts not being repaid—you don't get a choice as to whether you repay it because it's deducted out of your salary—because individuals are not earning the requisite income to start the repayment?

I think it is $69,000 or something like that at the moment. Part of that reason might be that people aren't in employment, they might be continuing their study or they might be not reaching that threshold. That might be part of it—that's right.
So are we funding courses that are not leading to employment outcomes?
I wouldn't necessarily say that. A lot of this depends on life choices—what students are doing themselves—so I probably haven't got enough data to do a causal link to that one. I'm sorry.
Were you surprised to see that there were fewer students completing year 12 and going on to tertiary study happy with their degrees and satisfying their employers?

I think there's more recent data, again, in schools, and we can probably talk about what that data looks like. Again, the Better Fairer Schools Agreement has a very strong focus on school attendance and school completion. We've set targets in relation to that, so I think we recognised this was an issue. There is a little bit still of COVID lag, dare I say, in terms of what's happening in schools, but we are seeing that there are some improvements in that data that states and territories are focusing on. This has lagged data. I don't actually know when the latest data set was. I should be able to find out what it is, but it's lag data in terms of it's not the most recent up-to-date data. If the schools group have more up-to-date data, we'll be able to share that with you in the next outcome.
I'll move on to a different subject, the Building Early Education Fund, BEEF. I want to ask about grant G08346. Can I ask that here?
Let's give it a go and, if we need to, the BEEF people can come back later.

Yes. I just wanted to check if it needed to be asked here because I wouldn't want to get to the end of the day and realise I should have asked it here. This is about the Building Early Education Fund. The Malangenna Children's Centre grant was a $4 million closed non-competitive grant which draws on the Building Early Education Fund, commonly known as BEEF. It was promised by Ms Urquhart as part of her 2025 election campaign and has now been delivered by the department. Is this just pork-barrelling?
My answer to that would be no. Again, I will need my BEEF people—that sounded weird, didn't it?—in the early childhood sector to be able to answer that in more detail for you.
Well, they're on notice, so I'll deal with that again later today.
But you said it was an election commitment. Is that right?

It was an election commitment. But I'm interested to understand the merit or value for money that this particular project has. BEEF, as it is designed, is there primarily for childcare deserts, yet we're seeing many go into areas where there is an oversupply of childcare services already. So trying to understand the merit and the value for money and the assessment that the department lays over it, notwithstanding there were election commitments. But, still, there must be some sort of assessment made, because it's a grant program, not just a—
There will be. My BEEF team will be able to give much greater detail in relation to that.
So that's a question for later today.
Yes.

I'll skip these and come back on that later, then. They've got a tip-off on where I'm going. I want to ask about the service delivery pricing project. For the Early Education Service Delivery Prices project, what's the total value of the department's contract with Deloitte?
I've got here $6.7 million.
Does that include any extensions or variations?
I don't think there were any extensions to Deloitte.
I'm not aware of it, but I can't absolutely say. I don't know.
You can come back to us.
The early childhood team will be able to answer that. They've got the detail around that.
Do you have the original contract dates and key milestones? Are there any delays at all?
I have the contract dates. Probably the milestones and the delays would be a question for our early childhood colleagues. But the start date was 6 June 2025, and the end date is 28 February 2027.
My understanding is the expectation is that a report will be delivered by the end of the year. I don't have any information that will say that's been delayed at all.
Have there been any requests or have there been any approvals for any changes to the contract scope, timeframe or cost, at all?
I'm not aware of any, but Mr Reed or Ms Crane can give more detail on early childhood. I'm not aware of any changes to that contract, but they can correct me if I'm not correct.
So a question on Deloitte's performance would be for them as well?
That's right, yes.
So the department hasn't withheld or adjusted any payment because of any delays or incomplete work?
Again, I don't believe so. But, again, the contract managers in early childhood will be able to answer those questions in more detail.
What's the purpose of the small provider relief payment?
In relation to the same contract? Or is it CCTV trial, or—
That's why I'm asking. What is it?

We have a series of funds that we offer to small providers. One was to assist them if they were involved in the CCTV trial, for example. Another one was in relation to possibly the Deloitte. But, again, I'm sorry, the early childhood team—

I think it's separate. Sounds like I've got to deal with that later today anyway, so I'll get some more info on that. I want to ask about the preschools reform agreement. How much funding does the New South Wales government receive under the agreement?
Senator, I'm sorry. We're really going into the early childhood outcome now rather than the department corporate outcome. I can do it. I'll drag out my early childhood folder.

I'm happy to deal with that later. Going back to Deloitte and the department's relationship with Deloitte, in the time since the last election, Deloitte has been listed as the inclusion development fund manager for the department. Deloitte is managing ECEC grants and grants for paid practicum and workforce development under GO7762, GO7760 and GO8344. Deloitte, as we've discussed, has been selected to deliver the service delivery pricing project. Is there any risk or any concern in relation to having so much of the core government work outsourced to Deloitte, to one organisation?

My understanding is that all of our contracts in relation to these were open, transparent processes. They went to the market. The market was able to tender for these particular projects that we're working on. There was expertise that we needed that was outside the department around this to support the department in the work that we did. In these particular instances, Deloitte was successful in relation to that. Our normal assurance process would happen around the work that we're doing with contractors. As far as I'm concerned, we've followed everything that we need to do in relation to the work that we need to do that we contract out. We're not a big spender on consultancies and contractors generally, but there are particular things—like the inclusion support program, as you raised—where we do have contractors assist us with some of the initial processing and then final decisions are made in the department in relation to those grants. I don't have that concern. We are very focused on contractors. We're very focused on ensuring that we're getting best value for money. We're very focused on making sure that our procurement process is very strict with a lot of probity around it, and we'll continue to do that.
How does that accord with the government's commitment to have less reliance on—
The strategic commission framework?
contractors and uplift within the public service to be able to deliver these projects more.

Our contractor numbers are 3.7 per cent of our total workforce. It's very, very small. In terms of our strategic commissioning framework, there are a number of core functions that we have ensured are kept within the department. Mr Markovic can probably help me in more detail around that. In terms of things like contracts and consultancies, that is something that we are focusing on to reduce our reliance on those. Mr Markovich can very quickly—I know you probably don't have much time, Senator—go through some of those core things and what we're doing particularly around some of the issues around contractors.

As the secretary has pointed out, the focus of the strategic commissioning framework is to ensure that core activities are undertaken by public servants. We, in our planning processes, have identified nine critical areas that we are keen to ensure are done by public servants. Then we have four additional areas that we are working on as a priority to bring back in-house. We provide transparency on our progress through both our annual report and corporate plans. Our focus has been on areas that we've identified that must be core—things like developing legislation, providing services to parliamentarians and national security matters in addition to those that are identified in the strategic commissioning framework. That's been our focus. As the secretary's mentioned, we will use contractors and consultants outside of that as appropriate to supplement our workforce.

In the last couple of weeks, Deloitte was heavily criticised for the inclusion of AI slop in its WA University merger report and an Australian welfare compliance report, which included hallucinations and fake references. Given you've got so much important work associated with and delegated to Deloitte, have you taken steps to assure yourself about Deloitte's use of AI in these very important core education and childcare contracts?
I don't know which contractors we had written to about AI previously or not. I'll just check with my team. I'm trying to work out whether we've actually written to any of our contractors around AI.

We do have clauses included in our contracts. If the department is undertaking something, we do have standard clauses around the use of AI by the provider—or the vendor, in this case—and then we have processes within the department on where the expectation is. All of that output—the reports, for example—would be reviewed by officers in the department.

In terms of ISP, for example, which is a significant work that Deloitte is doing, that doesn't involve AI in terms of reports. It's about processing and providing advice to us. The one that we particularly will be looking at is the service delivery price. I don't have a report from the service delivery price. But it's a fair point about us assuring ourselves around what Deloitte is doing around the SDP if they're using AI; they need to tell us about that, to be explicit about it and then assurances around—

They were hallucinations, right? We've all used it. We've seen how it can spit out some pretty spurious results. We don't need any more hallucinations when it comes to pricing in child care. People can see for themselves how the costs have been going up significantly.

ATEC—I want to ask about their establishment costs. Your report refers to a memorandum of understanding with ATEC around Corporate Enabling Services. How much did Education spend establishing ATEC?
We didn't really spend anything establishing ATEC as such, because they were staff within the department.
It was—sorry?

Staff within the department—I'm the accountable authority. Effectively, there's some additional funding that was made available to ATEC. I think it was $50 million that the government gave over forward estimates for ATEC. But otherwise—
You've just been able to absorb it.

Basically they're—I'm still the accountable authority. The staff are still staff of the department. There are additional costs for the commissioners, and those salary costs are built into the $50 million additional. But short of that—Mr Markovic?

Probably the only thing I'd add is the MOU and the corporate support. The corporate support services are provided from within the existing resources of the department. My group provides those resources. We didn't receive additional funding for that. It's done within the existing staff allocation. Both the set-up of the ATEC—we supported that—and also the ongoing functions, payroll, IT and property are provided within the existing resources of the department and not separately identified.
How many departmental employees were assigned to ATEC's establishment?
There's a budgeted ASL of 96 ASL.
Is that just for the establishment?

That's the approved staffing level for this year. That will vary over time in line with decisions of government to add resourcing and also savings that need to be delivered. It was slightly higher when the ATEC was established, but, for this financial year, it's 96.
Have you got an estimated cost of providing the corporate services to ATEC?

As I said, we don't separate it out. The ATEC is effectively running as a group within the department, and we don't attribute costs to each group. The costs of my area are borne by the department as a whole, as agreed with our executive board. We don't assign the costs.
So ATEC isn't required to fund out of their budget anything back to you? Do you just absorb it?

The arrangement is that there are commissioners for the ATEC and then the staff that support the commissioners are provided to the ATEC by the secretary. They do have their own group budget and group allocation so they can manage. But it is entirely within the resourcing of the Department of Education.
Do we know the cost of delivery of ATEC, then, as a whole?

ATEC have, for the staff—I've mentioned the NPPs that the secretary's described; they have an internal budget that's allocated. I can tell you that this year the internal budget is $21½ million. What that won't include is their contribution to corporate services because by their nature, as I've described, they're funded from within the department. But, certainly, we can ring-fence the cost of the commissioners and the staff supporting the commissioners in fulfilling their function.

But we don't actually know. I mean, it's not insignificant, though, is it? Corporate services come at a cost of time, and other on-costs, but that's not something that you are able to, say, put a dollar figure on?
We'd almost have to be a like a billing service to some degree.
We don't do that.
I mean, some of the work the corporate services does will be for ATEC as well as for everyone.
What about when it comes to new accommodation, ICT—those sorts of expected costs?
Again, part of the MOU outlines that we provide those services. But again, a number of those services staff were and continue to be departmental staff. We don't separate them out.
Which administrative functions previously performed by the department have ceased now that ATEC has been established?

ATEC particularly now plays the role around compact agreements. The department used to develop the compact agreements. ATEC is now doing that. ATEC is also doing some of the work around First Nations projects and grants that the department used to do. There's new work, of course, around needs based funding and managed growth, and allocation of Commonwealth supported places, which is all part of the compact process. Again, if you want more detail around that, both HERI and ATEC can provide that.
The ring-fenced—I think was the term you used—amount was 21.5. Is that—
That's their budget, yes.
Can you confirm that that's $86 million over the forwards?
I can't at the moment.
Can you repeat the question.
Is it $86 million over the forwards?

No. When the ATEC was established, two things happened. You would recall, the secretary described there were some NPPs specifically for ATEC, then there was some resourcing that was moved from the department into the ATEC for functions moving. I think you might be referring to the NPP number.
Yes.

We then put in the additional. I mean, over the forwards, the 21½ for this year is a good indication of what the next three years will look like. I haven't got the exact figure with me. It's more like that number rather than the $60 million that you've described. That will be the NPP. I think you're describing the NPP component.
Yes, I believe I am. I'll move on to APS redundancies. How many public servants accepted voluntary redundancies in 2025-26?
In 2025-26, there were 89.
What's the total cost of those redundancies?
The total cost was about $12 million.

I would say, in our annual report we disclose a total cost of all separations of just over $13.016 million. That is the amount we've disclosed, which includes some of the additional costs of, for example, providing people with financial advice as they separate. So there's a difference between the separation payment—the secretary's number—and what's in our published statements for that reason.
How many recipients were SES officers?
None in voluntary redundancies. SES are eligible for voluntary redundancy.
Sorry?
Voluntary redundancy is only available to APS staff, not to SES staff.
They get an invitation to retire.
They get an incentive to retire.
Yes, we heard that. We learnt that term yesterday. What's the difference? I'm just curious.
In terms of the contractual arrangements, that's what the difference is: SES have that available to them. APS has the VR process.
What was the largest individual redundancy payment?
I don't have that on me. We have to take that on notice. We've got the average but we don't have the largest individual.
What was the average?

To explain, there were two VR programs. One was an announced VR program, where I went out and invited people to apply for VR. But we also throughout the year have a normal VR process where people can approach us at any time. So within the actual announced VR program, the average payment was $132,000.
How many of the abolished positions have subsequently been recreated?
It would have been none, I think, because the whole purpose of the voluntary redundancy is to abolish the position.
I would have thought so.

A number of these positions were also terminating programs. As you know, governments give the funding for programs for three, four, five years, and then they terminate if those programs aren't extended. So a lot of the work that we were doing was around particular terminating programs.
Have any of the former employees returned to work for the department as contractors?
No. Not to my understanding. No.
No.
Yes, no.
How much was spent on labour hire last year?
Last year, Senator, the 2025-26 financial year was $17.5 million.
And what are the net annual savings from the redundancy program after accounting for replacement staffing and contractors?
We may have to take that on notice and calculate that one, Senator. In particular, the last bit about after accounting for contractors. Unless the CFO can use a calculator and—
Doing it on the fly. It'd be better to do it properly.
Yes, take that on notice, that's fine.
There's a bit of detail around that.

On notice, if you could, just to close out my ATEC questions, could you provide a full breakdown of the costs for ATEC, including a breakdown of the NPP spending. I want to make sure I understand that properly. More importantly, the internal budget allocation to the running of ATEC both for the current financial year and also over the forwards.
We can do that.
Good. Do we have some youth corporate?
Just a reminder, you're not the only one seeking the call in corporate at the moment.
We're almost about to finish.
There's a lot more for Schools.
Youth is in the start of the next section.
It wasn't in corporate?
Well we're going to ask some questions in relation to the Office of Youth. We do that in the next outcome.
In schools.
Yes.
It's in schools and youth, so the next outcome would be great, Senator.
One other area, I just want to ask where it is. What section is gender based violence in?
That's in outcome 2, in higher education, so it'll be later tonight.
We're good to move on.

Great. Thank you to everyone from corporate. We'll now call officers in relation to outcome 1 and schools. Before we kick off, we do have media in the room. With the committee's endorsement, we'll allow the taking of photographs subject to all the usual preambles that you would have heard a million times this week applying. Please let me know if anyone has an issue with it. Otherwise, we will dive straight into outcome 1, Schools and youth. Senator Scarr, you have the call.

Before I ask questions of the department—in particular, in relation to the Office for Youth—given we have the minister with us, I thought I might ask you this, Minister: are there any particular policy areas where, wearing your hat as Minister for Youth, you provided input into government policy decisions over the last six months?

The role of the Minister for Youth is to promote the engagement of youth themselves in the matters that affect them. The goal is to assist their voices to be heard on the issues that are important to them. We do that with the Office for Youth in a number of ways, including by having a number of bodies that young people participate in. Your question, I think, was if I then go and give advice to other ministers.

Or provided input. Presumably, that advice comes in. Are there any areas where, say, over the last six months, since last estimates, you've sought to elevate those concerns coming through the processes in relation to any particular policy areas or decisions of government?
I'm just trying to understand your question. Do you mean me, personally, as a minister?
In your capacity as minister. The government puts forward a policy. It could have a particular impact with respect to young people.
Yes.

Have there been any occasions over the last six months where you've given input with respect to the perspective of young people? You talked about young people providing their input through the processes or giving voice to their concerns through the mechanisms operated by the Office for Youth. Has that led to any particular policy input?

In terms of the mechanisms that are operated by the Office for Youth, we have five youth advisory groups that we're focused on, and they are engaged in policy. We have youth advisory groups on climate change and water, mental health, First Nations, sports participation and countering foreign interference. In addition to those specific youth advisory groups, the Office for Youth, as part of our Engage youth policy, assists departments to engage with young people on the issues that matter to them.
What's your role as minister, then, in terms of providing input—wearing that hat, as Minister for Youth? Do you have any role or is the Office for Youth coordinating that for you?
The Office for Youth is effectively my department in this portfolio. Our role together is to support young people to engage in the decisions that impact them.

That's helpful. Have there been any particular areas over the last six months which you can point to to say, in relation to government decision X, you made sure the government had the benefit of the views that you've received through the mechanisms you referred to?
We could go through the work of the youth advisory groups and give some of that information.
I'm looking for some concrete examples as to how the work you do has fed into government decision-making processes. Does that make sense?

I'm happy to take that question. As the minister highlighted, the Office for Youth's focus is around facilitating opportunities for young people to share their views and perspectives with government, and there are different mechanisms that we have in place to support that. As the minister mentioned, we have—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: Just to be precise, I understand the front end in terms of getting those views. I'm interested in the back end and how those views, when they're provided through the processes, have positively contributed to the development of policy over, say, the last six months.

Absolutely. Through our Youth Advisory Groups program, we have five youth advisory groups in place currently that partner with particular agencies across the Commonwealth, and that provides a direct avenue for young people to share their perspectives with various agencies and departments. For example, our Mental Health Youth Advisory Group works directly with the National Mental Health Commission and the Department of Health and Ageing to support the co-design of mental health resources and supports for young people. It also works broadly with the National Mental Health Commission on how they can support young people to engage and access mental health supports.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

I'm interested to know some concrete examples with respect to how the input you're receiving through those very worthwhile mechanisms have actually led to development of policy, to change or to reform, rather than a general description of the structure.

We can provide further detail of the work of all youth advisory groups on notice. But another example is our Youth Steering Committee, which we support through the Office for Youth. They supported and provided advice into the Anti-Bullying Rapid Review, which is obviously a priority for the Department of Education.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: That's what I'm looking for—that sort of concrete example.
There are certainly quite a few examples we can point to.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: Okay. I'm happy for you to provide that on notice, to give me a better understanding in that regard. In the feedback you've received from young people over the last six months, has anything stood out?

Yes, certainly. We recently published our 2025-26 annual report, which outlines the progress of our national youth strategy, Engage. Through that report, we were able to highlight some of the findings from our first national youth survey, which is another mechanism through the Office for Youth for young people to share their views and perspectives with government on priorities. Some of the pleasing findings in that report included that 70 per cent of program participants—the young people engaged in our programs—did feel that they'd influenced a government policy, and over 90 per cent reported a positive experience through their work with the Office for Youth.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

It was our first national youth survey.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: So top five?

The No. 1 issue that young people reported went to cost of living, No. 2 was around mental health and wellbeing, No. 3 was climate change, No. 4 was housing affordability, and No. 5 was education and training. As of last Monday we currently have our second national youth survey up and running and live. We are looking to, again, hear from young people about their priorities this year. We'll certainly be able to then reflect on the two reports and any trends.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: We're dealing with education and training here. What are the particular issues in that regard?

These can go to issues around access to education and training, support for developing job-ready skills, support for choosing appropriate courses and career paths and also transitions between education and employment.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: You might take this on notice. Can you provide details with respect to any topics—I'm not looking for the advice itself—where the Office of Youth has provided advice to government over the last six months, particularly in relation to young people's views of taxation policies. Obviously, there were some fundamental changes to taxation policy recently. Was there any advice on youth unemployment? I'm going to ask some questions on youth unemployment in particular, especially in the Queensland context, just to let you know. Was there advice on youth mental health services? Could you take that on notice and provide us any topics. How many FTE does the Office of Youth have?
We have 14 ASL.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, National Reform and Office for Youth

text: Can you also take on notice how many meetings and events with young people or youth organisations or on youth issues you've had in conjunction with the minister, and where those have occurred, including any that have occurred in Queensland. I'm particularly interested in a Queensland context as a Queensland senator. Minister, do you have any views with respect to the youth unemployment rate?
I know that the unemployment figures were released recently, and youth unemployment continues to be several points higher than unemployment in general.
What's the difference? What's the difference between that and the general unemployment rate?
The youth unemployment rate is at 11.1 per cent. I think the general unemployment rate is around 4.7 per cent.

As long as I can remember youth unemployment being reported, there's always been that that difference. It's always higher than the general unemployment rate. There are probably a number of factors in that regard. Is there any target with respect to where it should be? Any goal? What does success look like?

In yesterday's estimates we canvassed some of the issues that you're raising, which are about the difference between what the Office for Youth does and what the departments do and who has responsibility for particular areas of policy and delivery. Questions in relation to the youth unemployment rate, job creation and program delivery would have been relevant to yesterday's proceedings, particularly to employment services. What we do through the national youth survey, which has just been described and which is up now, is an attempt to understand young people's priorities, values and perspectives. They are published for everyone to see. Then we engage in what the priorities are for young people. We establish youth advisory groups, which have just been described to you, and those youth advisory groups then work on particular policy projects where they can have an impact, and they work directly with the departments that are relevant to those concerns. So it's a youth engagement strategy. The outcome that we want is for young people's voices to be heard and for them to engage on those issues with government.

The youth unemployment rate back in July 2022 was 7.1 per cent. It's now 11.1 per cent, so it's actually increased by four per cent. From a Queensland perspective, we've got one of the regions with the worst youth unemployment, the Queensland outback region, which is running at 18.2 per cent. Are you concerned about the increase in the youth unemployment rate over the last four years?

We may have data and information from the last youth survey about what the perspectives are of young people on that issue, and we may have data that is able to be disaggregated on a regional basis. But the point of the—
This question is: are you concerned by that increase in youth unemployment?

Well, I think the point that I'm making to you is that this is a youth engagement portfolio and that there are a number of policy matters that young people are encouraged to engage in. The questions that are appropriate, in my view, to be asked in this portfolio would be about how the minister and the department are working with young people through the structures and processes that we've put in place. Questions around the youth unemployment rate and policies and approaches to that belong yesterday.

Well, I actually asked if you were concerned. I think it's a pretty—are you telling me it's inappropriate for me to ask the Minister for Youth whether or not she's concerned about an increase of four per cent in the unemployment of youth?

Sure. I can talk to you, if you would like me to, from a general government perspective on matters like the government creating 1.3 million jobs over our term of government; the government presiding over the lowest average unemployment in 50 years; and the government making—
Not in terms of the youth unemployment rate.

investments in the jobs of young people, including increasing the minimum wage and supporting increases to the minimum wage, which young people rely on, by an additional $12,000 per year. I can talk to you about the government protecting penalty rates, which young people rely on. We can talk about the government supporting abolishing youth rates. I can talk to you about all aspects of government delivery. We could talk about specific youth unemployment programs.
But you can't talk to me about being concerned about the increase in youth unemployment of four per cent between July 2022 and September 2026. Is that correct?
I can tell you that I am interested in the views of young people about the issues that concern them—
Right. Okay.
and I know that young people care about having a job, and I know that they care about having a good, secure job that they can count on.

I would have thought it was an obvious answer. And I'm not being partisan. I've got a youth unemployment rate in a region of Queensland that is at 18.2 per cent. I would have thought it would be pretty obvious, if I asked the Minister for Youth if they're concerned about an unemployment rate in a region of my home state of Queensland of 18.2 per cent, that the answer would be, 'Yes, and this is what we're doing about it.' I'm not trying to be tricky. I've got an 18.2 per cent youth unemployment rate in a region of Queensland, which is just shocking—absolutely shocking. Thank you, Chair.
Senator Allman-Payne is joining us by videoconference. I'll give you a nudge at about 10 minutes, Penny, but you have the call now.

Good morning, everyone. My first lot of questions are about Redeemer Baptist School. Over the 10 years from 2015 to 2024, it has received $40.4 million in federal government funding, and the school owns 37 properties valued at over $67 million. As you're no doubt aware from media reports, there have been a number of complaints about the school over a long period of time. They started back in 2004 around systemic tax avoidance. They went through the 2000s. In 2008, a senior public servant compiled 147 allegations against Redeemer spanning three decades. My question is: how is it that, despite serious revelations about this school throughout the 2000s, it's continued to receive federal funding up until the present day?

Thank you, first of all, for giving us some advance notice on these questions so we could come prepared, and also Senator O'Sullivan gave us some notification for early childhood. That just makes it so much easier for us to help the committee. I'll get Ms Brighton to provide some detail on your question.

As we've discussed in this committee previously, in order to receive Commonwealth funding, all schools have to meet certain eligibility requirements, and that goes to being a fit and proper entity, financially viable and operating not for profit. As we've said at this committee previously, while we try not to get into specific commentary on individual matters for reasons of procedural fairness, I will do what I can to help the committee today.

With Redeemer Baptist, the department commenced its investigations this year. There are multiple regulators involved with Redeemer Baptist at the moment, and, as you'll be aware, there's also a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry. The case turns really on the employment relationship between Redeemer and its workers, and, as I said, there are a range of regulators involved in that. One of the things that we're doing at the moment is not only undertaking a pretty detailed analysis of the financial information that's available to us but also working closely with the other regulators. Findings that come out of either the other regulators or our own analysis may give rise to issues around that criteria of what makes a school eligible for funding, which is that fit and proper status. Are they a fit and proper entity, and are they operating for profit? Our investigation is continuing, and there is a level of dependency with the work of the other regulators who are also looking at this matter.
It seems to me that if I understand you correctly, Ms Brighton, the investigation is largely around the employment relationship. Is that right?

There are multiple components of the investigation. One lot of regulators are looking at the employment relationship. Other regulators will look at issues—such as us—about assets and monitoring of how funding has been spent. There are also, we understand, court proceedings around employment matters. All of those different dimensions feed into the criteria that makes a school eligible or not for Commonwealth funding.

Given that a publicly funded independent school is alleged to operate substantially on unpaid labour from an associated religious organisation while accumulating large surpluses, is the minister satisfied that the act's not-for-profit requirements are capable of detecting arrangements of this kind?

I think Ms Brighton was going to talk about those specific provisions, if that is helpful, but, from the minister's perspective, Minister Clare referred the allegations to the department. The department is examining the matters. Ms Brighton has talked about how that work is underway and how there are other inquiries underway, and the Commonwealth will consider those findings before taking any further action.

It seems that the focus is very much on financial arrangements. Some of the allegations against Redeemer Baptist include forcing students to stay in the homes of staff, dislocating them from their families; students being made to sleep in beds with teachers on camps; a homestay arrangement where the principal walked in front of a student naked; not allowing girls to play sport, not even handball; and compelling students to undertake a year 13 of unpaid labour after graduation. The allegations against this school go far beyond the financial arrangements and its not-for-profit status. Going back through the records of actions taken against private schools, no approved authority has ever had its funding suspended for its treatment of students. As far as we can tell, they've only ever lost their funding for financial indiscretion, and that's only happened three times. Given that's the case, Minister, is it your opinion that the fit-and-proper-person test, as it's currently legislated, is adequate?
Ms Brighton is going to give us some more information about that.

Perhaps it would have been helpful when I was talking about fit and proper just to explore that a little bit further. When we talk about the fit and proper requirements, it does extend not only to the financial management of a school but also to the school's governance arrangements and what we expect around approved authorities or schools about how their key personnel conduct themselves. Does the leadership foster a safe, respectful, supportive environment? So fit and proper actually has quite a broad definition. As the department, when we see allegations about the conduct of senior leadership or boards of schools, we actually also follow up with those schools under that banner of fit and proper person. So the points that you've raised are very much on our horizon and fit within the scope of the investigations we undertake when we look at these schools.

I'm going to come back to the minister, though. We've got a school here that has allegations as far back as 2004 around things that go beyond the financial arrangements of the school. Given that we clearly have a situation where that has been allowed to go on for several decades, is the fit-and-proper-person test fit for purpose if this is not the first school or authority to have allegations of this kind levelled before it, yet none has ever lost its registration? Is the test as it currently exists adequate, in the minister's view?

The deputy secretary of the department has gone through the arrangements and also the investigations and the inquiries that are underway. As that work is ongoing, there's really not much more I can say about it. It wouldn't be appropriate to comment further. These allegations are concerning, and the Commonwealth will consider the results of the investigation before taking any further action.

Thanks, Minister. We look forward to being kept up to date with how this investigation progresses. I think it's really important for the safety of staff and students, and we shouldn't have any kids being subject to behaviour like that in any school.

My next question is in relation to the Christian Brothers scheme, where the Christian Brothers transferred 26 separate properties for virtually a dollar or nothing to Edmund Rice Education Australia. My understanding is that the transferred property received by Edmund Rice Education Australia was worth $891 million. It's now valued up to $2 billion. We had a situation where they were seeking to deny any obligation for compensation, and, only after public pressure, they agreed to take on the responsibility for redress to the survivors of Christian Brothers abuse. Given that context, Minister, will the minister commission or support a review of related-party transactions and asset transfers between religious orders and school approved authorities given the royal commission's findings and the precedent now being set in the Christian Brothers scheme?
I'm advised that the department has written to the Edmund Rice Education Australia foundation or entity. I think Ms Brighton can give you more information about that.

My question is broader than that, though. This is one example of where that's happened. The question is: will you support a review into related party transaction and asset transfers between religious orders and school-approved authorities so that we can check whether this is going on in other instances?

I understand that the first step is that the department is seeking information about the asset holdings and disposals over time and that that is the step that the department has taken and that they're continuing to assess and monitor the situation and engage with agencies about those matters about asset holdings and disposals. Ms Brighton may be able to assist further.

The minister's completely correct. Our investigation is in flight at the moment. We are looking at asset movements across entities. It is a complex matter, and it is going to take us a little bit of time. We're also working with other parties to get underneath the covers. Like with most of our investigations and compliance action, if we find insights that warrant a broader look at a sector overall, then we will provide advice back to government. But an instance of one example that we're investigating does not necessarily point to a whole range of issues across an entire sector. But we do keep a pretty close eye on these things, and, if we need to provide further advice to government about a broader approach, we will do so. That advice will be determined based on the findings of investigations.
We look forward to an update on this one, too, and whether further stuff comes out of that. Chair, do I have time for one more question in this block?
You can place one more and then I'll rotate.

Okay. I'm interested in understanding what actions the department has taken to date with regard to the recommendations of the report into the national trend of school refusal. Are there any recommendations that the department is not progressing, and, if so, why not?

The references committee report, as you well know, has 14 recommendations. The Australian government agreed in principle to recommendation 1, which is about the research into school refusal, and also supported in principle recommendation 7, which is about improving awareness and understanding of school refusal. I'll ask my colleagues Ms Donegan and Ms Banerjee to elaborate a bit further about where we're up to.

The Australian government is working with states and territories and non-government sectors and other key stakeholders to address nonattendance and student absence, including school refusal, as part of the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement - Full and Fair Funding 2025-2034. This includes a national enabling initiative on collective work to better understand the advice to education ministers on student attendance; its impact on learning; and mechanisms to advance evidence based approaches in addressing nonattendance, including school refusal. At the moment, the Commonwealth with states and territories are working together to establish a work plan for that activity. That work plan has been consulted on quite broadly through the interjurisdictional elements of our work that go to supporting education ministers, including work with the non-government sectors as well. We are actively working to progress that work plan. In addition to that, the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership introduced a core learning requirement for initial teacher education programs in the December 2023 addendum to accreditation standards and procedures. All accredited ITE providers have been teaching that core content since semester 1 in 2026. That core content now includes classroom behaviour, responding to teacher components that focus on student behaviour and engagement in learning. It has strengthened the teacher capability to support students experiencing attendance challenges, including school refusal.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Improving Student Outcomes

text: But, Ms Donegan, certainly, what the inquiry showed was that there's a marked difference between nonattendance, where kids just aren't interested in attending, and school refusal. I note that, since we had that inquiry, off its own bat, without government funding, School Can't Australia is now a significant presence. They've got 16,000 or more parents and families who are getting help from them. They're running education sessions. There's a webinar tonight for parents who are experiencing school refusal. It's a really complex area of the attendance picture. Can you point to anything that's specifically addressing 'school can't', as people who experience this prefer it to be called, as opposed to just general nonattendance, because I certainly haven't seen anything? And even for behaviour issues, School Can't is not for behaviour; it's for kids who are distressed by school. They want to be there and can't get there. Can you point to specific things that address that particular issue?

In the agreements that we have with states and territories under the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement, you might recall we've got a reform domain called 'wellbeing for learning and engagement'. Each state and territory has quite specific actions that they are taking under each one of those reform domains to support young people engage with learning. That looks at engaging with learning in the broadest possible sense. If I look at, say, Tasmania, under their agreement they have quite specific actions that they are taking. They are taking an evidence-based approach to strengthening re-engagement support for students to engage with their learning. In the Northern Territory, they are doing a whole range of activity specifically focused on—and I'm going to use the language of 'disengaged students'. Sometimes that's disengaged students, sometimes that's school refusal. It's picking up the totality of the wraparound supports that those young people need to re-engage with learning, and that goes to psychosocial wellbeing and mental health supports, as well as to cultural and community supports.

My concern is that we're seeing the numbers of kids who are home schooling, in particular, rising. Certainly, the feedback that's coming from the community of parents, in particular—many of whom, as you would know, have had to give up work because they need to assist their kids—is that there seems to be still a lack of real understanding that this is a very specific issue. So my question is: is the department tracking kids who are experiencing 'school can't' or school refusal separately to kids who are just disengaged and have general attendance issues, or is it just continuing to bundle them all into one category? One of the recommendations of the inquiry was to be more specific in our absence codes, for example, to actually understand a kid who just doesn't want to be there, as opposed to a kid who really does want to be there and can't because of that level of distress.

This does sit squarely in the domain of each one of the states and territories in terms of the really tangible actions that they take on the ground for students. We are working with all those states and territories on the national Measurement Framework for Schooling in Australian. One of the components of that that we've committed to do together under the schools agreement is around attendance and better information and granularity around attendance, and it goes to the very matters that you've highlighted. That is a piece of work that we are working on with states and territories. It will take a while to work through, because, in order to collect better data, in the first instance, we have to have an agreement with states and territories about the data that will be collected, and then there will be the mechanism as to how that data is collected and then reported. We're in early stages of those discussions, and we hope that, over the coming 12 months, we'll have more to share with the committee about how those discussions are going.

My final comment is that I think there is a real role for the federal education department to play in educating states about school can't and school refusal. I really feel like there is still a lack of understanding in a lot of our school communities. Any leadership that the federal government can take in that space would be really welcome, and I look forward to hearing the results of the work that you're doing around absence. I think getting into the detail of that is really important. Thanks, Chair. I'm conscious of time. I'll leave it there for this block.

Thank you. That was technically two blocks. It's quite hard for me to interrupt via video. I'd just remind all to keep an eye on their own time. I'd appreciate it. I'll come back to the opposition now. Senator O'Sullivan.
Thank you, Chair. I'm sure you'll keep me to my time, because I'm right here in the room with you.
You can feel my eyes upon you!

I want to go back to those questions I was asking about the Preschool Reform Agreement. I want to ask about New South Wales. How much does New South Wales receive under the Preschool Reform Agreement?
Sorry, that's early childhood, not schools. You've got early childhood and after schools; I thought you were going to come to me about—
Oh—
It's outcome 1, but—
I thought it was part of Early Learning and Schools Support. No?
No.
Okay; we'll come back with those questions later then. I'll flick over; give me a second.

The year 12 completion people are here if you wanted to ask those questions you asked in corporate, about the fact that year 12—sorry, I don't mean to tell you how to ask questions. But I'm letting you know that those people are here.
But any suggestions—!
I've got a list, Senator, if that's okay!
I want to go to PISA. Let's start with that. Secretary, or anyone else on the panel, were you at all surprised by the most recent PISA results in maths and reading?

Senator, as you know, we've seen a trend in relation to the performance of Australian students. We've also seen that trend internationally. The actual thing that did surprise me to some degree was the impact on PISA data internationally; internationally, the data had actually decreased in terms of student performance. I'm pleased that Australia—even though I'm disappointed, obviously, that we declined—held our ground in a number of the areas and, in fact, our decline wasn't as significant as what was happening around the rest of the world. In science particularly, our performance continued to be strong. Literacy is one of the areas that we need to focus on, and the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement is focused on that. But if you want any more detail, I can ask Ms Brighton to provide more detail.

As you know, I chaired an inquiry into classroom disruption and behaviour in the previous parliament, and it's still a very serious issue. I'm disappointed to see that it continues to persist as an issue for Australian schools. In Australian schools, it continues to be incredibly problematic. Does that surprise you, and what's the government doing? What's this federal government doing to address it?

Obviously—being a classroom teacher myself—student behaviour is something that does impact on learning not just of the student themself but of the students around them. There are a number of things that we want to focus on. We've developed some training materials for teachers around classroom behaviour. We've enhanced and strengthened some of the initial teacher education requirements around classroom behaviour as well. But Miss Brighton can give you the detail about specifically what we're doing in that space.

To follow on from Secretary Cook's comments, we're looking at this in a variety of different ways. We're looking through the lens of needing to have a workforce that is well equipped from not only what they do at uni but then ongoing professional development about how they build strong cultures in classrooms and how they tackle how students behave in classrooms. Then there's an element of—we did see a slight improvement in the digital distraction in the PISA results. It is still pretty poor, and we recognise that. But you would also have seen that Minister Clare is talking to his colleagues about the impact of screens in schools and in classrooms, not only the impact that that's had on learning outcomes but also the impact that has had on distractions. A couple of years ago, all the education ministers made a decision to restrict mobile phones in schools or ban mobile phones in schools. Those different strategies are coming together as well as equipping teachers. The expectations in states and territories that schools are having a whole-school approach to behaviour and expectations and management—all of those elements combined—should reduce distraction and enable students to focus on their learning when they're in classrooms.

This committee recommended in its report a couple of years ago to have behaviour included in the curriculum. Has there been any progress on that front—explicitly providing guidance for teachers, particularly in those early years in school?

The Australian curriculum is a curriculum that's focused on content and achievement standards, but, sitting under the curriculum, there are a whole range of supports for teachers that a combination of the Australian government as well as states and territories put in place to help establish strong behaviours in schools and in classrooms. Under the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement we've got a whole pillar of reform that is expressly designed to improve and strengthen school culture. It's not the curriculum per se that goes to that but it's the support mechanisms that sit under the curriculum. When the UK talk about their behaviour curriculum, in Australian language it's talking really about the supports, the scaffolds, to establish that culture in a school.

We have developed training programs on behaviour that the Commonwealth has actually funded. They've been in place for a little while now. We've also had AERO develop some resources around classroom behaviour and classroom management as well. As I indicated, we have also enhanced the initial teacher education requirements to ensure that we've called out behaviour in what we would want our teachers to be trained in before they graduate and go into classrooms.
Yes, in the initial teacher education. Good.
I think your committee recommended that particularly, and the government fast-tracked that as part of the work that universities were required to do.
At a time when we're paying more than ever before in school funding, why are we continuing to see PISA results decline?
Past agreements—
Money doesn't seem to be the issue; that's my point.
I have to confess that I was part of every agreement that's been established since 2012, so you could say it's my fault, maybe. Let's not go there, shall we! But past agreements—
[Inaudible] 2012?

Actually, 2010, but let's not go there! Past agreements have provided funding, but the requirements that were placed on states and territories in relation to explicit reforms to address literacy and numeracy performance were perhaps not as explicit as the new Better and Fairer Schools Agreement. You would have heard Minister Clare talk about this. It's very explicit about requiring states and territories to implement things like phonics tests, numeracy tests, small group work. They are now required in the agreements, and they're required as a result of the funding the Commonwealth provided. The government will actually report annually to parliament, for the first time ever, around progress in relation to that. You'll be aware that Minister Clare did a report to parliament earlier this year. The report next year will be even more explicit about what we're seeing, about data to hold states and territories to account—including the non-government sector, dare I say—in relation to the funding that they've received. To some degree, we've learnt that we need to be much more explicit around what we're requiring. We have seen, and a number of states have seen, as a result of that—for example, in their phonics assessment—they are improving in relation to what literacy and numeracy, but particularly literacy, is happening in their schools. In the early years—every state, I think, other than WA is trialling a numeracy check this year. They're the sorts of things that we have to be much more explicit on, and I think we are now doing that.
Is the issue then around the pedagogy, the assessment and possibly the curriculum, rather than the amount of funding?

I'm not so much sure. I think it's absolutely about pedagogy. Again, we've had this conversation about—you know, 'the reading wars are over'. There was a contested debate, rightly or wrongly, about whole language versus phonics. The evidence is: absolutely. AERO is here later today. The establishment of AERO by ministers as part of previous agreements was to have the evidence base about what actually works. We are now implementing that, which is what BFSA is saying. It talks about evidence based approaches—and, again, you've heard Minister Clare talk about this endlessly—where we won't accept pedagogy that's not based on evidence. We are finetuning aspects of the curriculum—for F to 2, for example, in terms of maths—where we're looking at being explicit around that, and ministers are always looking at those things. Again, it's about what teachers are actually doing in the classroom. It's their teaching and learning practice and being much more explicit around those things which are so important.
Are all the states on board with this?
Yes. They've all signed up to the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement.
The other interesting thing I noticed was the drop-off in performance in relation to the higher socioeconomic quartile. Have you got any indication as to why that would be?
Luckily, Ms Brighton is on the international PISA board, so I'll refer to my expert at the table.

Certainly that was an area that drew our attention as well. We don't have at this stage a clear explanation around the why. Funding is important, but the reforms are important. What we've seen from the—
It sounds from the evidence that they're the most important thing.
The reforms certainly are.
The reforms are absolutely critical, but you need to have the funding in order to deliver the reforms.
Of course.

What we have seen and learnt from some of the work the UK has done is the importance of having the implementation with fidelity and sustained effort. The UK—particularly England, I should say, rather than the UK generally—phonics work has been sustained. The UK work in maths has been incredibly sustained, and they have not only looked at how maths is taught but wrapped around teachers with their professional learning. That has brought about sustained improvement in maths, and not only in the lower socioeconomic and lower-performing students but also in the top-tier students.
That's in the UK.

That's in England, yes. That gives us some pointers of areas of focus, and I think that we're certainly heading in that same direction of travel. As Secretary Cook said, we're doing that finessing and finetuning of the maths curriculum at the moment, and that will go to education ministers on Monday for their consideration. With all of these elements together, we do need to sustain them over a number of years to make sure that we deeply embed them so we can get the sorts of results that our students deserve.

That leads me to my next question. When the minister stood up in parliament to answer questions about the PISA results, he referenced the United Kingdom and Singapore as well. He also spoke about a digital detox plan for Australian schools and an F to 6 curriculum overhaul in mathematics. When did the department first start working on the digital detox program and the curriculum overhaul?
It was a while ago.

When we got the last PISA results—the 2022 results—particularly with what it was saying about the impact of digital disruption in classrooms, we overlaid that with what we were hearing from principals and teachers about the impact on devices. The first step ministers took around that was the mobile phone ban in schools. Then, as that evidence has continued to build over time, and we have been looking at the impact of screens and Minister Claire has been hearing from teachers and principals on the ground about the impact of screens, we've started to coalesce around this notion of digital detox. It started with mobile phone bans, but we started the policy work this year. I probably couldn't be specific about what date we started it, but in the last few months we've been doing a deeper piece of work around digital detox.

But the curriculum work—the maths work, for example—was last year. We started the work that we're doing around curriculum, on F-2 maths, last year, and all ministers agreed to start that work last year. As Ms Brighton said, on Monday next week education ministers will meet. They'll consider that work that's now completed.

I've been asked to rotate the call, so I'll finish with this. Back in 2013, the then education minister, Christopher Pyne, really pushed for phonics. It was almost immediately after being elected. He was criticised at the time, quite roundly, by the Australian Education Union and the Australian Association for Research in Education—and, indeed, by colleagues here and across other jurisdictions, such as Senator Deb O'Neill, the then premier, Jay Weatherill, in South Australia and others with vested interests. It's not something that's been championed by the Labor Party—by this government—but now it seems that the focus on phonics is being accepted as the right way to go. Was Christopher Pyne right all the way back then?
It's a bit of a political question. He was also my minister; I was the deputy secretary of schools at the time.
Was he the best minister you ever [inaudible].
I couldn't possibly say! I've had some excellent ministers at both state and federal level.
Fair enough. It's not meant to be a political question—
Mine was!

I get that it sounds that way. But am I right to take from the evidence that we're hearing here today that this is something that is now being championed, that it is accepted that this is the right path and that this is what we need for students in order for them to excel and achieve in their education pathway?

Absolutely. Again, Minister Clare's comments are:

The reading wars are over.

The reading wars were this motion about whole language versus phonics. This is why, as a requirement to get Commonwealth funding in school funding, you'll see the word 'phonics' in the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement. I believe—but I will stand corrected if wrong—it's the first time it's been in an agreement with that level of specificity. The evidence is, overwhelmingly, that that approach is an approach that is best learning for students.
Senator Allman-Payne, your second block.
Third!
Third.

I have a question about the independent performance evaluation from AERO. We've had a number of people try and get access to it by FOI, and we've tried in the Senate through an OPD. Are you able to elaborate on why it's expected that the release of the report would cause damage in relations between Commonwealth and states?

Thanks for the question. The Australian government, on behalf of all education ministers, commissioned that review. In that capacity it was all education ministers, as the company members of AERO.
