That report went to education ministers and, consistently with the conventions of education ministers, ministers make a decision whether they will release the report or not. The education ministers agreed not to release the final report. I believe Minister Clare also, as part of the response to the order for the production of documents, referred to that. It's a matter of convention that release of any reports and documents has to have the agreement of all education ministers. So that's the reason it hasn't been released.

In terms of the FOI considerations, the FOI decision-makers have regard to the various criteria that get applied to FOI decisions. One of those criteria is about Commonwealth-state relations, and that points particularly to the conventions of education ministers' meetings.

AERO's website says:

We welcome scrutiny to enhance the integrity of our processes.

Is refusing to release the report consistent with that?

Again, it's probably not for AERO. The decision doesn't sit with them. In these circumstances, the decision sits with all education ministers. The decision has been made by that committee for the report to not be released, so it's not so much AERO's responsibility. I get the point you've made, and AERO would absolutely say that they're about transparency. This is an education ministers' meeting decision rather than an AERO decision.

An open letter calling for the report to be released has been signed by 576 education academics, teachers and school leaders. Do you recognise that there is substantial interest from educators in the release of this report and that not releasing it actually reduces trust around why it hasn't been released, because the assumption is being made that those findings must be poor, particularly when one of the reasons for refusing the FOI was that it may damage people's confidence in the organisation?

Senator, I'm certainly aware that there's a lot of interest around it, absolutely; I take your point around that. Again—I'm not trying to be difficult—we can only operate within the education ministers' protocols. Ministers have decided not to release the report. I don't even know who or what ministers in terms of individual ministers, but that's the decision that's been made by the education ministers meeting as a group.

It just seems very inconsistent when teachers around the country are under incredible scrutiny and continually being told that they have to be held to account and when education ministers are refusing to release the findings of what is supposed to be the peak educational research body in this country. I find that astounding. I guess we will continue to lobby all of the state ministers to say that this is not okay. Teachers and educators deserve to know what that review said. I don't understand how people can be expected to have confidence in them if the ministers don't want to tell us what that found. But I'll move on.

It's my understanding that, in response to an increase in sexual harassment and assault amongst high-school students, the minister announced an independent evaluation of the CRRE framework would commence later this year. I note that that framework was only finalised earlier this year. Has an independent evaluator been appointed, and, if not, how will they be selected?

As per the announcement, you're right: there's a review underway for the CRRE measure, which aligns also with the expectation of the CRRE federation funding agreement schedule that there will be an independent evaluation of the measure during the life of the FFA schedule. The department is working on commissioning that work. We published a request for quotes on 6 October. That was open until 16 October. We did not receive a response to the request, so we republished the request for quotes on 21 October, closing on 10 November. Following on from that, we will identify a suitable provider to undertake that evaluation.
Do you have an expected timeframe for the completion of the review at this stage?
We are working towards findings to be determined and the review to be completed by March/April next year. But it's subject to finding a suitable provider to undertake the work.
Have you given any thought to who should be consulted for this review?

As part of the requirement, we would definitely consult with the variety of stakeholders that we consulted with on our Consent and Respectful Relationships Education work. We have experts on an implementation working group that we facilitate. We will definitely consult with those experts. We will obviously consult with the departments of education in states and territories, who are our key partners in the delivery of this measure. We will also consult with non-government school sectors who are delivering this measure in states and territories. Any evaluation, as you know, will start with a bit of scoping. As part of that scoping exercise, if there are other stakeholders that are identified, the evaluator will be required to consult with them.

The Monash University rapid review of CRRE called for a sexual ethics approach that addresses sex and consent explicitly. Those recommendations weren't adopted in the CRRE framework. Will they now be reconsidered?

If I can go back to the Monash review, that was undertaken in 2023. It was a point-in-time rapid review. When that review informed the RRA framework, that was one of the evidence bases that informed our framework. We also undertook extensive consultation with a range of other stakeholders. What came out in our RRA framework was a mix of all the views that we heard from a range of stakeholders, and the evaluation that we are undertaking will definitely look into what has been, what we are doing now and what should be. So the evidence will definitely inform the future work.

Perhaps I could just add to that. As Ms Banerjee said, those concepts that underpin sexual ethics and that are inherent to sexual ethics are throughout the framework. They go to consent and sexual consent, bodily autonomy, healthy and respectful relationships, sexual health and wellbeing, safety and violence prevention. A whole range of the dimensions that sexual ethics capture are actually embedded in the framework. The framework also has a whole series of resources and supports attached to it, including the UNESCO work on sexual ethics.

Yes. I'm conscious of time. I have a couple more questions. We've heard some members of parliament say that a feminised curriculum is contributing to young men's misogynistic attitudes. I'm sure you're aware that that's contrary to evidence. How will the government make sure that the evaluation of CRRE responds to expert evidence rather than conservative outrage?

The CRRE curriculum that's taught in schools is taught to all students, irrespective of gender or other specific categories. The curriculum is geared towards building lifelong skills and taught in an age-appropriate way. It's evidence based. The curriculum is expert driven. From foundation through to year 10 and senior years, kids learn how to have respectful relationships, and then that goes on to consent and other matters. So I don't think—
That's fine.
We would always take expert evidence, as opposed to unexpert—is that a word? I take your point. We would absolutely be looking at expert evidence, yes.

Great. This is my last question because I know that I have to wrap up. We're seeing a lot of female teachers in particular leaving the teaching profession because of the sexism and misogyny that's going on in schools. I'm wondering what actions the department is taking to address sexism and misogyny in schools, in both our public and our private sector.

Through the work of the consent and respectful relationships in education federal funding agreement, I can point to the 2025 activities, where largely the activities were focused on workforce development about how to manage these situations in schools, including through extensive professional learning—workshops, webinars, coaching—that focused on teachers and school leaders. There was also a significant effort invested in developing the curriculum and aligning teaching resources to make sure that teachers felt comfortable in schools to deliver that content.

We have an example that has occurred recently, so we understand that these issues are constantly being raised and are being raised in a concerning way. The Secretary of the NSW Department of Education has written to all school principals, as well as to all school staff, about these behaviours—about increasing misogynistic behaviours—to make sure that principals understand their obligations within that schooling context but also understand the resources that they have available to them to help them through these situations. That's just one example of a jurisdiction who is also focused on, outside of the CRRE teaching context, working with staff and making sure that staff are able to support the school environment, as well as students.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Improving Student Outcomes

text: On Monday, when education ministers meet, they will be discussing these issues—consent and respectful relationships—as part of their agenda with their ministerial council meeting.

I heard that announcement from the New South Wales minister and I thought, 'Oh, this sounds like they're just telling schools to fix it.' Obviously, resourcing is going to be important. If there's any extra information that you could provide on notice that's relevant to giving examples of the sorts of support resources that are being provided to help schools manage this, that'd be really appreciated. I'll leave it there.
Senator O'Sullivan, over to you.

Before I move on from this issue of PISA and funding, I've just been reflecting on the evidence that we've heard. Secretary, I want to take you back to your evidence when I asked why performance is so poor when school funding is so high and you specifically pointed to a distinction—that while there's been an increase in funding over the last 13 years none of those past funding agreements specifically had requirements around explicitly teaching phonics and small-group work, whereas the current ones do. You also mentioned changes to the maths curriculum. So am I right that the very clear implication from what you're saying is that, while funding is important, those other matters about the expectations around the explicit instruction of phonics and other things are actually super important to be able to lift performance? So it's not just a question of funding but we need changes to pedagogy and the curriculum? It's not just more money; is that fair? Have I understood your evidence?

Both are important. Obviously you need to have the funding to provide small groups because that requires additional teachers. So you need additional funding to enable teachers to develop programs in their schools around things like small-group teaching. The evidence is just as important. There's no point bringing together a small group of students if you don't actually know how to teach them explicitly the issues around phonics and things like that. So, together, those things are really important.

I noted your point about poor performance. I will say that Australia still is one of the highest-performing countries in the world around PISA as well. We're still generally around the top 10 out of the 80 or so countries that participate in PISA. Obviously as the secretary of the education department I want to see our performance improve. Absolutely. It's a combination. It'd be great to be No. 1. I love that idea. But it is a combination with the funding that's needed to implement the reforms. Those reforms are now very explicit in our agreements. My strong view is that those things together—and the evidence is starting to show that in the early days—will improve student outcomes.

Over a decade now we've had this constant focus on funding. Of course, funding is important, and the political debate often centres around that. But I'm pleased to hear that we are moving beyond just that element of it and looking at performance around pedagogy, around those explicit instructions and other things. Ultimately, that's what is going to really substantially make the difference. You can throw all the money you like at a problem, but, unless you've got the design and make-up of it right, you're just not going to lift the standards and continue to see improvements.

Minister Clare has been absolutely clear on that. If we just go back a little bit, the original Gonski report in 2011 or 2012 set a schooling resourcing standard, as you know, for all schools. Over the last decade, successive governments have put additional money in to reach that standard. As you know, non-government schools reached that standard several years ago. Government schools have yet to reach that standard. The Better and Fairer Schools Agreement that's now been signed by all states and territories will enable every school in Australia—government and non-government—to reach the standard that was set 15 years ago. That's what the additional money is about—actually setting the standard that was agreed a decade or so ago. But what we have fine-tuned or focused on, particularly over the last couple of years, is: how is that money best spent? It's best spent on evidence based teaching and learning and the things that you and I and all teachers, I assume, in Australia would agree will actually support students to be able to learn the best they can.

That's a good segue to bilateral funding agreements. I want to talk about the Victorian bilateral funding agreement. As expected, we saw their agreement out to 2034 announced as part of the Victorian state election campaign. Secretary, what reasons did Victoria give for the delay in signing the agreement?

Just a few things, because there are two agreements—Victoria signed the 10-year agreement last year. That 10-year agreement had Victoria agreeing to reach 100 per cent of the Schooling Resource Standard by 2034, I think. The second agreement that they signed just last week was the bilateral agreement, which showed what would be the trajectory of funding over those 10 years, and so they had already agreed to 10-year funding. That wasn't in doubt at all. It was how they were going to reach that between now and 2034. I don't think I've got a reason as to Victoria—they'd have to give that reason themselves, but we have been working with Victoria since last year about finalising that agreement, particularly around the funding trajectory. The reforms within that agreement were worked on last year and pretty much settled last year. It was the Victorian government themselves making decisions as to how that funding will flow over 10 years.
How many students in Victoria went through the government sector schools in the last two years while the Victorian government delayed finalising this bilateral?

I don't think we would know that. We'd have to take that on notice. I can give you the number of students in Victoria. In government schools in 2025, there were 665,683 government school students in Victorian schools.
There would be a flow, obviously—kids coming in and leaving.
Yes.

The Commonwealth's share of funding for the government sector increased incrementally for years. If you graph that increase in funding over time, it kind of looks like a bit of a hockey stick-style graph. Commonwealth contributions start at 20 per cent this year, then climb very slowly over the forward estimates. Then, suddenly, at the end of 2033 we have this really big spike in contributions from 22.5 to 25 per cent. Doesn't this just create a problem for future parliaments to have to contend with, because they will have to, all of a sudden, find the money for this sudden spike in funding?
No, it would have been funded as part of budget processes. Are you talking about just Victoria? It's different for every state and territory. For example, in WA—
I'm sure these figures here I've got are just for Victoria. It goes from 22.5 to 25 per cent, so quite a substantial jump, but it's in those outer years.

Yes, but part of our budgetary process would be to consider outer years as well. That's our normal budgetary process. In terms of what that would be in a dollar value, I don't think I've got that in front of me, but—someone's telling me to turn the page. Again, if we talk about Victoria alone—
We can get Mr Harding.
But, again, budgetary processes ensure that we factor that into any budget submission that we put into government.
Then have you found where you're getting that money from? Has the government already made budgetary plans for the sudden increase?

Obviously, we work over forward estimates, but, again, in terms of the way Finance allocate any budgetary decision, they don't just then—that would be part of the consideration over the medium term over the 10-year period, so every government would know what that requirement is.

I guess my point is that it's a nice headline. There's this big increase in funding. It's all the way out at the end of the forwards. There's not the pressure on the current budget to have to fund that. So is it not just a hollow empty promise for something further down the track where a future treasurer, whether it's the current one or someone else, has to actually find that money to fund all that and it becomes a problem for a future parliament?

That's the way government operates. I can't give any other reason around it. It's provisioned for in the budget. It's allocated in the budget, but, if there were a change of government, any decisions, obviously, can be changed by any government at all. It's not just schools funding; it's anything that's got an additional outlay in the out years. That's how we would normally do the budgetary process.
According to the projections, how much will the Commonwealth pay in SRS funding in 2033 for Victorian government-sector schools, and how much will it pay in 2034?
We can help with that.
I can talk about the additional funding that would be provided to Victoria in 2033. The Commonwealth—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Data Collection

text: I just want a total.
If you just give us a moment.
While you're looking it up, can you give those figures as both a cost per student contribution and in terms of the total budgetary spend?
We may have to take cost per student on notice. I'm not sure we'll have that level of detail. We can give total funding, I think.
We'll do that, and then we'll take a break.
Total funding for Victorian government schools in 2034, including the increased SRS contribution under the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement, is $4.9 billion.
I'll have to come back.
We'll now suspend, and we'll see you soon.
Welcome back, everybody. We are continuing in outcome 1, Schools and youth. Senator Dolega.
Minister, earlier on we heard about the National Youth Survey. Can you tell me some more about the benefits for young Australians and some more information that you can share with us.

Thank you, Senator, for the question. As we discussed earlier, the National Youth Survey is up online. It's the second National Youth Survey that we've done since we reinstated the Office for Youth, because we think it's so important that we hear the views and concerns of young Australians and that those views and concerns are available to be known to all members of parliament through the survey as well. We know that young people have so much to contribute when it comes to shaping Australia's future, and they absolutely deserve to be heard.

That's why we are creating more opportunities, including this National Youth Survey, for young people to have a say in the decisions that affect their lives. Of course, that's why we re-established the Office for Youth and support the important work that they do. It's why we have created this opportunity for young people to participate and have their views and their priorities directly inputted into the National Youth Survey, which will be published as well. The youth survey is open to young people across the country who are aged 12 to 25. They're invited to have their say on the issues that really matter most to them, and we launched the survey Monday last week. The survey was developed by OFY, the Office for Youth, and it gives young people a platform to share their views on a range of topics. This year, they'll have the opportunity to share their views on artificial intelligence and the impact that it's having on young people's lives, which we know is a big issue; on mental health, health and wellbeing, which always comes up as one of the top issues that young people face in our survey and other surveys; on climate, environment and sustainability; and on economic security and housing security. They're also invited to give their views on their experiences in education and training. The survey will really benefit young Australians because the feedback from the National Youth Survey will help inform the next phase of our youth strategy. Our youth strategy is called Engage! and it's up for review. The survey is a really important part of the process of developing the next youth strategy, because we want to make sure that young people can continue to have a meaningful role in shaping Australia's future. We want them to know that their voices matter. We want them to know that their ideas can make a real difference. We're really keen for young Australians to jump online and have their say. Again, the survey opened last Monday, and it remains open until the middle of December.
That sounds fantastic. Everyone should get on board and do the survey as quickly as they can so they can have a say in their future, right?
That's right. They should.
Thank you very much. I'm just a little bit ineligible now, sadly.
We'll get Senator Walker to jump online.

Yes, we will. Charlotte could do it. Can I ask the department some questions about Closing the Gap. Mr Mudford, you haven't let us down with another fabulous tie. I always look forward to seeing what you've got for us at each round of estimates. Can the department tell the committee about the First Nations Education Policy and what the policy is intended to achieve.

The First Nations Education Policy—as we've talked about previously, the department is working in partnership with First Nations partners and with states and territories. Our First Nations partners are the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Education Corporation, or NATSIEC; the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Principals Association, NATSIPA; the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Higher Education Consortium, NATSIHEC; SNAICC, the National Voice for Our Children; and the National Indigenous Youth Education Coalition, or NIYEC.

We're working with those partners to develop a policy that's a 10-year commitment to accelerate improvement in First Nations education outcomes, and that goes across the education lifecycle from early childhood education and care through schooling and then into tertiary education, which composes both the vocational education and training and the higher education sectors. We had First Nations partner led engagement earlier in the year. We then moved to co-drafting between the department and NATSIEC as the co-chairs of the policy working group informed by the perspectives of the five First Nations partners as well as the evidence base that we had developed through a range of engagements.

We then engaged through the Education Ministers Meeting architecture. That went through the Schools Policy Group, the Early Childhood Policy Group, the Education Senior Officials Committee and then the Education Ministers Meeting in July. We've continued that testing since then. NATSIEC coordinated with the four other partners to test the draft policy direction with First Nations communities, as well as the public consultation process and targeted stakeholder engagement that the department has been undertaking. We're doing further refinements through co-drafting at the moment, and we'll then again take it through our policy working group and the EMM architecture, as well as work with our skills colleagues in DEWR.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, First Nations and Closing the Gap

text: With the targeted consultation process, I understand there was also some targeted consultation at Garma. Can you give us an update on what you found through that targeted consultation.

At the Garma Festival, there was a roundtable discussion that was held with a number of attendees across education interests and the minister announced that further public consultation process that I mentioned that was open until the end of September. We had 117 responses to that and overwhelming support for the direction of the policy both from First Nations and non-Indigenous stakeholders across organisations and individuals. We tested across the elements of the policy, as well as the overall direction, and are taking into account that feedback to inform the further refinements that we're doing at the moment.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, First Nations and Closing the Gap

text: And, in parallel, the government's been working on the First Nations teacher and school leader strategy. What was the genesis of the work, and what's been the progress up to date?

Thanks for the question. The First Nations teacher and school leader strategy is the last remaining component of the National Teacher Workforce Action Plan for implementation. That action plan came out of a great need to attract more people to the teaching profession, equip those people to be successful in the profession and keep them in schools as well. This strategy is specifically around attracting more First Nations staff to the profession, keeping them once they're in and then giving them good and strong career pathways through. We're taking a very similar methodology to what Mr Mudford outlined. We are working quite closely with First Nations partners on the strategy. That strategy is going to education ministers on Monday for a first pass. Then it will go out for further consultation, working with our partners, the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Education Corporation and NATSIPA. They will facilitate consultation with First Nations educators. The department will facilitate conversations with departments of states and the non-government sector. Then we will bring those further insights and findings together, with a view to taking the strategy back to the ministerial council next year for endorsement.
Fantastic. With the long-term aims of the strategy, where are we going to go with that?

The long-term outcome we are seeking is really to have far more First Nations teachers than we currently do. I think our current proportion of First Nations teachers is in the order of 2.6 per cent of teachers or thereabouts, whereas the proportion of First Nations students in our education system is in the order of 6.8 per cent. So what we want to do is really even up those numbers, bring more teachers into the profession and keep them there, and have them be successful and see a career in teaching as a worthy endeavour.
What's been the Australian government investment in that?

The government's invested about $2.4 million in that. Some of that has gone to some preliminary work with external parties to synthesise the evidence, and the remaining component of it will be used to fund specific actions that come out of the strategy. Some of the early insights we're hearing from the consultation are about needing to have stronger and more culturally safe schools and do some work on building the capability of non-First-Nations staff around cultural safety and strengthening cultural understanding and awareness, as well as stronger mechanisms for mentoring of First Nations staff.

Fantastic. Thank you for the work you're doing. It sounds fantastic. I always look forward to hearing what you're up to and what work is being done. So, really, well done. Thank you for updating. Chair, I just have another quick block if I've got time.
Yes, just quickly, and then we'll move back to the coalition.

This is just to follow on from some of the questions about the digital detox, if I may do that. The minister was referring to that before. What does the recent piece of data tell us about how much time students are spending on devices, and how does this compare with international peers?

Thanks for the question. In that earlier block, we were talking about the heavy use of digital devices in Australian schools. The most recent piece of data—the 2025 PISA assessment, which just came out a little while ago—is showing that Australian school students, on average, are spending 2.6 hours per day using a digital device for learning at school. That's in really sharp contrast to what we're seeing across the rest of the OECD, where it is, on average, 1.7 hours. Something like 57 per cent of students reported using devices for learning at school for more than two hours a day, compared to about 30 per cent across the OECD. So it's a pretty significant difference. At the heart of this, we would say it's all about being purposeful. The importance of devices is about purposeful use of devices.

Yes. The minister was talking about how we were looking to see how screens and artificial intelligence and everything are affecting youth. Obviously, devices can have impacts on them. Is there evidence to suggest that screens are a big distraction in schools?

We've seen a couple of threads of that. At the headline level, the PISA data talks about classroom disruption, and when you dig underneath the data that disruption is that low-level disruption that comes from being distracted by one's own device or by other devices. That's what PISA is pointing to, but Macquarie University have also done some more recent research that talks to it. I think, of their survey, about 84 per cent of high-school students and 50 per cent or 57 per cent of primary school students are pointing to those levels of disruption and distractions from screens in class.
Does the data show that the distractions lead to poorer education outcomes?

In the work that we've been doing for education ministers for their meeting on Monday, we've been looking into what the research is saying about the impact of use. It's not all or nothing, but what the data is pointing to is that excessive use is having an impact on academic performance. I think the PISA data, with maths performance, talk to an excessive amount of screen use, and you saw a correlation to what was happening with students' maths results. Certainly, there's work out of Brookings in the US and a range of other leading research organisations about screen use.

What about student wellbeing when it comes to excessively high amounts of screen use? What's the data showing about wellbeing? Obviously, we're going to be really curious to see what the youth survey says about all the digital lifestyles and everything, but what are you seeing?

What we're seeing in terms of both in-school use and out-of-school use is the impact on wellbeing goes to students' interaction with social media and what's happening on social media. We had very strong feedback through the antibullying review that's been done around how screens and that form of communication was impacting overall student wellbeing. If we look at the impact of excessive use on student learning, combined with the personal use of devices and impact on wellbeing, there's this great opportunity for education ministers to get together on Monday and have a conversation about what they want to do collectively and nationally about how screens are used in schools.
With the work being underway, how are we going to be looking at what we can do about it?

Some of the research that our paper that we're preparing for education ministers has looked at is a meta-analysis of 23 different research limbs, and that pointed pretty significantly to a high use of screens and having poorer emotional regulation. That goes to one's ability to not only self-regulate but co-regulate with others, and it also diminishes your capacity to engage with humans.
Yes.
You start to diminish those core capabilities about how you get on in the world.

I have two nine-year-old nieces, and I see their love for Roblox and Minecraft and all these others that really can be wonderful things but can also really affect the ability to have that face-to-face conversation or to go out and play in the dirt and get dirty and everything, absolutely. Thank you very much.
I'm returning to Senator O'Sullivan.

Sticking to that theme of digital use, recently, we saw extensive reporting of a study in China on the impact of AI on learning for about 26,000 secondary students over a period of 30 months—a fascinating read. The study was clear that AI use lifted homework scores but lowered the monthly exam scores by 20 per cent within six months. This was reported extensively in Australian media in mid-September. The ABC ran a story on 20 September. Is the department aware of these impacts of AI use?
Absolutely, we are aware of that research. In fact, Minister Clare has been quoting that research. In fact, as late as this morning, he was quoting this research, I think, on media—
I missed his quote this morning.

and he was certainly talking about it in a number of forums that I was in this week as well. We are aware of that research. We've read that research. I think we're referencing that research in some of the work that we're doing as well. Ms Brighton?

In New South Wales, Deputy Premier Car has already made commitments in terms of restricting assessment and AI in assessment at home, in terms of what they were seeing in New South Wales students. I'm sure that the discussion on Monday with education ministers will point to AI and its use and when it should be purposefully used and when it shouldn't be used. All educators across the country want to see a correlation between what an in-school assessment looks like in a student's performance and what is happening with what they do at home. That's what the China data is absolutely pointing to.

I want to come to next week's meeting. Before I do, though, on 24 May 2023, at the AI in Education Conference in Sydney, the Minister for Education said:

AI can help us to personalise education and make it more engaging and more effective for individual students.

Similarly, on 1 December that year, the minister put out a media release calling for the use of generative AI to 'personalise education and make learning more compelling and effective'. The minister's 2023 comments endorsing the use of AI in schools are now at odds with his recent statements calling for a digital detox, saying that the more screens are used, the more results go down. Minister, to you: when did Labor and the minister change their position on AI use by students?
I have to reject the premise of your question.
Well, the premise is his quotes.

I think all the evidence about the minister's public comments and the work that he is doing reflects the fact that there are benefits and there are risks, and that is the approach of the Australian government in general to AI. It is why we have a government-wide focus on harnessing the benefits of AI and also approaching AI eyes wide open in terms of the risks. In terms of digital approaches in the classroom, as the officials have said, it is really important for students to have digital skills, and part of that is students learning when it's useful and appropriate to use AI and when it's not.

In relation to edtech and the potential uses of AI in edtech as well, the minister has been clear, and the officials have been clear, that that needs to be purposeful. All of that goes to what the minister means when he's talking about winding the prevalence of the use of screens in classrooms in particular back a bit. This sort of technology can be really useful for learning. We know that students do need to learn digital skills. But there is also a lot of evidence which the minister's really focused on that removing screens and going back to pen and paper where we can help students learn and retain information, and that's why the minister's talking about a digital detox. Of course, the minister's not talking about ignoring the existence of AI when it comes to edtech or when it comes to students' learning. What he is talking about is appropriate use and getting back to pen and paper where we can in the classroom. And this digital detox will be on the agenda for all education ministers next week.

You rejected the premise of my question in the first part of your long answer. The fact of the matter is that in 2023 we had comments from the minister in relation to encouraging people's use of AI. He is now being more circumspect in the way that he discusses that, so there has been a change. My question was simply about the fact that there has been a change. I was asking when he made that change. You mentioned the ministers' meeting next week with all other ministers. Will he back the coalition's policy? I commend my colleague Mr Leeser for his position on this, for drastically reducing screen time and AI use by students across Australia, particularly those very young students.
Sorry, I missed the last part of your question.
Will he back the coalition's policy to reduce screen time and AI use by students across Australia, particularly for very young students?

Well, from my participation in education ministers' meetings, I can say without disclosing all of the contents of those meetings that this issue has been discussed and has been raised for some time at those meetings. The department has given evidence to you today that work has been underway for some time in relation to digital detox. Decisions of the education ministers' meeting, of course, are decisions for all ministers. There's some really interesting work going on in the states and territories—in Victoria, for example, and in other states—that have started to implement screen time bans in different settings. We've been discussing that at education ministers' meetings for some time, and education ministers will come together to consider the work that is put before them on Monday.
Has the department ever specifically briefed the minister or his office on the impacts of AI learning, brain plasticity and/or development?

We probably have been briefing on AI for several years now, particularly in some of the work that was done in 2023, I think, around the development of the national framework around generative AI in schools. I will ask Ms Brighton because she will have the detail, but we've been briefing, not just this year but also in previous years, because education ministers did agree to a framework around generative AI in schools in 2023. That was reviewed again in 2024, I think.
Has the advice shifted over that time?
Oh, look, I mean—
I appreciate there have been significant advancements.
Yes, you beat me to it. I was going to say, even compared to—
So is that predicated? Has that meant that we've had to change the advice?

We would always change our advice based on evidence. You even quoted the Chinese research that's come out. AERO is with us a little later. AERO has done some really, really interesting work around this as well. As Ms Brighton said, New South Wales is doing some research into that, particularly around device usage, and they've made some of that available over the last couple of weeks. So I would absolutely say our advice has grown based on more information that's available to us, as it should. But in terms of briefing the minister or the government, we've been doing this for quite a while now.

The premise of the work that we've been doing with states and territories and education ministers is that technology has for some time changed in the face of teaching and learning. That technology presents an absolute opportunity. When I say 'technology', I don't mean just edtech but also AI and generative AI. It has an opportunity to have educational benefits, but systems and schools need to be ensuring that it's really quite purposeful and effective. If technology is going to be used in schools, it really needs to serve an education purpose. It's a pretty nuanced discussion. But if we take it back to the AI framework that was endorsed in 2023 then reviewed again in 2024—and that review has been published—the anchor point for that AI framework is all around purposeful and deliberate use. The increasing use of devices really is what has prompted us to be looking further into it. As I said before, it's not an either/or. It's about: how do you make sure that the technology is supporting and enabling teaching and learning, and not replacing it?

Some of the private schools are banning it completely, particularly the use of devices, and have been able to see improved not just results but also culture within the schools. I'm thinking of a particular school in Perth that's been well canvassed.
The issue—
Look, I'll move on because I've got a fair bit to canvas—
I'll let you move on, sorry.

and we're going to run out of time. Can I go to the Choice and Affordability Fund. What consultations or discussions have you had with the non-government sector about the continuation of the Choice and Affordability Fund, or CAF as we know it, beyond 2029?

The Choice and Affordability Fund runs until the end of the 2029 school year. I meet very regularly with both Independent Schools Australia and the National Catholic Education Commission. We haven't started formal consultation and engagement on the CAF yet, because that's got another few years to run, but, certainly, it is a feature that is regularly raised by my colleagues when they're meeting with me—the importance of that fund to them. That fund was worth about $1.2 billion over the nine years that it's been established, and it's split between the Catholic sector and the independent sector.
2029 is not that far away, though. Time flies, so—
It's still quite a few budgets away.
But you must be getting closer to commencing that negotiation.
Again, they've raised the point with us, and then it'll be a matter of government in terms of policy directions.
As you've pointed out, it ends in 2029. Has the department modelled the impact of ending the CAF funding at all, particularly in terms of the impact on school fees and potential school closures?
No, I don't believe we have.

No, we haven't done any modelling. The CAF was always set up as a time bound initiative for five very specific purposes. There are five criteria under which funding can be distributed by the entities in states and territories to independent and Catholic schools, and, no, we haven't done any modelling. The future of the CAF will be a matter for government's consideration.
How much has the Choice and Affordability Fund saved parents in school fees? Does the department model or measure those savings to families at all?
No. We don't even collect—well, at a high level, we collect school fees, but it's not verified data.

Secretary Cook is correct. We don't collect school fees—we have visibility of school fees, but we don't expressly collect it—but one of the priorities of the CAF is the choice and affordability priority area, and about 50 to 51 per cent of the CAF is spent on that priority area. That is around fees, I believe, but I'll get Mr Davern to jump in with a bit more detail.

Yes, Ms Brighton is correct in saying, in 2025, the choice and affordability priority, which is the first priority, accounted for 51.1 per cent of total expenditure, which was $74.76 million, and that priority is geared around fees and lowering fees.

Can I ask the inverse question. What are the savings to the Commonwealth for each student that attends a non-government school? You'd be paying X amount for every student in a government school and then the student funding is less.
It costs the Commonwealth government more for a student that goes to non-government school than a government school.
But your funding agreement with the states on the—you're paying it directly, I get that.
We pay 80 per cent of non-government, so I'm just saying now—
You're indirectly going through the states with the government schools. Are you not?
Sorry, I might have confused your question. Do you mind just asking the question again? I thought you asked what our save is on every non-government school as opposed to a government school.
Yes.
It's not a Commonwealth save. It's probably a state save because we are the—the more students that go to non-government schools, the bigger outlay the Commonwealth government puts out.
Yes, fair point. Is that tracked at all—the cost of a student in a government school versus the cost of a student in a non-government school from government funding, be it state or Commonwealth?

We do have that data. We also would show, through best estimates variation, the increasing cost to the Commonwealth with the number of non-government school students going to non-government schools. For each school there's a breakdown about what is the per-student rate, Commonwealth funding and state funding. Do we have an overall rate at all? No, not with us. But we can probably take it on notice.
That's okay. In relation to the negotiations that have not yet commenced on the Choice and Affordability Fund, when do you expect that they will start formally?
That's a matter for government about the future of the Choice and Affordability Fund. As Ms Brighton said, when it was announced, it was announced as a 10-year, time-limited program.
Minister, could I get a short response from you? Is there any decision from government about when that negotiation will start?
The program is funded through to 2029, so any further funding beyond 2029 would be a future decision for government.
What work has the department done to identify small regional schools that would face financial viability risks without CAF funding?

Remember that the Choice and Affordability Fund is to assist schools with coming down to what their entitlement actually is in the schooling resource standard. A number of these schools are getting more than what they're entitled to under the funding model. If there's an issue about their ability to continue, I'd question why, because some of these schools are currently getting more than what, under the model, they're entitled to at the moment. Remember: most non-government schools are above 100 per cent of the schooling resource standard. The CAF was to assist the transition down from above 100 per cent to 100 per cent. It's not as if they're going below what their entitlement is under the school funding model.

I'm not sure that I'm following, but my point is: if CAF support were to cease, if the negotiation didn't occur, what happens to small regional schools and their viability if there were no if there was no Choice and Affordability Fund.

Again, under the model, those schools are getting 100 per cent of the funding they're entitled to under the school funding model. If the question is 'Should they be getting more than 100 per cent of what they're entitled to?' not under the legislation but under the law, and they already get loadings in relation to small school size, and they also get loadings in relation to remoteness as well on top of that—
How many small regional schools currently receive CAF assistance?
I don't know whether we've got that data. The independent and Catholic systems will have to give us that data. We don't have it.

To wrap up: the department knows that the CAF is going to end. We know that it's ending in 2029. It's been raised by stakeholders. You've said, Ms Brighton, that it's raised in your discussions with the various peaks. But you've not consulted on what happens when the funds end. You don't know what the benefits to parents have been over time, you don't know what the impacts on parents and schools will be if it ends and you haven't yet started any of the negotiations. Ms Brighton, you specifically referred to its time-bound nature, and it was designed to end, if I understood what you were saying correctly. What confidence can schools and, importantly, parents have about the future viability of the non-government schools sector in Australia?

I think the confidence is that those schools will receive 100 per cent of the funding they're entitled to under the school funding model, which most government schools currently aren't receiving, as you're aware. All non-government schools—or at least the very large majority of all non-government schools—are. Again, the point was that the government of the day decided to give a 10-year transition period to assist those schools that are getting more money than they're entitled to with managing the transition down to the funding that they were entitled to under the model.
But, if CAF ends—
They'll receive 100 per cent of the funding—
then fees will have to go up. School fees will go up. How else will the school survive?

On the basis of already receiving everything they're entitled to? Again, they will be getting 100 per cent of the funding that they're entitled to under the model. It would take their socioeconomic status into consideration.
If CAF ends on a cliff, are you saying that there's another funding source that's replacing that?

If a school chooses to fund itself beyond the schooling resource standard, that's a matter for the school. But a model has been developed that's been supported by successive governments since 2011 and says, 'This is what every school in Australia is entitled to.' Every non-government school effectively is already receiving that funding plus more. If they want to continue to fund their own school above what the model entitles them to, that's their decision if they choose to raise fees in relation to that. But they're not getting less funding, in terms of what the model says they're entitled to, as a result of CAF ending. They're just not getting the additional, surplus money on top of 100 per cent.
Well, it sounds like school fees are going to go up then.

Again, that will be a school issue about whether they want to fund their school above the schooling resource standard. I've got no say over that at all. Almost all government schools aren't at 100 per cent. Almost all non-government schools are at 100 per cent—again, as the legislation entitles them to, which has been changed by successive governments. They're receiving the money they're entitled to under the legislation.

Alright. Hopefully, I'll be communicating to schools and parents about what the impact will be for them. As you say, it's up to them to do that. But that transparency would be important for parents to know.

I want to go to the NCCD and ask about the savings measures announced in the budget around the NCCD and disability loadings. How are you guaranteeing that those cuts do not fall disproportionately on independent schools which do not have the protection of a system that can absorb or distribute cuts? In particular, how are you going to ensure that those cuts do not fall disproportionately on majority-Indigenous schools or special-assistance schools?

I can contextualise that for you. About a third—about 27 per cent—of Australian students need an adjustment for a disability to access schooling. About 20 per cent of Australian school students—I think it's 19.7—receive an adjustment that is funded. The students-with-disability funding is for students with a disability. That loading is so that those students with disability can access education on the same basis as every other student. The funding is to provide an adjustment that exists because of the functional impact on disability. The reason I stress that is that the NCCD is not a general loading for disadvantage, complexity or vulnerability. We have other loadings. You mentioned majority Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander schools. There is a specific cohort loading around First Nations students. There are also specific cohort loadings around disadvantage. The work we have been doing around the NCCD is about making sure that students are getting the adjustments they need to access education. We've been working with the non-government sector and states and territories on clarifying the guidelines to ensure that students are getting what they need to access education.

When you refer to the cuts, the way we're looking at it is rightsizing and making sure the students are getting what they need to access education. One of the areas we've been looking at is where we have three categories of funded adjustments. The top category is what we call an extensive adjustment. These are the young people that, in order to access education, need the most personalised, targeted, intensive levels of support to go to school and to learn. What we have found through what the data tells us but also through our auditing program is that there are certain cohorts of students that have been funded at that level but actually don't have a disability that warrants that level of intensity, so we've been working with the states and territories and the non-government sector to clarify that.

We've heard directly from independent faith schools that have a majority Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cohort, and they say they now stand to lose between 25 and 30 per cent of their funding as a result of those changes. How is that an acceptable outcome for those students, particularly vulnerable students?

If, outside the committee, you would like to provide us with individual school examples, we'd be happy to look at that. The levels of supports that we expect for students at those higher classification levels have been very consistent since 2015 when the guidelines were first introduced. So it may be that some schools haven't been applying the guidelines in the way that they were expected to, and that might change the profile of a school and the funding that they receive. But, without the specifics, it's hard to talk in the general unless Ms Donegan wants to add.
We can get you that.

I can only talk in averages, but I can try to give you a bit more detail. When we look at the sectors specifically, I can talk about the total student population with a disability. For the government sector the total population of students with a disability is 28.6 per cent, in the independent sector it's 24.4 per cent, and in the Catholic sector it's 24.3 per cent. That's a lot of students with a disability. However, when you look then towards the students who require an extensive adjustment, that's 2.8 per cent of students, so that's a relatively small number. When you take into account what Ms Brighton has said and the stats that say that the overall level of adjustments that require extensive adjustments are around 2.8 per cent, we'd really need to look into the detail to be able to understand what's happening for about 25 per cent of funding.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Improving Student Outcomes

text: And we actually do that. When there's wildly different data that a school has from year to year—I know Ms Brighton has spoken to me about this—we actually contact the school and speak to the school about why their data is suddenly so different to what it was previously. I don't know how many schools we've done this year, but we have done quite a few. But again, if there are particular examples, we're very happy to look at those examples if you're able to give them to us out of session.

Ms Brighton, you use the term 'right sizing'. To me it sounds like a different way of saying cut, I suppose. So I use the word cut, because what you're talking about here is a measure which achieves $472 million in savings, if I understand it correctly, over the forward estimates. When you've got such a sizeable cut, how can that not result in a reduction in the delivery of support for students in these schools?

As Ms Brighton said, it's actually ensuring the right children are getting the right levels of support. When we have gone in with some of our audits where we've had children allocated to particular categories of support, we have found that some of those students either don't need that level of support or actually need more support, and so there's movement between the two. That's really important to ensure that that money is targeted in the best way possible. But, again, Ms Brighton will be able to give specific examples of that.

Yes. Some of the things we have seen, as Secretary Cook said, include the student at the level of support that they need as one element. Sometimes they are underdone, and sometimes they are overdone. But importantly are they getting that support? Is that support being provided by the school to the student? That's a really important part of how we're looking at it. It's not only what the student is assessed at and what do they need but also is the school actually providing that? Then through the consultation work that we did for these higher levels of adjustment, the requirement is that the student who needs the most intense level of support gets it over 10 consecutive weeks. We also heard through the consultation that sometimes that's pretty complex when you look at the characteristics of some of those students that need it. So in the new guidelines, we have also offered an option where it's either 10 consecutive weeks of evidence or it's 20 cumulative weeks of evidence to give schools a lot more flexibility about how they demonstrate the need of that individual student. What our audits have pointed to, just as Secretary Cook said, is that not only are some students not being classified at high enough levels but we've had other students that have had either the nature of the disability or the nature of the adjustments necessary overstated or sometimes there's not even a disability at all in that young person.

Have you had feedback from special assistance schools in particular? These are schools that are working with some of the most—definitely the most—vulnerable students in each state and territory. The ones that I've been to in Western Australia have students with very high levels of need. It might not necessarily be disabilities that might be measured or captured under this, but they might have very significant home lives and socio backgrounds and issues. They don't fit within a mainstream school system. They've maybe been expelled from those schools for behaviour reasons and other reasons. Essentially the next step for these students, to be really blunt about it—and I don't mean to be impolite—is either in hospital because of self-harming and those sort of issues or, in fact, suicide or going to correction centres because of the crime that they can lead to. These schools are on their knees. That is what I'm hearing. I know of one particular school that's having to close campuses around the state of Western Australia. It's a bit of a conflation of the change in how they're deeming or how they're assessed under the SRS, and then there is this issue here with the NCCD. Are you getting representations from those schools about the multitude of issues that that they're contending with and their viability going forward?

There are a few elements to that. There is no doubt that our schools need to be able to support young people who are impacted by trauma, who are homeless, who have a degree of complexity and vulnerability around their lives. Our schools need to be able to provide a supportive place for them to come to, to learn and to grow. Under the schools reform and funding agreement, we have a piece of work which is going to be a review of the Schooling Resource Standard. The scope of that review is in the process of being settled, but one of the things we will look at is does the SRS as it's currently constructed have regard to the contemporary costs of schooling, particularly as we look at those elements of intersectionality about different vulnerabilities. I've said to the SAS schools that I've met with that as part of the SRS review, we will—
They just seem to be in this no man's land. They've got unique needs compared to the rest of the school population.

Yes, and that's why as part of the SRS review we will look at that. The other thing I would say is that for specialist assistant schools the policy of the capacity to contribute doesn't apply to them. We have been working with some special assistant schools that may have made reference to reshaping of their programs. When that happens, we work with them. Some of those schools have significant asset holdings and cash holdings, and what they can actually do is they can deploy those holdings, which is often an accumulation of Australian government funding, that they can use to continue to support students.

I'm going to have to move on. I'd love to keep exploring that, but I'm going to have to move on. How much have you achieved or do you expect to achieve in savings in government schools, how much in Catholic and how much in independent schools across this $472 million? What's the breakdown?

The way we assess and fund schools is based on actual student enrolments, and how we assess that is through the schools census. We have a non-government school census and a government school census. Those two census periods have only just closed a little while ago. We're going through the usual data quality assurance process, and then, once those numbers are settled, it'll be part of the government's MYEFO process.
And the measuring starts this financial year—is that right?
Yes.

The NCCD portion of this measure only takes effect from the 2027 academic year, so we will only see that in the 2027 census, and we'll probably only be in a position to report in early 2028 on the impact and the sectoral split.
What's the largest reduction in funding to a single school under the compliance measures, both in nominal terms and proportionally?
The current compliance measures we've got in place, that have been in place for a year or two, or are you talking about this work that we're doing around NCCD?
Yes, NCCD.
Well, we won't know because it doesn't actually come into effect until 2027, as we've just indicated, so we won't get the data until next year to get a better sense of that.

Just to go back to something you said earlier in relation to the special assistance schools and their considerable cash holdings or assets, you're not suggesting that they would need to be selling land or buildings?

No, Senator. What I was referring to is that in some situations, as we're engaging with special assistance schools, if they express concerns, we work with them and, in working with them, we have a look at whether there's an accumulation of cash holdings. We have an integrity measure that was a budget 2023-24 measure. If there's an accumulation of cash holdings, we're having discussions with those schools about whether that is Australian government recurrent funding. The expectation is we fund schools on a school year, and the general expectation is that the funds that go to a school in a school year are for the provision of schooling in that year. So if there's an accumulation of cash, there's an opportunity, if that's the Australian government funding, for those special assistance schools to use that to service the students. No, I'm not suggesting that schools should be selling their buildings and lands, but we are also making sure that the funding for schooling is being used for the provision of schooling. Part of my evidence with Senator Allman-Payne earlier was that we do look at asset holdings and transfer of assets as part of our usual compliance work and as part of our audits.

I've been to a few of these schools, and none of them have got big grand facilities. It's amazing what they're able to deliver—many off the smell of an oily rag, I've got to say. I actually wish there was more support that could go to them.

I just want to deal with one more issue before we move on, Chair, if that's okay. I want to talk about, I guess, a generational shift that's occurring towards non-government schools. We've seen their enrolments go up in comparison to government schools. The full-time equivalent enrolment projections that you're using, which you provided on notice in response to SQ26-000676 and then again in SQ26-000662. Based on that data, in 2026 the share of school students in non-government schools is 38 per cent, with 62 per cent in government schools. By 2034 the proportion in government schools falls to 58 per cent, with 42 per cent in non-government schools. Now, that's a pretty massive change.
Sorry, did you say 2034?

In 2034, the proportion in government schools falls to 58, with an increase to 42 per cent in non-government schools. So it's a pretty big change. The department data is consistent with material released yesterday by Independent Schools Australia. Can you tell me what's going on? What information or feedback have you had as to why parents are choosing non-government schools? What do you think is driving this generational shift?

I'm not sure we'd have any data around that. Obviously we have conversations with both the independent and Catholic school sectors, as well as our state and territory colleagues. I think the opportunity for all parents is there's choice available to them in the education system in Australia. Funding is provided to both the non-government and government sector—which is a bit unusual, as you know, internationally—here in Australia. I think it's about providing parents that choice. I don't think we've got anything, sorry, to help you about why that is happening. No-one's spoken to us. We haven't done any research around that. Some states and territories might have done some research around that, but I don't think we have.

Okay. Across Australia this year we have over two million, 2,565,887, school students, but that's expected to shrink to 2.394 million by 2034. That's a decline of 170,000 students, or about 20,000 a year. Should we expect government school closures, and, if so, how many schools do you expect will close?
That's really a matter for states and territories rather than us. They make their own decisions. We don't make any decisions around school openings or closures. They make those decisions themselves.
So it's not something that's discussed in terms of viability of schools at this level.
Not really. As you know, in some schools in my home state of Queensland, they're a one teacher school with seven kids because it's the only school in cooee of anything.
Yes.
Those schools would not likely close down. In other schools in Queensland, we had 3½ thousand kids in a school.

The data shows that this year we have 1.573 million non-government school students, but by 2034 that number will increase by almost 150,000 to 1.722 million independent schools. Australia expects this will mean an additional 191 independent schools and presumably an equivalent increase in Catholic schools. What planning have you done in relation to the opening of these new schools—the capital funding that would be required and similar measures to accommodate that growth?

As you know, the Schooling Resource Standard doesn't provide capital funding. It provides maintenance funding. We have a non-government capital fund, which is about—Ms Brighton will help me—200-and-something million dollars a year.
Which is given to the states, and they—

No, that comes directly to us. We work with the non-government sector, and they decide where that funding should go. We tell them what is available. That funding is obviously directed at low socioeconomic non-government schools, of course. But as the ISA report said, it's really state governments that work with them around land provision, all the roles that go around local council approvals for building approvals—that's not a Commonwealth role.
Senator Allman-Payne has a couple of questions.
Yes, I'm happy to share.
Okay, Senator Allman-Payne, but we're due to move to the next panel.

Thanks, Chair. I'll be quick. Just around the SRS review, my understanding is that the review of the SRS base and loadings methodology is due to begin in the middle or early next year. Could you just clarify for me when that review is due to start, and when the terms of reference should be published?

You're right. You've probably got those dates from the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement. Ministers made a decision to bring forward the SRS review. The 2024 year?

On Monday.

In previous appearances before this committee, I've described the impactful work that Australia's national evidence body, AERO, does with schools and school systems. Most recently we published summaries of evidence about the use of AI in schools for policymakers and practitioners. AERO has also been charged by education ministers to conduct research in the early childhood education and care sector. Today I want to briefly highlight the important work we do to support achieving equity in education right from the start.

At a time when child safety concerns continue to challenge the sector, our focus has remained on identifying the system conditions and practices that make a difference to children's outcomes. Evidence based practice is a pathway to restoring confidence and improving education quality in the sector. We engage with state and territory governments and the federal government, who steward the system, and with key stakeholders across the sector. We also partner with early childhood services. For example, last month we published an intentional teaching model to help educators use intentional teaching to support children's learning. The model was developed in partnership with early childhood services to ensure that the resources are robust and relevant in real-world early childhood settings.

For the past four years, we've partnered with services to learn about what it takes to successfully implement evidence based practices. Working in 51 services, including long day care, family day care, pre-school and kindergarten. It's a genuine partnership where we learn together about how evidence can work in real-world contexts. Our early childhood work considers the entire system. We analyse national data sets to examine the impact of system-level settings and conditions. We look for what works by examining existing evidence and undertaking research to address gaps in evidence based practice, knowledge and approaches. We investigate what it takes and what is needed to make evidence based practice stick, and we consider context, engaging with our partners across governments and the sector to understand the context for policy and practice implementation.

Our study linking quality and child development in early childhood education and care is the first piece of empirical evidence linking quality ratings with child development. This analysis gives us confidence that our National Quality Framework is delivering for children. We've also identified specific quality areas that are associated with reducing developmental vulnerability. Through our work in both early childhood and school sectors, AERO's continuing to examine and strengthen the evidence base and promote practices and approaches that support the continuity of learning and development of our children and young people. Through our system-level evidence of what drives excellence and equity in educational outcomes, we're supporting the targeting of effort towards specific and impactful evidence based practices and helping to bridge the gap between research and action. Thank you.
We have both yourself and Senator Allman-Payne seeking the call and about 20 minutes. I'll come to you first, Senator O'Sullivan.

I'll make sure to leave some time. I want to ask about classroom disruption. As you know, it's a topic I've been very interested in for quite some time. The Centre for Independent Studies released survey based research earlier this year indicating that nine minutes out of every half hour of teaching time was lost to classroom disruption. Do you have any of your own data? Do you agree that the disruptive classroom behaviour is substantially reducing learning time in Australian schools?

There was evidence available from recent PISA surveys, as well, that have identified the fact that learning time is lost to low-level classroom disruption and disengagement. That was the reason that the Commonwealth government commissioned AERO to examine the evidence base for how to improve the quality of the classroom environment so that it is conducive to learning. Over the last three years, we've developed a suite of resources for teachers in schools to help them implement evidence based practice that helps to manage the way classrooms operate and enable good learning to happen. It's a feature of explicit teaching, making sure that the classroom is managed and that students understand the expectations of them and their behaviour provides the environment so that the learning can happen.
Do you have an estimate—the same way that CIS have come up with the amount of time lost around learning?
No. We used the estimate that was available from PISA, not the most recent piece but the previous one, which had quite a focus on that, which I can supply to you on notice.
Do you have an estimate on the amount of teaching time lost annually to classroom disruption?
Similarly, I'd have to supply it to you on notice.
Does Australia currently collect data on the extent of classroom disruption nationally?

No. It is part of the question that is asked through the PISA student and teacher survey. That's how we manage to get a bit of insight into that, but it's not something that's conducted as a national survey in Australia on a regular basis.

I'm not sure if you recall, but there was a recommendation from this committee that that be included in questions, as part of NAPLAN and in regular student feedback assessments, so that we're able to track improvement in this area. Would you endorse that?
Yes. I think there's an opportunity with NAPLAN to collect information about a range of things, and that would be one that would be really interesting to know more about at a national level.
Has AERO recommended that education ministers establish a regular national classroom behaviour survey?
We haven't made such a recommendation.

Right, but you would endorse that, which was your previous answer? Can we go to Senator Allman-Payne, and, if there is time before the break, I'll come back. I just need to table something, and I want to make sure I've got the right document.
Senator Allman-Payne, you have the call for 10 minutes.

I'll just start my clock so that I don't go over like I did last time. Hi, Dr Donovan. I have some questions around the independent performance evaluation of AERO that was commissioned by the minister in mid-2025, which we understand has gone to state education ministers. Are you aware that a number of people have tried to access that report under FOI and been denied access?
I'm aware that there has been an FOI lodged, yes.
Did AERO have any input to the education ministers on whether that report should be released or not?
No, none at all.

Much of AERO's work is around evidence based research, and certainly the government has a regime in the Better and Fairer Schools Agreement of holding schools and teachers accountable. Can you understand why education academics, teachers and school leaders are very concerned that the report and evaluation of AERO has not been made public, given that it's a means of showing the evidence for the work that you do and the accountability of AERO?

The evidence for the work that we do is transparently available already on our website. The ministers commissioned the report. It's the ministers' decision whether or not to release it, and they've decided not to.
In terms of how that report or that review was conducted, who from AERO was involved in being engaged with the reviewers for that review?
The reviewers sought meetings with several members of my executive team and our board, and we provided documentation to them as requested.
Did they do an audit of the operations of AERO? What sorts of documents were requested?
There were about 80 documents requested, but, as that goes to the content of their report, I can't give you detail about that. I would not describe what they did as an audit, no.
Have there been any actions that AERO is now implementing that flow from the findings of that report?

There were several findings that were about possible actions that AERO could take which AERO was already undertaking—for example, an annual report. We're not required to produce an annual report as a ministerially owned company. We report to the ministers on a quarterly basis about our progress and impact. But our board had suggested that an annual report might be a good opportunity for people to annually get a compilation of the work that we've done, and so we had already begun producing annual reports, for example.
Is that the only action that's flowed from that report—
No, there are—
noting that it cost $420,000?

Yes—several other actions that we have undertaken that were synchronous with things that our board had already made suggestions to us about. Another one is publishing our engagement plan, who we engage with and how we go about engagement and consultation around the work that we do.
Is there anything that you were not already doing that you are now doing as a consequence of the findings of that review?
I don't think so. A lot of the findings from the review—
Are you sure? Do you need to take that on notice?
I can take it on notice. Not all of the findings of the review were about actions for AERO's attention.

The reason I'm really keen to know is that the report cost $420,000. AERO has cost $65 million since its inception. I think it would be concerning (a) if we have a report that we can't get the findings of and (b) if there's nothing that flows from that. That doesn't seem like a good return on investment to me. Is there a work plan for AERO at the moment?
Yes, there's a work plan for AERO every year.
Is it publicly available?

The work plan is not published. It is made available to our members, the ministers. It goes into detail about the projects, the money that we're spending on them, the way that we're doing the work, the deliverables et cetera, and we report on our progress against the work plan to the ministers on a quarterly basis.
Is that work plan able to be provided to the committee?
I can check. I'll take it on notice.
When did AERO receive a copy of the evaluation report?
We received a copy of the evaluation report to our company secretary on 5 May this year.
Did you get an opportunity to see a draft of the report before it was finalised?
We saw a draft of the report around the middle of 2025.
Did you have any input into that draft report?
We were asked to identify any factual inaccuracies in the report.
Were there any changes that you recommended be made to the draft report?
Yes.
I think that's probably it. We will continue to press education ministers to see if we can get some transparency around that review. Thanks, Dr Donovan.
Senator O'Sullivan, you have the call, and we're due to break at quarter past.

We'll wrap up by then. Thank you for the work that you do, Dr Donovan, and for AERO and all your staff. It's important work. It's important that we have evidence based application in education, so thank you.
