PISA 2025 found Australian students spend an average of 2.6 hours per school day using digital devices for learning, compared to 1.7 hours across the OECD, which is quite a difference in Australian students' experience. It found that 39 per cent reported that other students were frequently distracted by digital devices during science lessons. What's your view on that?

We recently published some explainers for teachers and for policymakers about what is the evidence base around the uses of AI in particular but edtech generally in Australian classroom settings, and the truth is that the evidence base is very slender. The evidence that we have is derived mostly from overseas, from studies that are looking at higher education rather than school based practices—very short term studies, as you would imagine. We haven't had AI for that long. It's hard to do a longitudinal analysis, and a lot of studies go to perceptions and qualitative responses rather than hard data. So our advice in the documents that we published just last week is, in the absence of strong evidence about the positive uses, that it would be prudent to take a cautious approach to the amount of time that is spent using educational technology and AI in classroom settings, and that would be particularly the case for the younger children. Where AI in particular is to be introduced, it should be done in an explicit way and after solid knowledge foundations have already been established amongst the students.
Do you recommend in your report that you avoid entirely the use of AI in the first three years of primary school? If that's right, why stop at that point? Why not longer?

We haven't gone quite so far as to make that the recommendation, but we have suggested that that be a consideration for teachers. The reason is that the teaching happening at that time—when we're just teaching children about how to read and write, which are very complex things to learn—needs to be done in a very particular way, a scientifically based, evidence based way. That involves an expert, the teacher, leading the children through carefully sequenced, explicit instruction where the children get to learn and hear a new concept, see it modelled for them and practise it with the teacher before they move off into independent practice. That takes a while. Reading is really complicated; writing, even more so. If we disrupt that process with very young children, we run the risk that they never firmly establish that foundational knowledge and skills, and that will affect their ability to learn throughout the rest of their schooling and lives.
Is that neuroplasticity?

Exactly. They need to build up the cognitive architecture, and, increasingly, even once they've got beyond those basic skills, they need to be building up knowledge. They need to be accumulating knowledge in their long-term memories so that they can use it in application—in their thinking, problem-solving and critical thinking—throughout their schooling.
Given the importance of this, do you see that there are any gaps in our collection of data or our understanding of the issue that really should be addressed urgently?

Yes. We need to know more about what is happening in classrooms. We need to be able to do some research, set up some experiments and generate the kind of data that just doesn't exist for us at the moment around important questions: How much screen time is too much? At what age is it most appropriate to be implementing? And what is the most effective way to be introducing technologies like AI to children?
Is there any evidence you're aware of that demonstrates that AI becomes beneficial for students in years 3 and 4?

No, I'm not aware of any evidence for that age group. There is some evidence about good uses of AI driven technology for students using tools for tutoring, for catch-up, for multi-tiered interventions—systems of support interventions. There is some evidence that it can be useful for those. I have to say the balance of evidence available at the moment, though, points to the harm.
Would I be right in saying that it should only ever be used to augment explicit instruction and other pedagogies to make sure that the student gets the whole—

Yes. The foundational approach should be explicit teaching in the classroom setting. For those students who might need additional intervention, it is possible that there are some technologies' tools that could support that intervention.
Is there any reliable evidence that generative AI improves children's long-term retention of knowledge?
Not that we're aware of. At the moment, there is some evidence to suggest it gets in the way of their long-term retention of knowledge. It can—
At this point in time, are you—sorry?
It can create what we call an illusion of learning, if children are allowed to use—
What was that word you used?
Illusion of learning—if children are allowed to use a tool to produce an assignment, a project, an essay—
That seems to be the outcome of the study done in China.
Yes, really similar findings—exactly.
Yes. The exams didn't show that they had retained the knowledge.
Yes.
Would you therefore support requiring students to complete written assessments on paper?
Written assessments are going to be much more reliable indicators not only of their retention of the curriculum knowledge but also reassuring us that they know how to write.
What is AERO's best estimate of the amount of teaching time lost annually—it's a repeat of it. Don't worry about that. I seem to have a cut-and-paste of some questions on mine. Sorry about that.
Did you use AI to write these, Senator?

I haven't used AI. I've used a very reliable staffer, though I'm not going to throw them under a bus. I might wrap up there because that does conclude my AI questions. I was going to go back to disruption, which I've already covered.
And I do withdraw, because I know you wouldn't have done that.
Can I just say thank you so much for that work. It's very important.
Thank you. That means a lot to my staff.
Thank you, Dr Donovan, on behalf of us all. That was very interesting evidence. You are now free to depart and not return.
I welcome officials who are joining us as part of outcome 1, Early childhood. We'll commence questions. Senator O'Sullivan, you have the call.

I want to ask about safety in child care. The department's website says that Nous Group and KPMG have provided their final reports and advice. Have education ministers now considered those findings, and what decisions have they made in relation to CCTV?
The education ministers will consider the findings from that at their meeting next week.
Will the reports and summaries be made public?
That'll be a decision for education ministers.
Collectively?
Collectively, yes.
Turning to how CCTV is used in practice, did the assessment examine whether services routinely review the footage or generally access it only after a complaint, injury or other concern?
Without going to the content of what was in there, I'll get Mr Moon and Ms Hill—
What do we know about the practice?
to talk about the scope of services and who and what. To the extent that we can answer the question without disclosing what's in the report, we will do so.

As Ms Crane has said, the national assessment has studied a range of things in terms of the usage of CCTV in early childhood centres. That does include many factors such as technical standards, placement, whether things are reviewed routinely or post-incident and other matters concerning how the technology in the footage and the findings might be used.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: I'm sure everyone saw the Four Corners report on Monday night. I know, Minister, you were in it, and you were shown that horrible footage. Let's face it, it was very hard viewing to see that poor child abused in that way over such a long period of time. It should be said that was obviously terrible, and I hope that the child's going okay. The CCTV footage captured that abuse, and that footage was vital in the evidence, but it did not stop the abuse from happening. Do you accept that CCTV can document abuse without necessarily preventing it from happening or identifying it promptly?

Again, setting aside the assessment and what might have been in that process, I think the commentary that's been made around CCTV today from a range of players, including academics, the sector and ministers themselves, goes to there being a range of things in place to support child safety. To your point, the fact that CCTV is in place may not necessarily prevent an incident. It may deter somebody from doing something, and certainly in the tragic case that was shown there, it did not prevent that from happening.
Should there be a system for regularly reviewing CCTV footage to identify potential abuse rather than waiting until a complaint or a warning sign is raised before anyone checks it?

That would be going to a matter of opinion from our side, so we can't talk on that. But, as Mr Moon has indicated, the assessment did go to some of those matters and when it's reviewed and when it's not.

Minister, I'll ask the question to you then. Is the government considering changing the way that CCTV would be used so that it's regularly reviewed and not just acted upon when there's a complaint so that it's a more of a deterrent than just a way of recording instances?

As you said, that was a really horrific incident—we've all seen the footage of it—and it should never have happened. Of course—very briefly, Senator—the person who committed those offences is in jail. The service is closed. The funding was cut. In relation to CCTV, what I hear and see when I visit services, talk to educators and review the practices in services myself, and what I think we could see from the expose on Four Corners, is that CCTV itself is not a substitute for active supervision. There were many issues in that particular incident, but the fact that there was no active supervision of what was occurring in that room really is the issue. When it comes to whether CCTV can assist in helping to keep children safe and how we can better use it, including the question you raised about review, my general approach would be that we have a body of work coming to us. It's coming to us next week. We should all, and will, as education ministers, consider that work.

I suppose if CCTV were reviewed, the very fact that there wasn't active supervision would be revealed by the CCTV footage showing that there wasn't the active supervision. Do you know what I mean? It's not just the CCTV capturing harm perpetrated but also the improper practices of a centre in not complying with the requirement to provide active supervision. So it goes further than that. I'm happy for you to respond but I'm also happy to move on.

In response to question on notice SQ26-000699, the department said it 'does not hold or have access to' data on the prevalence of child abuse and neglect in early childhood education settings. Without that information, how is it possible for the government to measure whether its child safety measures, including the CCTV assessment, are actually improving outcomes for children?

The question as it was asked and as we've responded goes to a range of things in the early childhood system that aren't part of the data—not just that we don't hold it but that it doesn't exist. From recollection, in the last hearing, when we talked about some of this, we said the actual information, when it becomes available, is often made available to law enforcement before it's made available to regulators or others. When it comes to the measures that ministers have endorsed and that we are implementing at the moment, they are a suite of measures. When we're looking at the effectiveness of those, some of them go to, again, uplifting the quality and capability and understanding around child safety. The child safety training goes to that. There's the use of CCTV. The assessment goes to that. We've got the worker register. All of those measures individually address one part of what might have been a particular issue identified and raised either through the child safety review that was undertaken by ACECQA or through other actions that are there. Collectively, the implementation of those and the active monitoring of those are what's uplifting both the quality and the safety that we'd expect in that.

And thank you for that. My question really goes to this: if you're not, though, getting the data, how can you measure whether or not you've made those interventions that you talk about—good interventions—and whether or not they're having the desired impact that we all want?
In terms of the data—
Why can't we collect that data? Why would you not collect that?

It's certainly not data that we would collect as a matter of course. As a department, as an example, we have the right to collect information for the purpose of administering the childcare subsidy system. That information is gathered around a family, a parent, their income—things like that. From a provider's perspective, we gather information around fitness, propriety and their ability to actually administer childcare subsidy dollars. For the sorts of data that you're talking about, the regulators would have access to some of it—states and territories. But, for a not insignificant portion, as I said in previous testimony, actually federal police or state police or others would have access to it. I understand in other hearings there have been conversations about information sharing. That is certainly an active conversation that is happening across Commonwealth departments and with states and territories, but at the moment the information is certainly not available to the department, and it's not available collectively to any one of those individuals that I mentioned.

Minister, on Four Corners, you said:

There has been a reckoning in this system over the past 12 months, and it is changing in no small part because of the way in which you have shone a light on the problems in early learning.

Given that the department has said that it does not hold or have access to national data on the prevalence of abuse and neglect, what information is the government using to identify problems across the sector, and how does it ensure that those problems come to light without a media investigation?
I think there are a few different streams of answer to that. I know you like short answers, but it's a big and important topic.
I'm happy for you to explore it, if you can be direct, though, to the question.

I think there are a few things. One is that the reforms that we've put in place, which were recommended to us to keep children safe, are on track and on time. There's a body of work around what the recommendations were, whether we are implementing them and whether they are on track and on time, and all of that information is publicly available. Then there's a whole body of work around information that is available on issues in services which is published, as I think you would be aware, by ACECQA, but which we have also made available, as part of the reforms that we've made, to parents so that they have information about what is going on in their services.

In relation to the particular offenders that you're talking about there—particularly the really horrific sorts of offences that we've seen—I am briefed from time to time, as we know, from the AFP, and what the AFP said to me in the last briefing that I had with them is effectively that the changes that we're putting in place are breaking the business model of these sorts of perpetrators. Because some time ago there was, if you like, something of a revolving door of people coming in and out of the sector. There was really high workforce turnover, and that was a significant problem. The pay rise that we've put in place which stabilises the sector is incredibly important to that. It's not always seen as a safety measure, but it is foundational to keeping children safe.

If you consider what now occurs in early learning services because of the reforms that we've put in place, if you're this sort of perpetrator, according to advice from the AFP, not only do you need to be qualified and apply for a position in a service, you will now be on a register—which is the first ever register, of course, of early childhood educators—which allows regulators to track movements across the service. Every single person that you're working with and alongside will have been trained to recognise you and the behaviours that you are exhibiting in that service. These are difficult issues to talk about, but you will not be able to have a device with you in that service. They are so often implicated in these sorts of offences. Your provider will have triple the penalties that they had before for any breach, which puts providers on notice.

So I am really confident that the reforms that we have put in place are the right reforms. They're on track. They're working. The data that we do have says that more services than ever are meeting and exceeding the national quality standards, which is important data, but we would never say that it's job done. We'd never say that the work is done.
No, and I'm not hearing you say that.
We always need to do more to keep children safe.
Senator O'Sullivan, I'm mindful that we've got a number of senators seeking the call. I'm going to rotate now, but I'll come back to you after this rotation. Senator Hodgins-May.

I also want to acknowledge the horrific headlines that families and educators, many of whom are doing the right thing, woke to and are still reeling from and acknowledge that we're 18 months on from the original story—or stories. Despite the safety reforms, we are still seeing these harrowing headlines. It's a great tragedy. Minister, you said you've committed to reform, but can you explain to us how a worker studying towards a qualification can be left alone with babies?

This is part of the work that is being done by education ministers at the moment. This horrific incident at Injinoo occurred in 2024, before education ministers stood up and made the reforms that we have made. We have asked for a review into how working towards qualifications applies and the circumstances where it may apply. That review is under way. We'll be updated on it at—I think, Ms Crane—the next education ministers meeting. It's an important part of the work. In relation to that particular incident, though, Senator, I would go back to comments I made to Senator O'Sullivan and say that that service had responsibilities to ensure that that child was adequately supervised, and that child was clearly not adequately supervised.
Do you think that a review is enough if children are potentially being harmed right now? Will you commit to exploring an end to that provision, and shouldn't that be very urgent?

There is a body of work going on around adequate supervision in early childhood education settings. I think there can be a place for some educators in some settings to be working towards their qualifications, but those circumstances need to be very clearly specified, and they should only ever be used if the service can guarantee that adequate supervision of children is occurring. The review of the working towards qualifications provision is also part of a broader body of work on ensuring that children are adequately supervised at all times and that providers understand their obligations to do that.
Can I confirm that the next education ministers meeting is on Monday?
Yes.
That's correct.

You told the Four Corners program that 120 services had been put on notice by this government and that 12 had lost Commonwealth funding, yet Little Zak's—Four Corners identified enforcement actions at more than half of its centres over the past two years—does not appear on the Commonwealth enforcement register. How bad does something have to get at a large provider before the Commonwealth decides to intervene?
Senator, was that question to us—the department?
Both of you.

As you know, the close working relationship between the state regulators and the Commonwealth is important around some of this work. Some state regulators have taken action independently, as they should. Mr Moon can probably talk about that in terms of the work that we're doing and particularly the point you've raised about its serious nature. Also, the work that we're doing on unannounced spot checks will probably help around some of that stuff. Mr Moon.

I'll come to the nub of your question to start with and then I'll expand on some of the other activities. The intervention work that we do isn't always enforcement action. By that, I mean that enforcement action is a specific action taken under the act where there is a decision taken or a sanction imposed, and they meet the publishing powers under the Act. In the case of the action taken that you talked about in terms of the 127 notices, they were conditions placed on the provider's approval—to meet a certain requirement by a certain timeframe. In most cases, it was a six-month period in which those services were required to meet quality area 2 and attain a rating of meeting NQS. That's 127 services who we've issued conditions on. Inclusive of that, 65 of those services are now meeting the national quality standard, 80 have reached the timeframe in terms of what they were required to do, and we're taking further action on the 12 that remain. Within that, there are some services that are no longer approved. In addition to that, we've taken other actions that don't meet those publishing requirements, and they range from having very serious sit-down conversations with chairs of boards and CEOs, where we will talk about their track record and performance and show comparative information about how they're performing as compared to others and what market norms look like.

We've done a whole host of work with state and territory regulators, so a lot of the work that we have done has partnered with the states and territories to have a look at the combined picture, both in terms of the childcare subsidy risk and the risk in terms of what quality and safety across the National Quality Framework looks like, and additionally, what that risk profile looks like across jurisdictions. At times, it's difficult to ascertain the national risk of a provider because of the jurisdictional nature of the regulatory environment. What we've done over the last 12 or 18 months—nearly two years now—is bring that much more closely together. So we're having more conversations in a combined group, with large childcare providers with all of the jurisdictions in which they have services and the Australian government, to talk about where our concerns are and what change we need to see. I might leave it there.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Thank you for all of that information, but I do think it needs to be said that Little Zak's has a staff turnover rate of about 79 per cent and at least 25 staff ratio breaches in 2025. Only About Children is another large, for-profit chain, with enforcement actions at 27 per cent of its centres over the past two years, yet it also doesn't appear on the list. Other large chains are missing, I would say, too, and I'm just wanting to know—perhaps from you, Minister. Parents are saying these laws have been in place for a year now, so why aren't we seeing these large for-profits get cracked down on?

The government has taken significant action, and, of course, the department has outlined some of that action. In terms of some of the providers that you have spoken about there, I'm advised that regulators have taken enforcement action involving 24 Little Zak's Academy services, and our expectation of these providers is that they meet the standards and that they do everything they can to keep children safe in early learning. I think part of what Mr Moon was saying is that there is more coordination than ever before between the Commonwealth and the state regulators, and both of us have different levers. You mentioned Only About Children. Regulators have taken action across 24 OAC services, including enforcement action at 21 of the services. Again, our expectation is clear: these providers must deliver safe, high-quality early learning. Together, the Commonwealth and—
Do you think, though, that a provider with 25 ratio breaches—
Senator, could you just let the minister finish.

Finally, together, the Commonwealth and the states have put more resources into regulatory action than ever before. A record number of visits are being conducted. Compliance actions have more than doubled. There is a record number of service cancellations. There are thousands of unannounced visits from the Commonwealth, which has never happened before. When we came to office, around 88 per cent, I think, of services met or exceeded the national quality standard. There's been a massive uptick in the last year, and a record 92 per cent of services now meet or exceed the national standards. As a Commonwealth, we've imposed conditions, as Mr Moon said, on 120 services.
But do you think a provider with 25 ratio breaches in one year deserves to keep operating?
I think that all providers, no matter what their ownership structure is, need to deliver safe, quality early learning, need to comply with the law and need to address any failures—
So that would be a no then on that information.

that have been identified. Again, what I can say is that, together, the Commonwealth, states and territories are investing around half a billion dollars in keeping children safe. From the perspective of the Commonwealth, the Commonwealth introduced laws to enable us to cut the Commonwealth childcare subsidy from providers for the first time last year. We are continuing to use those powers. We're using those powers—

Can I draw you back to my question, please, Minister. Do you think it's appropriate for an organisation to continue to operate when it has had 25 ratio breaches in a year? Do you think that parents would have an expectation that that service would be closed down if there were that many breaches over such a short period of time?

Of course, it's incredibly important that providers address all of those breaches. It's important that that information is made public. It's part of the transparency and accountability that we require and that we've ensured that parents have available to them. Again, for the first time, the Commonwealth has the powers to withdraw the Commonwealth childcare subsidy, and we are using those powers, including withdrawing the Commonwealth childcare subsidy from providers who fail to meet our standards.
I've heard you say that; thank you, Minister. Has the department met and spoken directly to the CEO of Little Zak's?

We can't really disclose individual circumstances or information about individual providers. What I can say is that the department regularly speaks with each state and territory regulator, both bilaterally and as a combined group, in a number of forums. In the last couple of years—in fact, it's a little bit longer than that—there's been an acceleration of something called the focused deterrence initiative, which is led out of the states and territories. They will look at poorly performing providers across jurisdictions.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: But is Little Zak's on the list of providers that have been met with?
Again, I'm sorry, I can't talk about individual circumstances.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Minister, you said on Four Corners that you were using powers to stop big chains expanding if they have quality issues and that you had gone after two in particular. You mentioned Edge Early Learning. Which was the other chain?
I am unable to name the other provider, and that is due to the nature of the action that we are taking at present.

Do you understand the distress that parents are already in and how that can be exacerbated by knowing that there's a centre that is being investigated but that there is no certainty provided to families across Australia about which centre that is? That process doesn't necessarily bring them a sense of comfort—simply not knowing which centres are being examined for really serious potential incidents.
I'm unable to name the service because of the nature of the action that we are taking. It is to protect the action that we are taking.
What about protecting families in the meantime?

The action that we're taking is about making sure that early learning services are safe and that these particular services are safe. In terms of families, I think it's really important to know that, if a regulator views a service as immediately unsafe, it will be closed immediately. That is what happens when regulators find services that they think are posing an immediate threat to children, as families would expect. So I can assure families that the way in which the Commonwealth, the states and the territories are working together on regulation means that services that are immediately unsafe will be closed immediately. What we are trying to do and what we are doing with the regulatory action that we are taking is putting providers on notice that they stand to lose their Commonwealth childcare subsidy if they don't improve their standards. We are driving higher standards in the sector. We are seeing that both in the regulatory data that we have and also in the outcomes, with more services than ever moving from a rating of 'working towards the national quality standards' to a rating of 'meeting and exceeding the national quality standards'.
I'm returning the call to Senator O'Sullivan.

On 13 July, Hamish Tait was publicly named while facing 329 charges, with police alleging 136 victims. The AFP established the Operation Moonbi webpage to provide parents with information about his employment history, support services and who to contact. At the time, I could not find anywhere a public statement from you, Minister, or a post directing parents to that information at all. What I did find, however, was a post from you on your social media about Mr Tickle and other characters. I'm happy to table this if required.
Yes, circulate it.

I don't know if you are able to see the comments on that post, but it was overwhelmed by parents who were quite distressed at the insensitivity of your post and your lack of action and communication in relation to directing parents to a trusted page on an AFP website that gave parents information around the employment history of Mr Tait. Did you read any of those comments, Minister?
I'm aware of the post that you're talking about, but it is true that I don't generally read comments on my social media posts.

Why did you choose not to make any public statement about one of the most serious instances of child sexual abuse in a childcare centre over many, many years? Why did you choose not to make a comment about that but just simply went to talk about a release of Mr Tickle resources that the government is providing?

I can go through some of the matters relating to Mr Tait. I understand that it was on 13 July that the AFP released the media statement outlining the offences and establishing the local contact point which was set up with New South Wales. I think the communication with families on these sorts of matters, as we've canvassed in this committee previously in relation to the Victorian serial offender, is generally done in liaison with local state services, and I think this local contact point was in that category of having been established with New South Wales. From my perspective, the work that we have done on keeping children safe over the last year has never been done before. We have made the biggest changes to the National Quality Framework that have ever been made since it was introduced. There is half a billion dollars of investment going in across the country to help keep children safe.

During the week that you're talking about, education ministers met yet again to talk about how we can work together to strengthen safety and quality. Ministers were updated on the progress of the reforms that we delivered—reforms that were introduced through education ministers in a bipartisan way and with the support of the then shadow minister Senator Duniam the year prior, in August. What I have been focused on every day is the important work of helping to keep children safe in early learning. It really is my view, Senator, that this line of questioning is an unfortunate line of questioning, because apparently until now the opposition has taken a bipartisan-support approach on working on these matters of safety in early childhood education and care.
There is no question of our support for those measures. Minister, I'd draw—
We're focused on doing the work.

On a point of order, the minister is taking up enormous amounts of time in answering this question. I asked a very direct question, and I'll ask it again if it assists so that I can get a direct response. Minister, you are the minister responsible for early learning, are you not?
Early childhood education, yes.
So why did you decide not to provide any response at all to the announcement, to the media reporting, of this case?

I think the response that I have made as Minister and that the government has made is to introduce the biggest changes to the National Quality Framework that have ever been made and to make sure that those changes are on track and are on time. What we're focused on is doing the work every day to help keep children safe.

I take exception to your accusation that we are not united in ensuring that the protection of children and the measures that need to be taken are absolutely paramount. I'm going to the point that the community, parents—there is a massive distrust and a breakdown of trust in early learning and child care in this country, and we need to do everything together to make sure that that trust is rebuilt. I commend all of the work, and I go to great lengths to commend all the work, that providers and individual childcare educators and workers are doing to address those issues. My question is: why did you not provide any public statement related to this terrible case of abuse? And do you not think that it was insensitive that the next thing you posted online was about Mr Tickle?

I don't have my week's posting in terms of what I posted online that week, around the middle of July, in general. But what I would say is that the communication with families about these sorts of incidents is incredibly important. The AFP has a particular approach to the way they do it. I do think that when it comes to communicating with families about specific types of incidents and offences that that job is best done, as it was in Victoria, by the people who are standing up the operation to support families. What the AFP does, of course—and I know you wouldn't dispute this, and I'm not in any way suggesting that you would, Senator—is extraordinary work. We all support the work they do in communicating with the families of potential victims they've identified and then going about their work to identify further services where these alleged perpetrators have also worked. When they do that, and when they put that information up online, it is incredibly important that there is local support available, like the local contact point that was set up in New South Wales and like the similar arrangement that was put in place in Victoria to support families through these incredibly challenging times. So my evidence is that it is the AFP and the local contact points who are best placed to communicate with families.

When it comes to the broader focus of the government on helping to keep children safe, we are doing the right reforms. The reforms are on track. We are transparent about the reforms. Public reporting about the reforms is available. And of course families can access more information than they ever could before because of the reforms that we've made.

One of the reforms that has been introduced is the online training modules for educators. It's important that that's there, so I commend you for that. But I did ask you in last estimates whether you'd seen the modules and whether you, Minister, had undertaken them. Since then, have you remedied that problem and gone and had a look at the training and possibly even completed it yourself?
I have taken the advanced training and the foundational training.
How long did it take you?
In terms of logging on and doing the training?
Yes.
It takes a few hours to do each one.

Yes, it's about half a day. Since then, courses 3 and 4 have been released, followed by course 5, 'Leading and governing child safety'. Have you been able to review that content? Have you been able to complete that training at all?

I have completed the advanced training. There is a module that is for people who have management responsibility that was released at the start of September or during September. I'm yet to do that final module.
I haven't done the final one yet, either, so I'll let you off on that one!
We can do it together, Senator!

I'm happy to. I'll come to your office and we'll do it. It does take about half a day, I'm told, to complete that. I think it's a worthy investment of staff, and of course they're required to do it, but it's important that it gets done. There were issues—and this is a question for the department—in feedback I've received that it's easy to just skip through the video modules and then just do the questionnaire at the end. You can get it wrong and just go back and repeat it. So in a way you can truncate the amount of time it takes to complete the course, even by just going through the questionnaire at the end and doing it multiple times so that eventually you'll get it right. Is that being looked at? Can that be resolved?

After the last hearing, we went back and worked with Queensland as the contract managers and ACCP as the content holders. If the question is, 'Have we stopped people from being able to go through in a particular period of time?' the answer is no because the content is intended to be done at a user's pace.
And you don't want to make it clumsy, either.
Exactly.
I get that.

Correct. We did a couple of things. One, we looked at the data for, at that stage, the courses that were there to get a sense of whether what you were hearing something that was prevalent. It was not—the vast majority of users took the same amount of time you took or much longer, because you can start and stop. We also looked at whether, for anybody going through it particularly quickly, they were registered at a service or not. We are talking extremely small numbers. That information has been shared with states and territories so that, in their visits to particular providers or services, they can have that conversation. But, overall, the feedback about the training itself, including those new courses that you talked about, has been overwhelmingly positive—about the content, whether it's uplifted knowledge and capability, and whether people would refer it to colleagues. We've seen quite a good uptake of that foundation course that you referred to, with over 418,000 completions. For the first two courses of the advanced, we've got over 142,000 completions, and for that last, advanced course module, which has a more targeted audience, there were almost 22,000 completions as at yesterday. So there has been a good take-up and very positive feedback about the content and what it's doing.

My experience and the feedback I've heard is that it's a more engaging experience for people in those later modules. Would you go back and revise—if there was any feedback about how you could improve module 1, is there a chance to go back and revisit that as new staff members come on board? I take it new staff are required to do it.

New staff are required to do it, and in a much shorter timeframe. The ACCP, through the development of each of those courses, has taken on board feedback from the sector as it's been developed and research.
Yes, you can tell that.

So, yes, feedback has been taken on board. Apart from the courses that are being delivered now, there is a refresher that will come as well. The feedback has been on the course content and the delivery of the content itself, and of course the crux of this is actually being able to put it into practice. The bit that we probably haven't spoken as much about here is that this is supported by a community of practice, so the intent is that individuals do it individually or collectively but talk about what this means in practice in that site. All of those elements are what make a very good course and content.

I have a final question on this and we can move on. Some of the feedback I've had is that some providers would like to be able to include it as part of their training management systems, and there's an issue with being able to easily plug that into their existing system. There's a bit of duplication that providers are having to deal with—including, of course, the educators themselves. Is that something that can be resolved?

No. The decision has been taken that it will not be shared in that way. Part of the concern with that is about the integrity of it and the data, so it is hosted in one place. It is centrally owned, managed and controlled.
Could an API or something that enables the completion of those courses be fed into it?
In that respect, the completion—
I'm saying not necessarily the content but the completion of the—
We will be looking at that component in some of the future iterations of the register.
Thanks.
Senator Dolega.

I would like to get an update on the new services recently announced for Devonport and, in addition to that, the six additional services for Tasmania, the amount of Commonwealth funding that will be included and how many places it's going to deliver for the community.
We're talking about the Building Early Education Fund and the six projects, as you said, including two election commitments in Tasmania. Mr Smyth, I'll hand to you.

In Tasmania we have three election commitments. Westbury Primary School is $5 million for 36 places. Huonville Primary School is $5 million for 130 places; additional, I think, is around 45 for that particular service. The other election commitment is Devonport Childcare Centres, which is Malangenna. That is in the process of negotiation. The other two were finalised through Federation Funding Agreements with the Tasmanian government. This is actually a grant, and we've issued grant guidelines. Malangenna have responded. We're in the process now of negotiating the grant agreement. We haven't reached a final conclusion yet. It also relies on land transfer from Tasmanian TAFE to the operator as well. We hope to conclude that over the coming weeks.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: It's a fantastic place. The early childhood education minister visited there with Anne Urquhart not long ago. It was absolutely fantastic to have the minister down. Any other centres or opportunities for Tasmania at the moment?

Yes, there are a number of others. There's St Marys, which is a $4 million commitment for 24 places; Rosetta, a $5 million commitment for 36 places; Bruny Island, $3½ million for 20 places; and Bothwell, which is a $3 million commitment for 20 places.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: Fantastic. When can we expect these to be delivered, and when can families expect to see these additional places in the community?

Our expectation at this point is that Bruny Island is the first one, to be delivered in September next year. Then, following that, we have two expected to open in March of 2028, Westbury and Huonville. Then, in September 2028, St Marys, Rosetta and Bothwell.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: Fantastic. That is all I have for that one. Thank you very much.
Ms Cotching just had one point to raise as well.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: There is also one project we recently announced in Trevallyn, in Launceston in Tasmania, through our large grants funding round as well, which we've just announced with Goodstart, who is our recipient from our large grants funding round.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Building Early Education Fund

text: Fantastic. Thank you very much. Thanks, Minister, for your work in Tassie as well.
Can I ask just one follow-up question just in relation to that? I had a visit recently to Weipa in Far North Queensland.
I know Weipa very well.

You know Weipa very well. It's an extraordinarily remote town. It's also an extremely important town in terms of the support it provides to the bauxite mining operations in Weipa, which are conducted by Rio Tinto. They had a single childcare service that was unable to be continued. So you've now got a town with quite a reasonable population with so many working parents, including amazing women in the mining industry, some of whom I've met, who don't have child care available. It's actually having an impact in terms of people's lives, being able to work and continue generating the economic wealth which my state and the country depends upon. To what extent is the department looking at other regional and remote centres around Australia, where there's this desperate need for child care? I'm giving a plug to Weipa here as an example.

Sure. Obviously, one of the criteria for BEEF is looking at childcare deserts, rural and remote, and we can give you stats around that. BEEF is particularly focused on new services—additional services on top of existing services.
What if there's no service? Say there's an existing service and it's closed down.

To the point you've raised about Weipa, I'm not aware of that issue particularly, but it doesn't mean we can't at least talk to the Queensland government around that. I'm just not aware of the particular circumstance that you've raised.
Mr Cook, I'll contact the wonderful mayor of the Weipa Town Authority and get some further detail and provide that to you.
Yes, that'd be useful.
Literally, I spoke to wonderful women in the mining industry—and we're trying to get more women into the mining industry—who were telling me how difficult it is.
It'd be useful to know why they closed. Any of that information that would help us understand.
It's a remote site. It's a remote place.
It is, but it's a moderately big remote place compared to some other remote places we've got.

Yes. I think it'd be a beautiful place to live, and everyone tells me anyone who leaves Weipa inevitably comes back to Weipa. It has especially got a wonderful caravan park for people to visit during the dry season.
If it was because they couldn't get staff—they're the sorts of things we'd need to know.
Yes. I'll get the local town authority to pull some material together and provide it to you.
That'd be useful. Thanks.
Back to you, Senator O'Sullivan.
It's a good question Senator Scarr was asking and a good segue to the topic that I now want to raise.
It wasn't coordinated.
It wasn't at all. Great minds!
I think we all knew that.

ELACCA, the Early Learning and Care Council of Australia, report that their members closed 152 long-day-care centres between 2024 and, year to date, 2026 and identified a further 276 services at risk of closure over the next 12 months. That's 221 long-day-care services and 55 preschool and kindergarten services. These figures are drawn from the 13 ELACCA members rather than a national census. I don't have access to national figures. On the Four Corners report, Minister, you said the government was seeing record service cancellations, with 600 reported in the last period. What does that figure refer to, which reporting period does it cover and how many were service closures by state regulators versus Commonwealth funding withdrawals? That could be for the department.

There are a couple of different issues there and a couple of different data points. The 600 service cancellations, I understand, were by state and territory regulators, but we can probably also assist with information about service closures in general and the number of additional services in the last period as well.

We don't have access to the data that you're referring to, so the information that we will talk about comes out of what is the ACECQA reporting. The first thing I'll say is we don't have disaggregated data, so what we'll talk about will be at national or state level where we can. That data is owned by states and territories, so for anything lower we'd need to seek their approval and authority to discuss. If we look at the 2025-26 financial year, there were 494 service closures in that period. Over the same period of time, there were 734 new services that were approved. That kind of number, where more services are opening than closing, is a repeated pattern over a number of financial years. That's not just a one-off in that sense. I'll hand over to Mr Moon, who has some of that other data.
Can you reconcile that 600 figure?
We've got this by financial year. Chances are that's probably calendar-year information, but we'll take that on notice.
Take it on notice; that's perfectly fine.
Yes.
Sorry. Were you going to say something else?
No, that's alright. Mr Moon is ready to go.

If it's helpful, I can provide a little bit of historical information about the number of cancellations and new provider approvals. One quick caveat is we will generally look at what we call the national law cancellations and approvals. Because of the dual regulatory system, there are two factors here. The first is a service has to be approved under the national law before it can be approved for the childcare subsidy. The second is for a cancellation. Often—in fact, most often—a cancellation is first enacted under the national law, and then the childcare subsidy cancellation takes effect under something called an operation-of-law cancellation. In the 2022-23 financial year, there were 455 closures compared to 832 new service approvals; in the 2023-24 financial year, there were 391 closures compared to 799 new service approvals; in the 2024-25 financial year, there were 436 closures compared to 783 new service approvals; and, in the 2025-26 financial year, as Ms Crane said, there were 494 closures compared to 734 new service approvals.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Do you have data on permanent closures of early childhood education and care services?
Senator, those are permanent closures.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: They're all permanent?

Again, I'm a regulator, so I will always caveat. That is where a service provider has permanently closed a service. It doesn't go to say that the physical building won't at some point in the future be used again for child care, but it will be shut down at that point.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: I have a line of questions here which I'll put on notice for the sake of time. Does the department track where closures are occurring—for example, in metropolitan, regional or rural and remote areas—and identify communities where families have few or no alternative services? This is to Senator Scarr's example.

We can get remoteness classification around that data that we talked about to understand whether the bulk of this has happened in metro areas or others. Certainly of the ones that we have seen in the last 12 months, the vast majority of closures have been in areas where there is existing capacity elsewhere in other services. So it would be an area that you might hear the sector or others talk about. It has been oversupplied, in that sense. There are places there to take. That's not to say that is in 100 per cent of cases. Yes, we are aware of some areas where there hasn't been something else. Depending on what the reason is for a service looking to close—and this is a before-it-happens piece—there are programs that the department has and will work with the provider and states and governments around sustainability funding and the like. Where it is an individual business decision and they are shutting doors, we might work with states and territories around what other offerings might be there. In some instances—which we've spoken about previously in this forum—other service delivery means that we are trying to explore in-venue care or family day care capability trial, where we are looking particularly at those areas where centre based day care in and of itself may not be the viable option, which may be one of the reasons why it closed, and other forms of care may be appropriate.
Did you get a report? Is there any information sharing back to you in relation to why the service closed? Is that collated?
They certainly have to give us notification beforehand. Is the reason mandatory?
I'm relatively confident there is information on the notification of closure form. But, Senator, just so that I don't mislead, we'll take it on notice and bring back exactly what information we have.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: I'm keen to understand whether it was financial pressures, low enrolments, workforce shortages, voluntary closure or regulatory action—those sorts of responses.
We can certainly look to get it for you.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Does the department monitor services or providers at risk of closure?

Senator, when you say 'at risk of closure', what we would have visibility of and what gets talked about most predominantly is financial viability. In financial viability, we have the large provider recording—which Mr Moon can talk about—which was implemented quite a number of years ago, for exactly that reason, to look particularly at the large providers and what might be generating behind that or if there's anything at risk. We do not get that same data from small or medium providers.

I go back to ELACCA's report which says there are 276 services at risk of closure. Do you get intel from the sector as to their status and how viable they are? I'm hearing across the country, particularly now in metropolitan and urban areas, that viability is a problem because of oversupply of service providers. So occupancy rates are low. Some are reporting operating at about 50 per cent. I don't run a childcare centre, but I'd imagine that it would be pretty hard to be viable and continue. Do you get that sort of intel so that you've got a bit of a desktop dashboard of the state of the sector?

Anecdotal information, yes. I wouldn't go so far as to say that it's anything that would even be a desktop-worthy piece. We have a sector stakeholder group that we meet with regularly. Through that and other correspondence or meetings, we will hear about certain things in certain parts of the sector or certain parts of the country, depending on what is happening. So, to that extent, yes. Nothing as rigorous as what you have described in the ELACCA information that you have.
Can I keep going, Chair?
Yes.

I'll just move to a slightly different track. The department's factsheet says that BEEF is expected to support around 160 new or expanded services and deliver around 12,000 additional places. Does that remain the government's current estimate?

The answer is yes, noting that it's in two components. The first $500 million is what we're working on now. The second $500 million is part of the business case that's being developed at the moment. We're still in the first $500 million, and that's the 48.
When will all those places be operating?

It's going to take a number of years, obviously, for construction of a number of those sites, and we are yet to finalise grant agreements through our ACCO round, our small-scale round and our large-scale round. We intend to maximise the full $500 million to build as many services as possible. The funding that we have runs until 2028-29, so we are trying to get as many sites as possible. Certainly the 160 number is a target that we're working towards. At the moment, I think we're actually doing pretty well in relation to how we're tracking against that.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: What's the net additional number? If services are closing, there are a number of places that have been lost as a result of those closures. You've got 12,000 additional places. What's the net addition?
That's outside of BEEF. The additional we're talking about is the 12,000 for BEEF.
I guess I'm talking about the aggregate. There's 12,000 for BEEF; I get that.

The other bit is a bit hard for us because new services will be opening which aren't related to this program. For-profit and not-for-profit services will be opening. We don't have a forecast of what that looks like. We can look at an average, I guess. We know on average there are about 700 or so new services opening at the moment per year. But we just don't have that data, Senator, I'm sorry.

Sure. But we hear that there's this sort of trading almost. You've got services closing; you've got services opening. Media announcements say there are 12,000 additional places as a result of BEEF. What's the net addition? If you take into account those that are closing—how many?

I'll start and let the department help with the numbers that you want. There are two different issues there. The Building Early Education Fund is entirely focused on areas that are underserved, unserved and disadvantaged. The effort there is to build services where they are really needed. Mr Smyth can talk about that, if he would like to, around the criteria that is used to identify those places where those numbers of services have a really big impact. You're also looking at the overall numbers in the sector. As you pointed out, Senator, there are some areas of oversupply. Again, I'll just give the top-line numbers, and then you can explore them as you would like with me or others. I think in the last year, as has been discussed, there were 734 new services and 494 surrendered or cancelled.

One of the other policy responses that I think are important to talk about is the potential for an early education commission, which is a matter that's coming to education ministers next week. We can see from all of the discussion that we're having here right now that there are areas that are underserved and there are areas that are oversupplied. We're seeing that play out. We think a commission could assist with better strategic planning of the kind that we're talking about.
Senator, if you want to put this question, you can, because I know that was a partial answer. Then we were going to the department, and then I was going to rotate at that point.
I'm happy to come back.
Yes, or I can do it at this point. I know the department was going to provide some data. Did you want me to rotate?
I'm sure I'll want to explore their answer.
We found the number. I'm sorry. I was grappling with it. Approved childcare places have increased by 25,000 places from June 2025 to June 2026.
Thank you.

I'll come back to you. I'm coming to you now, Senator Hodgins-May. I'm just drawing the committee's attention to the program. We are breaking at 3.45, which is when we are due to conclude early childhood. We'll obviously continue whilst there are still questions, but I just draw your attention to the fact that both parties have requested all of the agencies seeing us for the rest of the day, and we do need to get to them as well. Senator Hodgins-May.
We know that around 70 per cent of the sector is for profit. We've established that. Minister, can you please explain what your government is doing to change the composition beyond the BEEF.

Thank you, Senator. Around 70 per cent of early learning services are operated by for-profit providers. It's important, I think, to note that the majority of those for-profit providers are small providers that are family owned and are independent, and a proportion of those services are larger corporate providers. We are, as you know, focused on supporting the not-for-profit sector. You asked me not to talk about the BEEF, but, of course, the Building Early Education Fund is only available to not-for-profit services. We, of course, could talk more about that.

More broadly, we are exploring and taking opportunities to support not-for-profits to expand where we see them. An important and recent example of that would be the support that we've provided to Goodstart Early Learning in relation to its bid to take over a number of Edge Early Learning services. Edge Early Learning is a provider that I have described as having significant compliance issues. It's a provider that was impacted by our Commonwealth regulatory action and went into voluntary administration, and we are focused on supporting Goodstart to take over as many services as is practicable to provide not-for-profit learning to those children.

Minister, what about those ones that are actively closing? I'm thinking of, for example, Uniting Merri-bek back home in Victoria, who have had to fight against closure despite multiple for-profit centres opening in that same area of the community. Thank you for letting us know about Goodstart, but is there anything beyond the BEEF happening for those smaller community run centres that are feeling immense pressure due to oversaturation, often, of the for-profits in those areas?

I have a couple of things there. One, of course, is the CCCF funding that we provide to support the viability of services, many of which are smaller community and not-for-profit services. We concluded a round of $106 million of support to a range of services to assist with their viability. You mentioned your example there—and it's one that I don't have particular background on, but I heard how you described it, and I've seen ABC reporting about it as well—and what you've described is a situation where there's a long-running community or not-for-profit service and there's siting of larger for-profits around. You cited a situation where that may affect the viability. Again, I don't have information about that particular circumstance, but we can certainly see that, in some areas, there is oversupply, and we are starting to see the implications of that over supply, particularly in the viability of those services who do the additional siting around services that already exist. As I have said, we are interested in whether an early childhood education commission could assist with providing a better basis for coordination for the Commonwealth and states and territories, who have different responsibilities in relation to coordination, and we see a need for better stewardship of those approaches to make sure that we can better match supply to where it is needed.

I'd be very happy to facilitate an introduction with those families fighting to keep their much-loved centre open if there was interest in doing so. I'm going to pick up on your point around the CCF. In particular, I want to draw the department's attention to a question on notice, SQ26-000703.
Just to confirm, this is the one about applications for childcare viability?

Expenditure figures under the Community Child Care Fund. The department has provided expenditure figures under the Community Child Care Fund up until financial year 2024-25. Expenditure has been falling over the last three-year period, and I also note that, in the last two years, you haven't expended the appropriation of $4 million that I was told is available under this fund. First of all, are the 2025-26 figures available now?

I believe your question is about the 2025-26 CCCF special circumstances grant round. As you said, yes, we have $4 million in special appropriation available. We actually paid in the 2025-26 year $2.8 million to services for the year, and I've got the breakdown on a state basis if you're interested.

Are you able to explain why the department is not spending that entire $4 million? It seems like a fairly modest amount in the first place if we've got community centres closing down basically everywhere and if you are committed to keeping those not-for-profits open, as you say.
It's a grant process that stays open for the full 12 months of every year. We can accept a grant application that addresses the special circumstances grant criteria at any time in a 12-month period.
The financial year is finished now though.

We've got different types of programs under CCCF. We've just concluded a competitive round 4 grant process. The special appropriation round of $4 million is an annual round that stays open every year.
So it's not operating on financial years?
It operates on a financial year.
We just need people to apply for it. We've allocated $2 million or so for the people who have applied for it so far.

The figures that I gave the secretary were for the 2025-26 year. In the 2026-27 year we've currently received 25 applications to date. A number of those have been assessed, and we've got about 15 applications that are working their way through the process of assessment currently.
In the previous financial year, none of that $4 million was expended. Is that because people didn't make applications for that money?
That's right.
That went through the process.

Were they notified? If a centre is closing, is the department notifying them about that potential? Do you have any information on why those applications aren't going in? You said there were 26 applications already in this financial year. Do you have the figures for how many applications were made in those earlier financial years?

To add to Ms Hinds's statement before, the special circumstances stream is quite specific. As Ms Hinds said, you have to apply for funding through the process. It's really about those services that are experiencing unforeseen or specific events. We find that the pool of applicants for that type of funding is a bit narrower than it might be through our open competitive round, which is the round that has just opened and closed. So it's a separate stream within the overarching CCCF.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Quality, Workforce and Stewardship

text: In terms of the number of applications that were received and those that were approved, do you have those figures?
We never took that on notice. I don't think we've gone back, by the looks of it. I haven't got any historical data with me. We're happy to take that on notice.
If we're not spending $4 million—it sounds like, as I said, such a modest amount of money. Are those conditions specific, and are they all available for us to look at?

The criteria are relatively flexible. They talk about an unforeseen or unexpected circumstance where, if there were to be a closure of that service, there would be a market failure. Often it's the sole provider. An example would be an extreme weather event. The grants don't preclude other special unforeseen events.

On notice, could you please provide applications made, supported or denied, but also the number of community-run centres, in particular those that closed on those years. That would be useful information.

To your question around how people know about this, all of this information is available on the department's website, and it is provided through the sector newsletter that we have, which we periodically send out as well. This isn't information that's only put up and then taken down. It is available permanently up there.

This is to the Minister, I suppose. You regularly hear about centres that are closing down. Have you told them that there's money that's sitting there that hasn't been spent, with its purpose being to keep these types of centres open? Is that something that concerns you?

We are supporting services with the main CCCF round. Certainly whenever I hear of a service that may face challenges or may have missed out on the substantial CCCF round, I tell them about the special circumstances grant. Obviously, it's important that the department does what Ms Crane has indicated that it do, which is provide that information on a broader scale than I would be able to provide that information.

This particular grant is actually supposed to be a one-off. It's a particular circumstance that just needs a small injection of funding once, effectively. That is the purpose of this grant. All the other CCCF grants are for more of a long-term scenario. This is to help with why perhaps there are not as many people. It's because it's a one-off amount.

Yes, it'd be good to have a bit more data around why, if there are a number of applications being made and how many are being approved. Minister, does the government have a target for the proportion of child care delivered by not-for-profit and public providers?

As I said on Four Corners, which was aired on Monday, the government wants to see more not-for-profit early learning. We're taking a number of steps to do that. The Building Fund Operational Support, as we've described is taking those opportunities where we can, like, for example, supporting Goodstart in securing some of the edge services and continuing to explore how we can support the not-for-profit sector to grow and expand. The main body of work that really underpins next steps in the work that you're talking about there, Senator, that would inform future considerations, including the types of considerations that you're talking about, is the service delivery prices project. That is the foundational piece of work that we are doing to understand the cost of delivering early learning across different provider types, different locations and different cohorts. That is—
I've got more questions about that coming up shortly. It's more about whether there's a target set by government.
That is the work that we need to complete before we make further policy decisions.

I was really hoping to know whether there was a figure yet. I suppose, if government does have this plan to move towards a universal system shaped by community need rather than when commercial operators choose to invest, it seems like a fairly important step to take. Has a department modelled what the provider mix will look like in five or 10 years if current trends continue?
No.
Is that something that you think is potentially worthwhile doing, with a view to moving towards a universal system, as the Prime Minister has indicated?
That would be a matter of opinion.
I'll ask the minister.
You just asked me a question that was very close to that, and I gave you an answer. The next step of reform for us is the service delivery prices project. That work's under way.
Since 1 October, businesses have been unable to charge a separate surcharge for most credit-card payments. I assume this applies to child care and early learning services too.
Yes, that's right. Our understanding is it does apply to child care.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: What engagement did the department have with ECEC providers before that change took effect?

We have discussed it with stakeholders. It was discussed at one of our stakeholder reference groups that Ms Crane referenced earlier. Generally, Treasury would have been responsible for communication of that measure, but we have discussed it with stakeholders in our formal forums.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: Are you at all familiar with how many services previously charged surcharges?
I'm not sure I've got data on that.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: I don't think we collect that data.

The Guardian reported on 29 September that Cubby OOSH, the out-of-school-hours care provider, told families it would stop accepting credit card and debit cards because of the new surcharge rules. Has the department received advice that other ECEC services are restricting card payments for the same reasons?
I haven't had advice from any services that they are stopping accepting credit card payments, but I assume it's a business choice that some would make.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: Is the department aware at all of how many parents are using credit cards to pay for their childcare services?

We don't collect that information. In the discussions that I mentioned before where this was discussed at some of our stakeholder forums, like our formal reference group, I understand it is a fairly significant proportion of families that use credit cards, but we don't have figures or a percentage on that.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: Before the decision was made to ban the use of surcharges and pass on the surcharge, did Treasury or the responsible agency consult you at all in relation to how many parents might be using credit cards?

I'd have to take on notice whether they consulted the department. What I would say is that most services and most third-party software providers that interact with the financial side—the interaction between parents and provider systems—offer a range of payment methods. It could be direct debit, or it could be that parents can choose when to transfer the money. There are, usually with these software providers, a number of payment options that parents can use.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: The government's promoted this as a cost-of-living relief, but providers still face payment-processing costs. Has the department assessed whether or not they're able to absorb those costs or whether they're simply just going to have to pass it on by way of other charges?
We haven't modelled—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: You haven't modelled that? The services—
I would say that the service delivery price project that the minister referenced before is collecting cost information from services, and that would be factored into that—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: Does that include the cost that service providers are having to incur for credit cards?
It would include that cost. It includes all current costs.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: For services receiving the worker retention payment, were card-processing costs considered when the fee cap was set, and how are those services expect to manage these costs now?

All available information was considered when the fee cap was set. I don't have the timeline on me of when that information was available. What I would say is that the fee-capping for the worker retention payment gave a buffer. It takes into account several ABS indices when we determined that amount, and there is a buffer. It is something the department would continually look at and provide advice to ministers. If we think that cost pressures are exceeding the available cap, then we can provide advice to government. At this stage we think that the cap is a reasonable amount, and the feedback that we've got from the sector is that the cap is a reasonable amount. I would say that, where a particular business—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: That cap's going to have to absorb this surcharge now?
It will form part of their cost base. Where a service is—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: Which is why you can understand why they're saying, 'We just won't take credit cards anymore.'

Yes, and that would be a business choice. In relation to the fee cap, services can apply for a higher fee cap if they are under viability stress. While the current fee cap is in place for the majority of services where their costs are exceeding their revenue, they can apply to the department to get an alternative fee cap to raise, but they have to show evidence that their costs are exceeding their revenue to be able to get that higher fee cap.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Funding and Evidence

text: Apologies for the interruption, but we're now overdue for our suspension. We'll be continuing with this outcome.
We're returning on outcome 1, Early childhood. Senator Payman has the call.

Good afternoon. I understand that on 14 October the department met with the Shire of Mukinbudin regarding the government's election commitment to spend $5 million on a new early childhood education centre. The CEO of the Shire of Mukinbudin told ABC Radio Midwest and Wheatbelt: 'Based on the discussions that I had with the Department of Education staff on Wednesday, it sounds like it's not going to go ahead.' Why has the government broken its election promise?
I'll ask Mr Smyth to make some comments around that. He was part of the meeting. My understanding is discussions are continuing in relation to that particular site.
There has been no decision about that. We are still in ongoing negotiations and discussions with the Western Australian government as well as the shire council.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: So is the shire lying to us?

I'm not aware of exactly what was said there. We had some confidential and without-prejudice discussions with the shire council on the date that you said. It's not my decision. The decision is one for the government. Obviously, it was an election commitment. The discussions and negotiations are ongoing with the Western Australian government and the shire.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: I'll just give you a timeline. The shire office told my office earlier this month: 'First, the department verbally told me that they would not be honouring the commitment. Then Channel 7 called me yesterday afternoon and said the department had told them no decision had been made. Then they reported that the government will honour the election commitment. So who knows at this point?' Do the government and the department believe this is an acceptable standard of communication?

I'm not privy to what the Shire of Mukinbudin says to the media or to anyone. I've had discussions with them, as have my staff. Those discussions are continuing. We have not made any change to the fact that we are looking to honour the election commitment to the Shire of Mukinbudin.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: I understand that the CEO was told the project would not be going ahead due to a lack of demonstrated demand. If there was a lack of demonstrated demand, why did the government make this commitment in the first place?
The government made election commitments in the first half of last year. This is one of those commitments. We are continuing, as Mr Smyth has outlined, to work on delivering that commitment.
So you can confirm on the record that you will be delivering this commitment to the Shire of Mukinbudin?
We are working closely with the WA government. I am of the understanding that discussions are continuing with them and with the council to deliver on the commitment.
That's not a yes, though, Minister. It's still sitting on the fence.
