Some of the information that you've given us here is difficult for us to square with the work that I'm advised the department is doing and believe that the department is doing, because the department is working to deliver the BEEF and the election commitments that have been made. I can confirm that the department is working on all aspects of the BEEF and delivering all aspects of the BEEF. We are continuing to work with the WA government and the council to deliver on the commitment. We intend to deliver the commitment.

It's just that that vague wording actually allows you the room to break the election promise. That's why I would like a definitive answer. Is this going ahead? Is that a yes? That's so that the Shire of Mukinbudin, who are probably watching this right now, can know that that election promise is going to be honoured and that the government's not going to break that promise. Candidate Karen Wheatland announced that a re-elected Albanese Labor government would invest up to $5 million towards building a new childcare centre in Mukinbudin. Are we saying that she wasn't speaking on behalf of the government if you're not going to give me a definitive yes?

We made the commitment. We are working to deliver that commitment. We've made election commitments across 17 locations, and 13 of them have been delivered. We are working through the final four, including in Mukinbudin. The only issue that I have with what you're asking me or what you're saying to me is that it does take work to deliver the commitments. That work is underway.

Minister, the Marrickville Golf Club, which the Prime Minister is a member of, received $6 million from the government's taxpayer funded slush fund. Does the Albanese government only do pork barrelling in the eastern states? Because we're waiting in WA to have this commitment honoured.

I sort of reject all of the premises of your question there, but I can talk about the services that we've committed to build in Western Australia. We have signed a Federation Funding Agreement with the WA government, and we have announced that we are working with them to build an early learning service at Maarakool Primary School and at Greenmount Primary School. We have a third commitment there that we'll be announcing soon. We have also worked with the WA government to announce a service at Derby in WA, and we continue to work on the Mukinbudin commitment.
I'll just move on to my other questions, Minister. There's another time to talk about what the government's doing. But can you just clarify the primary school that you referred to?
Maarakool Primary; Greenmount Primary.
'Greymount Primary'?
Greenmount Primary.
Okay. To the department: can you please provide any record of a meeting with Mukinbudin Shire on 14 October 2026?
I'll have to take that on notice.
witness_position: Senior Responsible Officer, Building Early Education Fund Taskforce

text: Thank you. On the Four Corners episode, I understand that Four Corners displayed a figure stating that 98 per cent of new early learning services opened over the past two years were for-profit. Does the department confirm that figure?
We'd have to take that on notice. I suspect what has occurred in that is that they're looking at, potentially, some of the data that ACECQA has. We wouldn't have that in our folders.
Do you know what the breakdown of for-profit and not-for-profit is?
Not over that period that you're referencing, no. We'd have to take that on notice.

Thank you. The Commonwealth directs substantial public money into the for-profit system through the childcare subsidy. When a corporate early learning provider faces pressure, more margins and returns, while also deciding what it spends—whether that's on qualified educators, supervision and quality—what guarantees that the child's interests win in that situation, when they've got competing priorities?

As we've given testimony today and in previous hearings, no matter the provider's size or type, all governments have an expectation of quality service provision. Whilst there might be individual business decisions made within those entities, the expectation is that those services are safe and they are quality. Some of the changes that ministers agreed to, and that were implemented in national law earlier this year, go to the paramountcy principle, where a board or others responsible for that entity need to take that into consideration in the decisions that they are making about staffing, layouts, program design, food choice et cetera.

This year we've watched quite a number of large for-profit providers shut their doors, leaving parents without answers about their children's ongoing education and care. Did the Commonwealth ever consider buying back those centres and running them directly to plug the gap?
Not to my knowledge.
Why wasn't this considered?
That would be a matter for government.
Minister?

I gave evidence a bit earlier about Edge Early Learning, which has gone into voluntary administration. We have been engaged in that, and we have been engaged in working towards as many of those services as possible being able to be supported to transition to a not-for-profit provider. Goodstart Early Learning has entered a conditional agreement to acquire 31 edge learning services, and we have supported them in that proposal.

Are you suggesting that another not-for-profit should take over from the for-profit providers who may be shutting their doors and the Commonwealth won't step in? What I'm asking is will the Commonwealth step in and buy back those centres to ensure that families aren't left without ongoing education and care for their children?

In some of the earlier evidence in the committee, we were talking about areas of oversupply and undersupply, and there are two slightly different things happening in your questioning. In relation to closures that are due to oversupply, we are monitoring that. We are concerned about that because it is incredibly disruptive to children and to families, even if there is another service that is there and that is available. We are, as you would know, exploring with education ministers around the country the potential for an early education commission, which we think could help with those issues of oversupply and undersupply. When there are services that go into administration or are at risk of closure, we are interested in supporting the not-for-profit sector where there are viable services in areas of disadvantage and undersupply. We are interested in supporting not-for-profits where it is possible to do so—to step in with those services. That is what we did with Goodstart Early Learning, and we're very pleased that Goodstart Early Learning is in an arrangement and has conditionally agreed to acquire 31 of the Edge Early Learning services that are in areas of need.

This question is about disadvantaged communities. We know that the childcare subsidy helps families purchase care, but it obviously doesn't guarantee that a service will exist where a family lives. If a regional town, an outer suburb or a disadvantaged community needs early childhood education centres but operating there isn't commercially attractive, who's responsible for making sure that that service exists?

I don't think there's a responsibility per se in terms of the work that we do in the department. But, if a service is interested around that and they need some sort of financial support, there is a range of financial support mechanisms in place: CCCF, which we talked about earlier; the childcare subsidy; and applications through the BEEF project, if they're a new project around that. As the minister indicated, one of the things that we're looking at is a new commission. The potential of that new commission would be to look at supply across the country and provide advice to governments in relation to that. That's work that we are progressing, and ministers will have further conversations around that in the coming weeks.

As long as providers aren't only focusing on the money they'll make but are ensuring that those childcare deserts that we're seeing around the country are being fully serviced and those families are provided with the essential service that early childhood education care is. Thank you.
Senator Hodgins-May.
You alluded to this earlier, but what are the precise criteria that the department used to identify the 120 services subjected to funding conditions?

Those were some of their more straightforward ones. In the context of those services, they were rated as below meeting the NQS initially for seven or more years after multiple assessment and rating visits and assessments and ratings and they were assessed as not meeting quality area 2. The further tranches of the work then tightened in and went from five or more years. So the whole cohort is five or more years rated as below meeting NQF and not meeting quality area 2.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Sorry, was it seven or more years or five or more years?
It was seven to begin with, and then we broadened to the five or more.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Were there any services that did meet those criteria but were not placed on conditions, and can you provide the committee with the complete assessment methodology?
I don't have the full sample here. I don't believe so, but I'm happy to take that on notice.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Do you know whether Little Zak's was assessed at all?
Again, we might take that on notice. I don't know how much I'm able to disclose, because of the secrecy of revisions under the family assistance act.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Can you also check whether it was only about children?
We can look into what can be disclosed. I can certainly tell you the methodology. I'm pretty confident I can't, but we can see what we can provide in terms of individual identifying data.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Ideally, if you are able to provide specifics about why they did not meet the threshold—if they are in that assessment pool.
We'll take that on notice and see what we can do to help.
Does the department have to hand how many childcare services have failed to meet the national quality standard twice in a row and are still receiving Commonwealth childcare subsidies?

I don't have it in the folder. Our ACECQA colleagues—it's not Commonwealth data, I should say to start with. It is state and territory data that ACECQA manages on behalf of states and territories. There is some public data on this, so I understand the ACECQA national registers would likely hold data that could tell you that.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: We don't hold the data—is what we're saying. Again, we can take it on notice to see if we can access that data. You're after services that didn't meet national quality standard 2—
Yes—twice in a row but who are still receiving the subsidy.
We'll have to work that through with ACECQA to get that data.
We can definitely work that through with them.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: My understanding is it's about 350 services that have failed to meet the standard in two consecutive assessments, with an average gap of more than three year assessments between—but you can't confirm that today with the information you've got in your folders?

No, we can't confirm the number. What I can say to a couple of the other points that you've just made is that, certainly, that period of time between assessments was overall for national—the assessment rating was something that education ministers discussed last year and agreed to timeliness provisions around that. To some of the points that you've made around—there are large gaps between those assessments for some of those services. The second piece is that, with the announcement of the extension of the worker retention payment, QA2 and meeting that is a requirement in that for any of those services that—
Sorry, what was that? QA2?

The QA2 that we're talking about. Whilst what Mr Moon has just discussed has been about the conditions that have applied to a very specific group of services and about whether they expand or other things, QA2 will also feature in the worker retention payment for the extensions. It will be a requirement that those services that receive funding under the worker retention payment also meet it with that. So there will be two levers that the Commonwealth will have as means to ensure that services are meeting QA2.

Minister, seven or five years sounds like an exceptionally long time for a centre to be failing to meet standards. Our kids have well and truly gone through in that time. If a service has failed the national quality standard twice in a row, why isn't that automatically enough to trigger a Commonwealth funding review? Do you think that that's an appropriate timeline?
I'll get Mr Moon to repeat the criteria, because I think the criteria that you've just outlined did enliven the action.
It did. It was rated as below meeting the national quality standard and not meeting quality area 2 after multiple assessments in five or more years.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: So do you think that five or more years is reasonable?

What I can say, and Mr Moon can help if required, is that education ministers have said that when a service is working towards standards it must be visited more often to make sure that it gets up to the standard. There are 590 more services that are meeting the standard under the last data than there were a year ago. This means that they've moved from working towards to meeting the standards, so almost 600 more services have moved from working towards to meeting the standards. We think that's a good thing where services are failing to meet the standards. Mr Moon's given that five-year timeframe. That is generally going to involve more than one visit—probably a couple of visits that they've had—and they haven't met the standard. Mr Moon's evidence was that for all of those services that met the criteria the compliance action was taken.

An important explanation or piece of context in terms of the different elements of regulation here or how the safeguarding works, the assessment and rating part of the process is incredibly important and gives families visibility as to whether a service has met each of those quality areas and to what level. It is an incredibly important part of the system, but so too is the ongoing monitoring and oversight that their state and territory regulators undertake. It is not the case that a service is assessed and rated and then they're not looked at again for a period of time. There is regular and frequent monitoring.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Is there data, even if it's de-identified for senators just to see, around how often 'regular and frequent' is and how many checks there are?

There is. There are a couple of things. We can take on notice exactly what we can pull together. But to be helpful, again, the ACECQA national registers disclose the last visit by a regulator, and that is complemented by further transparency in terms of regulatory action that's been posted both on starting blocks for families and the national registers for broader visibility.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: You can see the last check. Does it show each visit?
I believe it's the last visit.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Is there any data to get an idea of, when you say multiple visits over five years, whether that's two or more, given the seriousness?
We can work with colleagues to see what we can pull together.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: I might move on. I was out of the room. If you have been asked these questions, just let me know and I will keep moving. I've previously raised service closures and viability at previous estimates. Since then, Edge, as we've discussed, has confirmed 11 centre closures and Shared Beginnings has entered administration with further centres closing. Did both of these providers notify the department about this within the satisfactory notice period?

The short answer is yes, but let me explain so I don't mislead. The legislative notification period is 42 days unless there is an exceptional circumstance. In each of those cases, the companies had entered administration under different and varied terms. I received a personal phone call from the CEO of Edge as they entered administration, and we got phone calls from the administrators of Shared Beginnings as they entered. It wasn't before the 42 days. It was as they entered administration, but given that it was unforeseen it did meet the legislative requirement.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: It seemed like it would be a fairly common one to be used. Is it discretion that you have around exceptional circumstances?
Yes, it's discretionary.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: When Edge's 11 centres were confirmed for closure, it was reported that some families had only 48 hours to find alternative care, which mortifies me as a working parent. What role did the Commonwealth play in helping those families, and what support was actually provided?
An important distinction is that when a provider enters administration the administrators become the approved provider. We do a whole bunch of processes to make sure that that's OK.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: What sort of processes?
We make sure that we understand who the person with management and control is and that they have got working with children checks and understand their obligations.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: But they are administrators, really. They're not—

They're administrators, but we need to be satisfied that they understand the childcare subsidy; for our state and territory colleagues, that they understand the national law; and that they understand their obligation.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: How do you understand that? What rigour is behind that process?

Given time, I might take on notice what we look at in terms of fitness and propriety. There are a wide range of things, and it's probably best to take on notice just for utility. In terms of coming back to those closures, we've involved ourselves and our state colleagues in a couple of instances or situations. The first one is that, on entry of the administration period, both we and the relevant state regulators made very clear our expectations in terms of communicating and engaging with families. We made it very clear that, although there is uncertainty with some of those services, it is incredibly important to us, and to the states, that families are notified as early as possible if there's an expectation that services will close. We provided examples of better practice in terms of things that the administrators—or any provider, really—could do to make it easier for families. It was quite a good response, in a sense; it's not taking away from the disruption and distress it causes children moving between centres. It has been increasingly common where administrators particularly will have a look within their existing footprint, their service footprint, to figure out where their capacity is and think about arrangements to transition between sites or services in the smoothest way possible. I would say that's increasing, which is a good thing to see in troubled circumstances. We are also seeing, increasingly, administrators get on the phones and call around other providers, other services, that are near to where those services operate so that they can not only provide as early as possible, noting that in some instances—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Did this all happen in the case of Edge?
It certainly did with Shared Beginnings, and I believe it did with Edge as well.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Would you mind taking that on notice, just to be sure?
I can take it on notice to confirm.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: What is the role the Commonwealth plays in supporting? Once you've approved that administrator, as you see fit, to run that centre, is that when you step back?
Certainly not. We remain engaged with the administrators throughout the duration. We provide advice in terms of what we would be looking for in terms of a fit and proper and suitable—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Moreso to the families. Do you have any contact with the families?

In limited circumstances we have direct contact. It's generally done through the approved provider and sometimes through the state regulator. The general advice is to go to the StartingBlocks website.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: Minister, what is your plan if another major provider collapses or announces dozens of closures at short notice, especially if your department uses discretion to waive that 40-day notice period, which is likely to leave families with 48 hours to scramble if you know they are going into administration. That sounds like it's an exceptional circumstance. What assurances can you give us today that, if something like that were to happen, the government is ready and prepared to respond to meet the needs of those families under that very stressful situation?

I think you've just had evidence from the department about the responses that they put into place. For my part, as the minister, I have asked that the department support families as they can when these instances happen, and that is what they do through the work that Mr Moon has described but also through the work coordinating with the states and territories, who are working on the ground to support families and children as well. I think, more broadly, we see that there is an issue with oversupply and undersupply. That is the challenge that we are facing at the moment. We've talked a lot, and we've talked a lot today, about those things. I can go over it again, but, at the end of the day, there are issues with oversupply and undersupply. We think that a commission could help to better steward and coordinate supply in the sector.

I suppose I'm talking about a large for-profit provider going into administration, closing dozens or even hundreds of centres. Can you, hand on heart, say that the department is ready for that? I think it's a fairly possible scenario when we look at the context that we're in at the moment, hearing about lower birth rates, the cost of living and so on. Do you, hand on heart, feel that there are safeguards in place to ensure—
I gave you a brief answer because we've already canvassed some of this, but I'm happy for the department to provide further information.
Thanks.
Then I do need to provide the call to Senator O'Sullivan.

I'll move through them as quickly as possible, and we may need to take some of them on notice. Senator, you may have been out of the room when we referenced the process that exists for large providers. We have a financial viability process for large providers. In the examples that Mr Moon gave to you, they were not large providers, and therefore we would not have visibility of their financial position, or what might have them moving into administration. We would not have seen. When it comes to the large providers, we have a lot of information on them, and that process has been in place for quite a number of years. All large providers, for-profit or not-for-profit, must report to the department, and there is a pretty forensic analysis of the financial information that's provided, to understand exactly those sorts of things that you were talking about.

And, just to be absolutely clear, they're not major providers. Edge was subject to large provider financial reporting. Also, to confirm, all jurisdictions where Edge was trading were engaging deeply with Edge—I think there's been quite public reporting of the South Australian services in particular and the work that the Education Standards Board has done with Edge—leading up to the administration and throughout.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Child Care Integrity

text: So there is a provider-of-last-resort plan ready to go to ensure children aren't left without care when a private provider exits the community. Is there any provision for government to take over and run services?
No.
There's no provision. Okay. Do we need to rotate, Chair? I've only got a couple more questions. If you want me to, I can finish my block and then I can put the rest in on notice.
I know Senator O'Sullivan is seeking the call. Senator Hodgins-May has a couple more questions. Let's finish here, and then I'll come to you, Senator O'Sullivan.
Yes. Then we can dismiss them.

Thank you. I still don't have complete confidence that no children will be left without care if there isn't a provider-of-last-resort plan. Is this something that is intended to be discussed with state ministers?

I think the department would say that that would be a matter for government, so I will jump in and say that we monitor these providers. The department has just given that evidence. When these circumstances occur, the department works closely with administrators. They work closely with the jurisdictions. We had an example recently where we intervened and supported a not-for-profit provider to take over 31 of the Edge services, and we are continuing to work through the lessons of that. We are supportive, where possible, of not-for-profit providers being supported in the circumstances that you are outlining.
Otherwise it's left to the market, essentially, to take over closing centres?
I'm just going to repeat my answer that I've given about five times, which you don't want me to do.

If you're going to repeat it, don't worry. I don't. I'll put the other ones on notice. Finally, I am really encouraged to hear what you're saying about the Early Education and Care Commission, the EECC. I know stakeholders are very enthusiastic about this, as are we. Will you be tasking the EECC with monitoring service openings and closures, local vacancies, provider viability and unmet demand and with using that information—I think you've said this, but I just want to confirm—to plan where new services are needed?

The sorts of issues that you've just described are within the scope of what we are discussing. That is the answer that I can give you because it's going to education ministers on Monday for their decision.
Should the sector expect to find out after Monday's meeting?
It will be a progress report on the consultation around the commission. There are decisions to be made. I can't pre-empt what those decisions will be.
Thank you.
Senator O'Sullivan.

We're just wrapping up. I wrote to you. We covered a lot of the issues; in the interest of time, I'm going to put the rest on notice. But I want to say thank you for whatever work was done to prepare to come with those answers today.
Thank you for the heads-up on the questions.
Putting them on notice means that you can now answer them quickly.
We've got them ready for you.
Great—thank you. That's it.
Thank you very much to officials for this outcome. You're free to depart.

text: We'll just jump straight into the questions then. Senator Scarr, you have the call.

text: Hello everyone. This is my first estimates with this committee, so it's lovely to meet you all. It's a very pleasant environment, I'm finding, but I do have to familiarise myself with how to pronounce the acronym.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: A lot of people struggle with it.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: As I understand it, the ABC reported that 473 services operate outside the National Quality Framework, and the government plans to bring 142 of them into it. Can ACECQA confirm those figures? What are the figures from your perspective?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Those figures—the data around out-of-scope services—are really a matter for state and territory regulatory authorities. We are not in a position to confirm the data on the number of out-of-scope services.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Presumably, you liaise with the states and territories, so are you able to provide the latest data which you have on your records that's been provided by the states and territories?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I will have to take that on notice and discuss it with the states and territories.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: What's the current data you have from the states and territories?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The data that we hold is in relation to the National Quality Framework, and out-of-scope services data is held by state and territory governments.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Maybe you can give just a bit more background in relation to what types of services operate outside the National Quality Framework. What are we talking about?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes, certainly. My understanding is that it is Commonwealth-funded childcare-restricted program services as well as services that are regulated under state and territory residual legislation. But the question is probably better directed to the department, who would be able to answer that.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The sorts of services that we're talking about, in quite a number of instances, wouldn't meet the definition of 'education and care'. They are playgroups or creches, occasional care and community centres. The 120-odd number that was referred to does refer to ones that the department funds in terms of Community Child Care Fund-restricted, but the gap between the full number that was reported and the others are a range of other services, as Ms Buchanan has said, that are regulated under state and territory legislation.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Ms Crane, this figure of 142 that's been described as the number that the government plans to bring under the National Quality Framework, what can you say about that?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The Community Child Care Fund-restricted sites have a long tail. Last year, education ministers agreed to bring them in under the National Quality Framework and that involves an actual change to the national law. At the moment, it explicitly excludes them from being in there and, by extension, what that means is, even though they are still regulated, the data cannot be held by ACECQA because, under national law, they are not a nationally approved service in that sense. So the work that will happen with states, territories and the Commonwealth will be national law changes to allow them to be brought in, and obviously work with those services to ensure that they meet the standards under the National Quality Framework, as has been discussed in the previous session.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Does ACECQA have any role in terms of advising the government in that regard?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: No.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: So you haven't—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Sorry—while we don't have a role in terms of bringing them into the legislation, there are teams within ACECQA that work closely with the Australian government to support some of those services through quality improvement type programs. I don't know whether Ms McCoy wants to elaborate a little bit further on some of those programs that sit in her area.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, Policy and Regulatory Systems

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes, in terms of some of the out-of-scope services, since 2021 we have worked with CCCFR services on a quality and safety training package project where we have supported services to strengthen their capability in the key areas of quality, safety and supervision. We're currently in our fourth stage of that project, and that continues until mid next year. Another key area where we're also working with the Australian government is for in-home care services, where we have developed a framework, which was published yesterday, in consultation and collaboration with the in-home care sector. That provides a framework consistent with the National Quality Framework, which sets a benchmark in terms of the quality and safety standards. That's to support and strengthen the existing frameworks that are in place for in-home care.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, National Register and Innovation

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: How long are these projects going to go on for? Is there any time line in that regard?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: At this stage the CCCFR project is due to conclude mid next year. We're also supporting the Australian government in terms of implementation of the new framework, and that is due to finish mid next year as well.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, National Register and Innovation

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: What's the difference between the safety and quality requirements that apply to services outside the National Quality Framework and those that are covered by the National Quality Framework? What are the sorts of differences?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Apologies: I don't think I can go too far in answering that question, because our focus is the National Quality Framework. It would be a matter for state and territory governments that are regulating those services.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay. Well, in terms of the work Ms McCoy's doing, presumably through the work you're doing it might have given you some sort of insight in relation to the sorts of issues, at least, at a high level?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The work we've done is helping the services in, for example, home care, to meet the ministers' rules in terms of providing high-quality education and care, in terms of the types of things that surround alignment with the child safety reforms that have been taking place in the last few years, and a lot of consistency, as I said, with the National Quality Framework, taking into account that, for example, home care occurs in a child's own home.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, National Register and Innovation

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Sure. So there's a difference. I understand that. So you're working on these projects, and that's to effectively bring the standards up in relation to the services that aren't covered by the National Quality Framework, presumably, to assist them to meet those standards. Is that an appropriate description?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's to support those services for the in-home care and CCCFR services to meet the requirements to provide quality education and care and evidence as to how they meet those requirements under the ministers' rules.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, National Register and Innovation

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Taking into account that the environment is somewhat different in some cases.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Exactly—taking into account the context of those services.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, National Register and Innovation

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay. I might leave it there, if I can cede the call to Senator O'Sullivan.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I have just one last block. What role, if any, did ACECQA play in designing and conducting the national CCTV assessment and trial?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We were consulted as part of the process by governments to undertake that evaluation.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Did the assessment and evaluation examine whether CCTV is being reviewed routinely or whether the footage is generally just accessed after a complaint or incident?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'm unable to answer that question, as we don't have—those are matters for governments. The department who led that project may be able to answer that.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: So that wasn't part of your evaluation?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We didn't undertake the evaluation. We were—
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Sorry, I thought you just said you did.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: No—sorry. We were consulted in relation to the evaluation undertaken by the department.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I see. Did you provide any advice to the government about the use of CCTV to identify possible abuse or neglect, rather than to simply preserve evidence after an incident?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Our 2023 child safety report did touch on this. We reiterated, as part of the consultation, the findings in that 2023 report. I might ask Ms McCoy to speak about those findings in the 2023 report.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: As Ms Buchanan said, in our 2023 review of child safety arrangements, we did cover CCTV. Consistent with what was discussed earlier with the department, we found, based on the research we did, that CCTV didn't prevent matters of abuse from occurring, but it certainly did support regulatory authorities particularly, and also services, in being able to look at that CCTV. Our recommendations in the review, which have been implemented by governments included on the tracker on our ACECQA website—there are recommendations that have been followed up and that are about having policies about CCTV in place. Policy information advice has been developed for services to use, to enable parents to have an understanding about CCTV, consents in place, how it works, the data and security issues around that.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, National Register and Innovation

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Does the NQF provide any guidance requirement around the review of footage?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I might ask Ms Weldon-Chan to talk to that.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The NQF includes a requirement for services to have policies and procedures. There are a whole range of different ones they need to have, and they need to follow them. One of those is about the use and storage of images of children, and that does cover—if they use CCTV, then they need to have a policy and procedure in place for how they manage that. As Ms McCoy mentioned, it is about things like ensuring that children's privacy is upheld, who has access to those images—those kinds of things. But that's as far as the framework goes.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
witness_position: General Manager, Policy and Regulatory Systems

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: What national guidance are you providing in relation to CCTV, including who should be able to access the footage—that goes to the point you were just making—how long it should be kept and how concerns are identified? Is this something that is promoted in terms of—are providers fully aware of their obligations?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I think those questions go to policy decisions of governments through EMM.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Do you have an educative role, though, with providers?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes, certainly we do. We develop resources and provide guidance, training and support. But the matter of CCTV is still subject, as I understand it, to governments' consideration through EMM.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Four Corners showed CCTV footage capturing serious assaults on children at a centre up in the cape, in Injinoo. What lessons does ACECQA believe the sector and regulators should take from cases where CCTV provides evidence of abuse but may not prevent it?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I think the CCTV evaluation report will go to those matters, and, certainly, we will stand by for the decision of governments in relation to that report and then look at what actions we may be expected to take by EMM in relation to those areas.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Was Injinoo outside of the NQF?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: So you would have limited direct authority over that service in [inaudible].

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That's correct.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: What arrangements, then, should exist to share child safety lessons between NQF and services regulated under other systems?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I think the question of out-of-scope services really is still a matter for governments. We obviously work closely to provide resources and guidance where necessary, where we can, when those areas cut across both the NQF and out-of-scope services. But I would say that it really is a matter for further consideration of governments.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Senator, if I may add, the service that you've referenced is regulated by the Queensland government. When it comes to matters that were discussed in the previous session, around the engagement between Commonwealth regulators and state and territory regulators, certainly with the services we've just talked about, in terms of Community Child Care Fund Restricted, they would be part of that conversation as a funder and, in many instances, state as regulator. That information is shared as and where relevant.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Just finally, on a slightly different—well, very different—topic, earlier I was discussing the national child safety training modules with the department. What role does ACECQA have in that? Are you the host of the—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: No, we're not.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Have you had any involvement in it at all?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We were consulted as part of the development of the package, which was led by governments.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: So the contract with the provider is directly with the department, not with ACECQA?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Correct. The contract is from the Queensland Department of Education with the Australian Centre for Child Protection.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Good, good. Someone's going to message me to say if I can let you go. Yes, I can let you go. Thank you.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: You don't have that authority at all—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Sorry, Chair! I'm overstepping my bounds here.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: but I do. Thank you, Ms Buchanan and your officers, for your evidence today.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you very much, Chair.
witness_organisation: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I am standing in the way, though, if I keep going. I do have some power!

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: They're already gone! I'm now calling officers from outcome 2, Higher education. I'll start by giving the call to Senator Dolega, who I believe has a block on Closing the Gap.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thanks for coming back this afternoon. At the previous estimates, we talked about some of the changes that the Albanese Labor government has made to ensure that all First Nations students are provided with a Commonwealth supported place at university, where they meet the entry requirements. Last time, you mentioned that there'd been a five per cent increase in First Nations students starting their degree each year over the last couple of years. I think it was for 2024, and you provided some preliminary data for 2025. I'm wondering if you have any updated information that you could share with the committee on the number of First Nations students starting a degree in the last 12 months and the trend that you may find over the last couple of years.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Chair, before we do that, Ms Mohr is at the table. It's her birthday today.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Happy birthday!

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I would just like to share that she's thrilled to be here for her birthday at this time of year.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That's so good that you're starting with a government senator, and I'll go very easy on you.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We're not going to ask how old you are! Sorry, I've destroyed the committee. Over to my team.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: On behalf of the committee, happy birthday! Your gift will be that we won't sing to you.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you. Thank you everyone; I really appreciate it.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Good on you for being here.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Back to the question—over to you.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I am actually going to go straight to Dr de Crespigny to give you an update. We're seeing some really promising results, and Dr de Crespigny will talk you through those details.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
As Ms Joldić said, there are very positive indications that efforts to increase participation of and improve outcomes for First Nation students are paying off. In the last four years, between 2022 and 2025, the number of First Nations students starting higher education has increased by over 18 per cent. That's an increase from 9,668 to 11,431. We have preliminary semester 1 2026 data which indicate a further eight per cent growth in commencing Indigenous students compared to the same time last year. Based on historical trends, it's estimated that this is going to translate to between 12,000 and 12,400 commencing First Nations students in 2026, representing an estimated growth of around 24 per cent over the past five years.

I'd also like to add that, in the past five years, the success or pass rate—that's the proportion of students who are passing their subjects—for undergraduate First Nations students has been increasing, reaching a record high in 2024. I think it's also important to note that the gap between First Nation students and non-Indigenous students is narrowing in this respect. We also know from our graduate outcomes surveys that First Nations undergraduates have higher full-time employment rates and higher median salaries in both the short term and the medium term compared to their non-Indigenous counterparts.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Market Analysis and Data

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That is fantastic to see. Congratulations to you for the work that you've been doing on this really important measure. I do know that, from January this year, the government extended the demand driven places for First Nations students who want to study in medicine. Can you provide any update on how that sector has responded to the change and any early numbers that you may have as a result of those extended places?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'm afraid I don't have data on First Nations medical students with me, so I might have to take that on notice.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Market Analysis and Data

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Jessica Mohr, First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We won't just call you birthday girl.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Please; thank you! As Dr de Crespigny said, I don't believe we've got preliminary data on that with us, but I will say that, obviously, as a result of that reform, once it's fully implemented, we are expected to see an increase. We are expected to see around 30 more First Nation students studying medicine each year, and that will be an increase of around seven per cent. That would be a fantastic outcome, if you want to check.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Has the response from the sector been positive?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It has been very positive. It is very much welcomed by the sector, including the medical deans, with whom we've had a number of conversations about this.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you very much for the work that you continue doing. I really do genuinely enjoy hearing from this department, through Senate estimates, the work that you're doing on First Nation stuff. It's something that we very much care about, so thanks for coming with the update, and have a lovely birthday.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'm handing the call to the opposition—Senator O'Sullivan. At this stage, I don't believe I have another senator seeking the call, so I won't interrupt you.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay. We'll just be going between ourselves.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes, so you might want to organise that amongst yourselves, but I'll let you know if I have another senator seeking the call.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
Okay. We may ask for a short pause between—we'll see how we go. On 13 October this year, in the House, and then again in a press release two days later, the Minister for Education said:

… this year more Australians than ever before have started a university degree.

That wasn't true. In fact, when the minister's office was questioned about this by Future Campus, they claimed that the minister had been referring to unpublished data held by the department, which showed an end-of-year projection based on a May year-to-date trend. Did the minister mislead the House?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: My response to that would be no. The data is accurate. But I will go to Dr de Crespigny to give you a bit more of an update on how the data works and what's behind the numbers in that media statement that you're talking about.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The minister did not mislead the House. Those data are actually available in our preliminary data release. There was a bit of additional work to project those to the full-year value, but, if you take a look at the preliminary data, you can see that 2026 undergraduate commencements are ahead of where they were in previous years. So I don't think it's fair to characterise that as misleading.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Market Analysis and Data

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
Well, I'm only asking because, to me, it's black and white. The minister said this:

… this year more Australians than ever before have started a university degree.

But Future Campus said:

… the Minister's statement was incorrect and total domestic commencements for 2026 remain below 2021 levels …

Future Campus also said:

However, the Minister would be right if he stated that 'More Australians are forecast to commence an undergraduate degree this year than ever before.'

Can you deal with that discrepancy.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Well, we probably should have included that word, potentially, but—
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Market Analysis and Data

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It has a very different meaning.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Well, yes, but I think it's also worth bearing in mind the longer term trends. The 2021 years were associated with very high enrolments due to the pandemic-related border closures. So we've been in a state of flux with enrolments in the sector, and it's my view that those years really should be considered outliers in a trend analysis. If you look further back, you see a trend, now, of increasing growth. I think, this year, when we look forward, with the enrolments, it's pretty clear to the department that we're going to be exceeding those pandemic related highs.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Market Analysis and Data

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Your statement just there provides that caveat about the trend and about the COVID years. But the minister didn't make that statement at all. It didn't include anything to couch what he was saying. We can all make mistakes; it's whether or not we're prepared to admit it. So should the minister correct the record and go back to the House and apologise and make sure his statement is accurate? As you pointed out, he could have said, as was said by Future Campus, that more Australians are 'forecast'. There's a very different meaning—if you say that 'there are' versus 'it's forecast to be'. We read the weather forecast each day, and sometimes they get it wrong. It's not what actually happens. They have very different meanings, don't they?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Senator, the department's not going to make commentary about what the minister should or shouldn't do; you wouldn't expect us to in relation to that. I think the point we've made is that, based on our data, the data would indicate that there'll be more students starting domestically this year than ever before.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Secretary, are you prepared to tell this committee in evidence that, as of 13 October, more Australians than ever before had started a university degree?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I already said just a minute ago what I'm prepared to say, which is that, based on the data that we've got, it's our expectation there'll be more students in 2026 than there ever has been in relation to starting domestic undergraduates—just checking that's right?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That's correct—undergraduates.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's still a projection though.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Well, it's always a projection. That's how the data works for us, because they start at various times throughout the year.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I didn't ask about expectations. I asked if more Australians than ever had started. You don't have the commencement data?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Commencing happens through various times of the year. It doesn't just happen at the start of the year. Commencing can happen mid-year, and there are various aspects of that, so my statement remains the same.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The data shown in the Future Campus report—I'm going to table this; thank you for that assistance, Senator Scarr—which I've just tabled, for domestic undergraduate commencing students between 2016 and 2027, with a projection for 2026, shows that the highest year on record for undergraduate commencements for which we have actual records and not projections was 2021 and in that year the figure was 290,901. Is that correct?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Based on the information you've just given us, that's correct.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: On your website, there's information in relation to preliminary trends in higher education, and the data on the department website—other than its underlying data file, which you can download from that page—shows that there were 971,638 domestic students but in 2026 there are 942,111 domestic students. Have you got that there?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I don't have the preliminary data report with me today, sorry.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'm sorry; I don't have that.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Market Analysis and Data

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I beg your pardon?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I don't have that that underlying data with me today. Sorry.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Policy, Data and Strategy

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We've got copies of it here. You don't keep that in your files? Can we table that as well, please.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: If you distribute it, we'll check that it's able to be tabled.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I might come back so you've got that in front of you.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Sure.

text: That'll be fairer for you to be able to answer those questions. I'll deal with a different issue and then come back to it.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: On notice, the department provided copies of letters between Ms Joldić and various institutions relating to research security, one of which reveals concerns about recent researcher-to-researcher collaborations between Iran, Russia and North Korea. Which university is that, and to your knowledge is the collaboration ongoing?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I will need to check which letter you're referring to. There were multiple letters that I sent in that period. I have sent a letter to multiple universities. I just need to check which one—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Are there multiple that have collaborations between Iran, Russia and North Korea?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Earlier this year, I sent a letter to all of the vice-chancellors, and there were follow-up letters, so I just need to understand exactly which letter you're referring to.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We reminded all universities about arrangements with those countries. That was the same letter that went to every university. I just don't know whether there's a—I think that's the one you're talking about. It went to all universities.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: This is in relation to the Trailblazer Universities Program. Are you aware, then, of how many universities have engaged in research-to-researcher collaborations with individuals in Russia, Belarus, North Korea or Iran this year?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I don't think we have that data, but I will—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Do you have the data? No, I don't think we do have the data.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Do you have any awareness of that?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: In general terms, the number of researcher-to-researcher collaborations across the university sector is quite astronomically high. Some of those are formal arrangements, some of them are non-formal arrangements. As Ms Joldić indicated to the committee earlier, there are three main criteria that we look at. The first is whether or not a discipline is in national skills shortage. For that we look at the Jobs and Skills Australia occupation shortage list. The second criterion we use is the completions data for those disciplines—how many students are completing that course at university. We also sought advice from the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, which has policy responsibility for the health workforces. You will recall that the CPP is not a universal payment; it's a targeted program. The two major objectives of the program, as you've already mentioned, are to look at relieving cost-of-living pressures for students who have to undertake mandatory placements as part of their study and also the investment in the critical workforces.

On your question around medicine, when you look at those three criteria that I indicated, the completions data for medicine is usually very high. On that basis it wouldn't necessarily satisfy a particular need for the mandatory payment to provide that cost-of-living relief under this program. We did want to spend some time in our posture—which you've probably read from some of the documents on the website, the regulatory statement and what have you—working in that education and engagement space, educating the sector around what we were looking for and what 'good' looks like to get that balance between prevention and response. agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: When we received all the plans and it was clear that there was a lot of work to be done across the sector, we considered our posture as a regulator and the need to educate and engage very early on in the life of the code. What we decided to do was hone in on three core requirements of standard 1 that we believe, for year 1 of the regulation of the code, are critical to success for the four years of the life of these plans. agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
