text: We're now bringing ATEC to the table. Welcome, Professor Glover. It's nice to see you in this capacity. Would you like to make an opening statement tonight?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
If I may, yes. Thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to provide an opening statement. I'd like to acknowledge that this is the Australian Tertiary Education Commission's first appearance at Senate estimates with our own session on the program, for which we are most grateful. ATEC now has its full cohort of five commissioners in place, with three of our ongoing commissioners present today, including Professor Mark Rose, our First Nations commissioner, Professor Stephen Duckett and myself as chief commissioner. We also have our chief executive, David Turvey, here. We welcome the opportunity to respond to questions from the committee regarding the important work of the ATEC.

I would also note the passage of relevant legislation with the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Act 2026, which amends the Universities Accord (Australian Tertiary Education Commission) Act 2026 and now provides ATEC with decision-making powers in relation to the allocation of domestic and international student places. I also note the announcement of the higher education support total allocation pool determination 2026 by Minister Clare earlier today. This is an important step in that it allows the ATEC to finalise the first round of the mission based compacts with 42 table A and B providers for 2027.

The negotiations that have taken place over the last couple of months with the universities have been very positive, with extensive discussions about each university's mission, strategies and plans and how they relate to the ATEC priorities for the sector. We will likely release the final compacts in mid-November, subject to data finalisation, and the ATEC will now work with the two new table B providers—the Australian University of Theology and Alphacrucis University College—to negotiate their mission based compacts for 2027. The process illustrates the stewardship function of the ATEC in understanding the unique missions of our universities, the challenges they face and the basis for investment in them through the allocation of additional domestic student places. This highlights the move from an essentially transactional financial engagement to a deeper mission based negotiation.

Another important milestone for the new ATEC was achieved today with the release of our efficient costing and pricing consultation paper, titled Towards a costing and pricing framework for Commonwealth supported places in universities. This is a significant step in the development of ATEC's advice to government on options for the pricing of higher education qualifications and reflects our commitment to deep engagement with the sector in the formulation of high-quality, evidence based advice to government. Professor Duckett is a renowned expert in pricing and is leading this work and can answer questions on it today. Bringing expertise like Professor Duckett's to bear in complex policy issues like pricing is another feature of the ATEC model, as is the very important work supporting First Nations peoples in tertiary education that will be led by our inaugural First Nations Commissioner.

The ATEC has recently taken on the responsibility for providing advice to government on the Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards). We have established a legislative consultation forum to ensure expert advice informs the ATEC's views to government on the threshold standards through the Higher Education Standards Committee. We've been recently engaging the sector on questions about how the threshold standards could accommodate a greater focus on research and national security, as well as considering how to facilitate specialisation in research for universities that may seek to do so.

We are also currently consulting with the sector on the next statutory statement of strategic priorities for 2027. This is a foundational document because it frames the discussions we will have with universities in 2027 on mission based compacts that will span 2028 to 2031. This is another important feature of the new model: a four-year compact timeframe, providing greater certainty and a longer planning horizon for universities in their relationship with government, contributing to sustainability and stability for the higher education sector and stronger and more coherent collaboration with the VET sector.

Finally, we have opened consultation on our work plan, engaging with the sector on the urgent areas of priority attention for the ATEC in 2027-28. Thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to address the committee.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you, Professor Glover. Senator Scarr.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you, Professor Glover, and congratulations to the other commissioners. Thank you for your service in relation to this important role. Professor Glover, I very much enjoyed your testimony when we were having the inquiry in relation to the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill. It gave me every confidence in terms of your experience and expertise. Given that experience and expertise, do you have any reflections on this difference between the national planning level for international students of 295,000 and the fact that it appears that, at the end of the year, we're going to undershoot that by 50,000, and what that means for universities?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
Thank you for your comments, Senator. One of the key aspects that we incorporated in our conversations with universities in the negotiation of mission based compacts for 2027—even though, for 2027, we're not responsible for allocating net overseas student commencements, NOSC places, we nevertheless engaged with universities to discuss with them their international strategies to understand the type of conversation we'd have with them in 2027 for 2028 to 2031. It was a matter of some discussion—how they were tracking in relation to visa processing and the number of students arriving.

As you pointed out, of course there are challenges for some universities in the sector due to a downturn in the number of international student commencers. The quality and integrity of the Australian international education system is of paramount importance to the government, and that, of course, is an important consideration. As the secretary pointed out earlier, some universities are tracking better than others in terms of visa processing and admissions—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The corollary of that is that some are tracking worse.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: There are some universities that are seeing a significant downturn, and one of the conversations that we were having with them, in anticipation of the discussion for the 2028 to 2031 compact, was about what their emerging strategies are to deal with what is a downturn in international student commencement load and how that will be managed over time. I think those universities are very engaged with the challenge of managing what will be a different profile for them, in many cases, for international students alongside the conversation with the ATEC—as the secretary pointed out a moment ago—as we discuss the allocation of increasing numbers of additional domestic student places through the managed-growth funding system alongside needs based funding for equity students. So we're in a situation where there's investment in the domestic side of higher education and management of the stabilisation of international student profiles.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Did the universities request additional places for 2027, in discussions with them? I've received some advice that the universities were seeking an additional 83,140 places for 2027. Are you aware of that?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes, we're aware. In the initial draft mission-based compacts that universities provided to us, they indicated their needs in terms of additional places for 2027. That did account for a significant number of places. It involved, though, not just places for new commencements, because we'll see growth, we anticipate, in higher education next year, as we've seen growth in higher education this year, in commencer load. It was also additional load in some cases for universities that were underenrolled, and it was also additional load for some universities that were overenrolled to address the underfunding of marginally funded places. So there was a significant request for places.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's all coming back to me now—the complicated issues from the bill. It makes my head hurt a bit. But your evidence was extremely well put. So there's an available pool of approximately 37,000 for 2027. Is that correct?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: There are additional places available now that the minister has made the determination on what's called the total allocation pool, which is 624,590 places next year. That is approximately 35,000 to 36,000 places more than were utilised this year, in 2026. So, yes, there are additional places to distribute.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: This comes back to the point you made. These are genuine additional student capacity rather than existing commitments or conversion of overenrolments. Is that correct? How would you describe these 37,000?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's a good question. Some of the 36,000 places will be provided to universities for growth in commencer load. They will be new commencer load places. Some of them will be used by universities to address overenrolment. That will be to convert marginally funded to fully funded places. And some will be used to support the universities that still remain below their funding floor to compensate them while we transition those universities to the new system. So it's spread across three categories as well as some load for things that we support, like Regional University Study Hubs.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: What was the first category?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Growth in commencer load.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That seems to be the growth element. How many are in that category, approximately?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: We're finalising data at the moment. It depends a little bit on the finalisation of verified data, which we don't yet have, but I would anticipate growth in the system of somewhere between 12,000 and 15,000 additional places in commencer load next year. We'll know more in the early part of next year when universities provide us with more of their data on their admission processes in 2027.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Should we be comparing that 12,000 to 15,000 range to the 83,140 additional places requested? Is that comparing apples to apples?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: No, not quite. The 83,000 included a significant request from universities that have significant overenrolment for support to convert that overenrolment from marginally funded to fully funded.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: How much of the 83,140 fell into the—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'd have to take that on notice. I don't have that figure in front of me.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Could you take that on notice.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Of course.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I understand it's early days. Have you given any advice to government yet in relation to additional funding that may be required to meet the objectives the universities have given in terms of increased places?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's a matter for government to determine the total allocation pool for 2028 to 2031, so that's a matter for government. We are certainly at the moment looking at rolling out the 2027 total allocation pool. The government will make a determination on the next TAP, I think, under the act, by 31 May next year, and that will give us certainty. Under the act, of course, the TAP can't decrease from one year to the next, so we anticipate significant growth, and the minister's on the record as indicating significant additional places over the next four years and beyond.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: As I understand it, the ambition under the universities accord is for 55 per cent of young Australians to hold a university qualification by 2050. Is that correct?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: By 2050—the actual target is an attainment target. It is 80 per cent of the working age population to have a tertiary qualification. At the moment we're working through the balance between higher education and vocational education and training, but it's around about 55 per cent with a higher education qualification. That's a matter that we're working through in more detail at the moment. That was one of the early forecasts in the accord process.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I've got another series of questions I would like to ask. I'm not sure how you're going to go with this, because I'm going to ask you a question about Jobs and Skills Australia. For the benefit of the Hansard, could you say what your previous role was, Professor.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I was previously the Jobs and Skills Australia commissioner.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: For how long?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: For a little over two years.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
As I understand it, earlier this week, your previous agency came out with a report which identified a potential oversupply of university graduates relative to trades. I want to quote to you from the report. It says:

There is potential misalignment between student demand for higher education and employment demand for VET.

Have you had a chance to have a look at that report and consider the modelling in that report? It might have even been commenced under you, Professor. I'm not sure, but I'm interested in any views you have with respect to that observation.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That work began when I was the JSA commissioner and when Mr Turvey was the JSA chief executive.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: You've come with the director? You must enjoy working for him.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text:
It's based on some very important modelling of growth in employment in Australia over the next five to 10 years and some very interesting modelling that Mr Turvey commissioned to look at what that modelling would generate if we changed some of the input parameters around the post-secondary education profile of Australians. When you do that you see some recalibration between higher education qualification demand and vocational education and training demand. JSA continues to do that very important modelling, and it shows that, in that unconstrained context, we will need more people with vocational education and training and slightly fewer than might have been anticipated in higher ed.

Overall, as I think the JSA report makes very clear, we need significant growth both in vocational education and training and in higher education. It's something both Minister Giles and Minister Clare have been saying frequently. I think it's one of the challenges for Australia. We talk about parity of esteem between the two sectors. We need to encourage young people into trades, and there are great examples of that around Australia. But, equally, we need to see growth in higher education and, particularly in the case of higher education, to attract more students from educationally disadvantaged backgrounds, equity students, to participate so we have some chance of reaching that very ambitious attainment target for 2050. So, yes, I'm aware of the work. I think it's very important modelling. But it doesn't, I think, subtract from the very clear need to increase significantly the number of people in both higher ed and VET. The balance between them is something that we need to do some more detailed analysis of.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Do you have any views with respect to the balance between them? What should be the target balance?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I think it's 55-45, which is the figure you quoted earlier. Of course, we need to appreciate that we're also entering a period where you've got generative AI and you've got changes to the labour market.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: That's the other point, isn't it?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's another potential area of impact. You also will have more flexible qualifications. You'll have lifelong learning as a much stronger component of the future than we see now. The blend of vocational training and higher ed might also change significantly in the future, so it's hard to make predictions about it. I certainly see a balance between our vocational education training and higher ed as a desirable outcome, but we need growth significantly in both.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'm just trying to get my head around growth in both when you're trying to balance the proportions. If you've got any other thoughts or information that you could provide on notice, I'd appreciate that.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It would all be referenced in the JSA report.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Could I offer one brief thing. The figures you're quoting are proportions of the labour market. They're not absolute numbers of people. So it's the share of the labour market that has VET and higher education qualifications. So you can still have growth in both, but the proportions might differ.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I understand that, but there's also the risk of cannibalisation of one by the other.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Absolutely, and that's one of the key reasons why we're very focused on tertiary harmonisation as a policy objective.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Understood. Professor, you do have a wonderful turn of phrase. I might use some of your phrases. You used the phrase 'in an unconstrained context'. What is 'an unconstrained context' in this context?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It might be a wise moment to ask Mr Turvey, who is an economist, to explain that particular characteristic.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: The modelling is based on a computable general equilibrium model of the Australian economy which is run by Victoria University. Essentially, it produces projections of the likely employment in the Australian economy based on the demand required by businesses and industry. The way the modelling works is that it projects that demand—what employers are anticipating they will need for the production side of the economy—and then it looks at the supply of labour based on the qualifications that people have and how people move through the education and training system and into the labour market. The model brings those two together and converges to an equilibrium employment projection. That's the mechanics of the modelling. When I was working at Jobs and Skills Australia, what we did in that modelling was essentially say, 'What happens if you turn off that supply constraint and just work out what would happen if you could supply the demand side of the labour market?' That just showed that there would be a slight rebalancing of the proportion of the labour market that would have VET quals versus higher education quals.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: On that language around 'unconstrained', the constraint in the model is the supply of labour based on expected qualification utilisation.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay. When we're talking about the 55-45 split, it's a split within the 80 per cent cohort that we need to get advanced qualifications, yes?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Yes, and I think the JSA work is suggesting—is it 55-45 or is it 52-48?—that we need to do more work on this to be able to give some more detailed advice to government.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: But when we talk about a slight rebalancing, we're talking in absolute terms about tens of thousands of people. That's correct, isn't it?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Correct.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: What sort of quantum are people—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I wouldn't like to—

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Is it 140,000 or something moving from one pool to the other?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's probably a better question to put to JSA in the next estimates, I think.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Alright. That was a polite prompt; thank you. I've just got two more questions. Why does the National Credit Recognition Framework initially focus on recognising TAFE qualifications for entry into university rather than the reverse?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: It's a good question, actually, because reverse articulation arrangements—that is, recognition of higher education in vocational education and training—is also a focus of attention in the long term in relation to tertiary harmonisation and the work of the Tertiary System Advisory Council. But the initial focus for many universities in the system is how we can provide more block credit arrangements that are more seamless and more systematic for students who have completed a diploma or certificate IV in the TAFE system so they have a more seamless entry to higher education. You may know, from the relevant background consultation papers on this, that we see great productivity benefits here and equity benefits and also links to national priorities through this. The National Credit Recognition Framework will, I think, be an important way of setting for the system more seamless movement from VET into higher ed. I think we also need to be focused on how we ensure we have the higher ed into VET. A lot of students complete a higher ed qualification and then go and do a VET qualification. It helps them in the labour market. It gives them the practical skills they need. We need to make sure they get the appropriate level of recognition. Considering both directions for credit recognition is certainly on our agenda.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Okay. I might just leave it there. I might, though, just ask your colleagues whether they have anything they want to add in relation to the discussion we've just had. I just want to give you an opportunity if you've got any observations.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thanks, Senator. I think this credit recognition stuff is extraordinarily important. You're right; the reverse articulation is also on our agenda. My main background is in health policy. The movement from enrolled nurses into registered nurses training, for example, is something that's really important in the health sector. So thank you for raising those issues.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Professor Rose?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Senator, can I just say that, in Aboriginal education, I can name you five very significant professors who were only allowed to go to TAFE in the early days of our entry into education.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Is that correct?

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Absolutely. I can name them if you'd like me to. TAFE has been a catalyst for our people to move in, so that's why I'm really curious about the harmonisation and I'm really excited about its potential. For our people, our first entree was into TAFE education, so I'm excited by the nuance in the ATEC.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Excellent. Good on you. All the best to your team.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you, Senator. We appreciate it.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: I'll put the rest on notice.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you, Senator. Thank you, Professor Glover, and thank you to the team from ATEC. It's lovely to have you at your first estimates officially.

agency: Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority
text: Thank you, Chair.

I welcome officials from ANU, including the interim vice-chancellor and president, Professor Brown. Welcome to you all. Would you or Professor Leach like to make a statement? Does anyone have an opening statement?
Yes, thank you.
Please proceed.

Thank you, Chair and senators, for the opportunity to appear here this evening. I'm delighted to be joined by our new chancellor, Dr Gordon de Brouwer, and members of the ANU executive leadership team.

Our global and diverse capability underpins our excellence in research and teaching. This year alone, we've welcomed students from over 80 countries to our university, and our community is enriched by our students, leading academics and educators from all over the world. Just in September, 20 ANU researchers were awarded the prestigious Australian Research Council Future Fellowships in research areas spanning quantum technologies, climate and environmental resilience, food security, health, mathematics, and the humanities and social sciences. Only last week, the Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences awarded ANU Professor Lisa Whop the Outstanding First Nations Researcher Medal for her work in advancing equitable cancer screening. This month, we announced that researchers from ANU have received funding to build a sustainable materials workforce, answer fundamental questions in earth science and further advance computational modelling to solve real-world problems, adding to critical national, national capability.

The quality of our teaching has been recognised by the international Times Higher Education rankings this year, with our strongest teaching performance in six years. We also rose three places this year in the international QS rankings to 29th in the world, our best position in the last five years. The Department of Education's recently released QILT 2026 graduate outcomes survey report showed that ANU's graduates are in high demand by employers, with our domestic graduates recording a full-time employment rate of 96 per cent, ranking first in the Group of Eight universities and second amongst all Australian universities.

But, of course, we have work to do. We're well placed to address the governance related conditions applied to the university's registration by TEQSA last month. Our chancellor and council will oversee the program of work to address these conditions, and we'd welcome the release of TEQSA's more detailed statement of reasons for the conditions.

We are committed to providing a safe, inclusive and respectful environment for our students, our staff and our wider community. We've been consulting deeply with our community on the new anti-racism definition requirements, and we believe we're well placed to meet the obligations that apply to all Australian higher education providers from 1 January next year.

In August we kicked off our 80th anniversary celebrations with the reopening of University House, the launch of our new university strategy, ANU by 2030, and a community day with more than 6,000 registered attendees. A few weeks ago we welcomed thousands of concertgoers to ANU for a student-led celebration of Australian music—a fitting way to celebrate 80 years.

In summary, while we have significant governance reform work in front of us, we are really proud of our ongoing achievements of our people and what we've achieved in teaching and research. We look forward to continuing to deliver on our mission as the Australian National University, and building capability in areas that are of priority to the people of Australia.
Dr de Brouwer, congratulations, and welcome.
Thank you.
We'll go to Senator Pocock.

Thanks for being here this evening, and congratulations to Dr de Brouwer—welcome back to Senate estimates. I bet you didn't think you'd be back this quickly, or at all! Thank you for the work that is happening at the ANU. It is obviously a very turbulent time and there's lots more work to do, but I recognise how far things have come since this time last year, and how much work has gone into that. I'm certainly hearing a lot more optimism from staff and students. Thank you for the engagement on a bunch of individual matters that people have brought to my office recently.

The cost of living is a big issue in this country at the moment, and it's something that a number of students have raised with me. I want to ask about the recent rental increases announced for those living in ANU campus accommodation. I know that it is somewhat separate to what you have control over, but I think it has a big impact on your students. I'm told the increase is above inflation, and brings the cheapest accommodation on campus to just under $700 per fortnight for an individual, self-catered, shared amenities room. That's 325 bucks for a room where you're sharing a bathroom and you have no inclusion of food. Looking at what that means, students in on-campus accommodation have had their costs go up 30 per cent in five years. If you look at rental costs for Canberrans, they've gone up 17 per cent. You're running at double, and campus accommodation is not protected by the ACT tenancy act. Are you comfortable with those rates and increases? What can be done and what is being done?

Thanks for the question. I will ask the COO to provide more information should it be needed. We've spent a lot of time talking with our student representatives from the ANU Students Association, ANUSA, about this matter, and we are very concerned about the impact of the cost of living on our students. As you highlighted, some of these costs are out of our control, because they're set by private providers. We have done what we can to offset and reduce some of the utility costs that are within our control. I've had a number of conversations with the executive of ANUSA in relation to the tenancy act, their rights as tenants and what that means, but if you need more information I could ask our Chief Operating Officer.

Thank you for the question. Not all increases in the operating costs can be absorbed, as the Vice-Chancellor said. We do take steps to try to minimise the impact on residents wherever we can. This year, for example, we did absorb those utility costs rather than passing on costs through rent increases. But, in all cases, the weekly tariffs are independently assessed by an external valuer. Our accommodation tariffs cover not just rent but also direct and indirect costs such as amenities, and other service costs such as utilities, IT and various other student support services. We're conscious that the cost-of-living issues are significant, but we also believe that the cost of living on campus at ANU will remain competitive in 2027 compared to other options around Canberra.
Thank you. That's good to know. Is it correct that the ANU sold management of its on-campus accommodation to Dexus in 2019?
Yes, I think that's the right date.
That's correct.
It was before me, but yes.
Would it be possible to table the terms of the current accommodation contracts between ANU and any management partners for its student and on-campus accommodation?
COO?
I would have to take that on notice if I can, purely because of the commercial arrangements of those contracts.
Sure. Maybe you could take on notice, as well, the current vacancy levels of all ANU accommodations.
I could give you some vacancy figures now if you'd prefer.
That'd be great.

At the moment, in terms of our occupancy levels, essentially we have quite a number of different colleges across the campus. Occupancy levels currently range from about 98.7 per cent occupancy through to 68.7, so it's quite a range. If you like, I can table the full list or I can run through them now for you if you're interested in any particular numbers.

Tabling would be great. Thank you. Have you done any modelling or cost-benefit analysis of ANU ownership and management of these facilities compared to the current and future private management agreements? It just looks like the costs are higher than in comparable cities like Newcastle and Wollongong.
I don't think we have. We have talked about this.

No. I think it's fair to say that we haven't done specific modelling because there would be quite a few things to take into consideration, including the existing contracts and how they would be dealt with under such an arrangement. So we haven't done that specific modelling.

I want to really acknowledge the ANU's efforts to grow enrolments for lower-SES students. I know that's a real focus, and you're doing a lot in that area. There are some issues with the way that we collect data in this country that mean that, say, Canberrans don't get much support with that. But do you see how on-campus accommodation costs like this could really hinder those efforts and make it very hard for kids who don't have rich parents to actually enjoy the on-campus experience that ANU is well known for?

We do see that. To that end, this year we launched a new set of scholarships, 150 vice-chancellor's scholarships targeted specifically for those students, which include full accommodation in our residential campuses. That's supported by our alumni and our donors.
Brilliant.
At the moment—obviously we won't know till census date next year—I think that we've had full acceptance of those offers that went out not so long ago.
Well done. That's great to hear. I've got more questions. I'll put them on notice because I'm really keen to get to TEQSA. Thank you.
Thanks, Senator Pocock. Senator Scarr. I just note we're breaking in about 11 minutes.

Okay. I'll be very quick if I can. Congratulations on the work that you're doing. If Senator Peacock's complimentary, that means a lot, because I know he's well connected with the community in Canberra. So I acknowledge that. And that 96 per cent figure is quite outstanding in terms of successful job placements for your graduates.

I suspect you are going to anticipate the first question I'm going to ask you. I'll be impressed if you do. Has the ANU successfully managed to get its whole-of-organisation gender based violence prevention and response plan signed off by the Higher Education Gender-based Violence Regulator?
Yes.

Thank you. That's all I need to know, so people can work through the process of elimination as to who hasn't. Excellent.

The Australian newspaper reported in August that Chinese police had confiscated the passports of ANU academics and PhD students during a May 2024 visit. Do you know, or does anyone at the table know, what the circumstances of that case were and what steps ANU took in response?
We do, and we do think the reporting was exaggerated or a misrepresentation. In terms of the detail, I might ask our provost to answer that question.

With that episode, I think it was distressing for colleagues who perhaps do not travel in China often. It was a routine check, as I understand it, of the hotel where colleagues were staying. There were language difficulties between staff and the officials that were coming to check the passports, so there were some moments of confusion. But colleagues from the university came to assist. Passports were checked and returned to colleagues.

Okay. In a previous life I used to travel to China quite a lot and I never came across an episode like that, so it does surprise me somewhat. Is that the only information you have—there was regulatory confusion or confusion on the part of authorities?

As I understand it, yes. There was a language difficulty where colleagues' passports were being checked. They weren't able to speak across the language barrier. But, once colleagues from the university they were visiting came to assist, things were clarified rather quickly and passports were given back. I believe—
So just explain: was it at the hotel, where the passports were confiscated?
Yes. The local authorities, as I understand it, were coming to check everyone who was staying at the hotel there.

Again, I never came across that during the many times I travelled to China, so, again, that is interesting. Did you liaise with the embassy in China? Did they give you any explanation as to what had happened?

We did. We spoke with embassy staff. They were super helpful. They indicated that they thought it was a confusion, a problem of a language barrier. No staff were detained. Indeed, during this bit of confusion one member of staff left their passport with the authorities, was allowed to go and teach a class they had to teach and was then given their passport upon return. It was fairly orderly, I think.
How long did the authorities have the passports?

For the group in the building, I think, not for very long at all. It might have been a matter of an hour while things were being worked out. I'm not quite sure of the exact period. And for that one member of staff the passport was returned to them the next day.
How many people were on this delegation? How many people were impacted—even if you've got the ballpark figure?
As a ballpark figure, I would say six people.
Did you get anything from the embassy confirming an explanation? Have you got any document you could potentially table with us—take it on notice—just to corroborate—
Yes, I'll take that on notice.
from, say, the embassy's perspective that this is the reason for it and additional things shouldn't be read into it? Is it possible for you to take that on notice?
I'll take that on notice. Thank you.
What was the purpose of the particular visit where this occurred? What was the purpose of the visit and what areas of expertise or professions were members of the delegation in?
These were colleagues going for, I believe, a two-week intensive teaching period.
In relation to what discipline?
I believe this was the biological sciences, the chemical sciences and perhaps mathematics. Again, can I take that on notice to give you the accurate identification of those disciplinary areas?
Okay. And which university were they visiting?
I believe it was Shandong University, Weihai.
And the partnership with Shandong University continued after this episode?
The partnership with Shandong University was, at that point, in teach-out, so—
Sorry, it was what?
It was coming to an end. It did continue after that episode, but that was in a teach-out period.
It was coming to an end in accordance with its terms, its written terms?
That is correct.
It didn't have any possibility for renewal on it's own terms?
It may have had.
Can you have a look at that and perhaps come back on notice.
Okay.

I'm trying to reconcile that with what I thought, which was that the Foreign minister had cancelled the partnership earlier this year; I'm trying to reconcile 'it was coming to an end' with 'the Foreign minister's cancelled it'.
That is true. The Foreign minister has asked us to end that agreement, and we are in full compliance with that. The end—
Sorry, if it was coming to an end and ended in accordance with its terms, that's different from a cancellation, isn't it?

Yes. I do understand that. The end of the agreement, I believe, was later in time than the date that the Foreign minister would like us to end the agreement, so we brought that forward to end the agreement early.
The Foreign minister cancelled the agreement prior to it coming to an end?
Yes.
What was the reason for that cancellation?
That would be a matter for the Foreign minister.
You haven't been advised as to the reason for the cancellation?

As I understand it, in broad terms, the concern is about the nature of the institution in relation to specific areas or domains of study and the potential, for example, for research collaboration around dual-use technologies.
You didn't receive any indication that there was a connection between the cancellation and that incident where the passports were detained?
No.

Can you just take on notice to check if you've got anything else, any other communication from government, from any agency, with respect to the reason for the cancellation. There was a reference to dual-use technologies. Can you just explain what you mean by that?
The usual referrals of dual-use technologies are technologies that can be used in a non-war environment and in aggressive environments—technologies that can be used for good or for bad.
Did you receive any indication of any concern from the Australian government prior to the cancellation?
No, we did not.

If you can, on notice, check that. And could you also provide on notice, details of if you've ever had any other security incidents of that nature or something similar in China or potentially elsewhere involving ANU researchers, students or employees in a foreign university. Could you take that on notice as well, please.
I will do.
Thank you. I'll go to the timeline. This incident occurred when, in terms of the authorities coming and taking the passports?
I believe this happened in 2024.
In January? December? first quarter? second quarter?
I would say in the second quarter, although I would have to check to be absolutely certain.
It was then a year and a half later that the Foreign minister directed a cancellation of the partnership, is that correct?
Yes.
When was it going to expire in any event?
I believe it was going to expire in the first semester of next year.
I believe, but I will double check that for you, Senator.
If you could, thank you. If I can move on to the issue of—
We are due to break.
Senator O'Sullivan has the call.

At last estimates, it was revealed that Dr Andrew Hammond, an academic responsible for teaching Middle Eastern politics and history has, under his aegis as an ANU professor, publicly endorsed and promulgated antisemitic conspiracy theories. Can you confirm that he's still employed at the ANU, still teaches and has not been stood aside.
I remember that from last Senate estimates. What I can confirm is that there is still a process afoot, so that's not something that I can discuss. In terms of his status in relation to teaching—
That's all I'm asking.
I'll ask the provost.
He's currently not teaching.
But still employed while the process works its way through.
That's correct.
It was publicly reported that there was a complaint about this matter. What's the status of that complaint?
That's part of the process. It's being addressed through our processes.
What was the selection process of the combating racism special committee?
We established that special committee earlier this year. The provost is the chair of that committee, and I'll ask the provost to talk about that.

That committee was initiated earlier this year when the university was looking at a definition of antisemitism. Then our legislative requirements changed, and we have to consider further definitions of racism, Islamophobia and anti First Nations hate. When that committee was first called into being, I made a general call to the university to ask people to join the committee, but especially reached out—
You sought nominations, did you?

We sought self-nomination across the community. It was especially attentive to members of our Jewish community because, at that point, we were looking at only that definition. When that legislative remit expanded, we reopened the committee to see if there were other people who would like to join the committee to assist us in other areas.
Just to confirm, the selection process was that you sought expressions of interest. Did you appoint everyone that expressed interest, or did you have to make a selection?
No, we appointed everyone who expressed interest.
Then, because of the expanded scope, you opened it up to others. Was that the same process to find those people?

It was absolutely the same process to find those people. I think the committee was well underway at that point, and we probably had gotten many people who were already interested in general issues of antiracism, so the committee was not much expanded, but anyone who has wanted to join the committee has been welcomed.
So no-one that wanted to join has missed out.
No.

Are you aware that Jewish members of the committee wrote to its co-chairs in July 2026, objecting to the adoption of the first paragraph alone of the Universities Australia definition of antisemitism?
Yes, I'm aware that some members of that committee did so.
Was that letter or part of it put to the council?

That letter was written to me in the context of the committee. The role of that committee is to put recommendations forward to council. At that point, that work really had not begun, and, now, that work is coming to completion, so, yes, that will go to council with the recommendations across the committee.
But it hasn't yet.
It has not yet.
Has the ANU received any submission from any Jewish student, staff member or organisation supporting that first paragraph alone?

I can't point to any individual who has made a recommendation of adopting only the first part of the UA definition. What I can say is that we have had an open consultation across the university where colleagues could answer or make their preferences and their analysis known anonymously through a consultation process. So I do not know, from that open consultation, who said what, but there are a variety of views, and I have spoken to our Jewish community about this, and there are differences of views amongst that community.
Interim Vice Chancellor, you presented in front of the royal commission.
That's correct.
When was that? I'm trying to get the chronology. Do you recall?
It was in June.
I don't need the precise date. You gave evidence there that the definition had not yet been incorporated. Where is it at now? Has it been adopted?

I gave evidence to the royal commission that council had adopted the first paragraph of the Universities Australia definition and that council needed further time to consider the other paragraphs of the definition, and that was to the best of my knowledge in June.
Just so I understood the evidence before, it's been—
I think it was July instead of June.
Did you say it's going before council soon?
That's correct.
Since that time, we've had the regulatory requirement of all higher education providers to have those definitions in place by 1 January.
So it will be done?
It will be done.
Thank you for your time.
Thank you to you all. I believe, Mr Schwager, you have an update?

I do. If I could just update a response we gave to Senator Pocock's question on our Dexus accommodation arrangements for our purpose built student accommodation, the premise of Senator Pocock's question was that we originally sold the arrangements to a company called Dexus. In fact, the original sale of the purpose built student accommodation arrangements was to a company called Morrisons in 2016. They then sold that arrangement themselves to EMP in 2019, and then EMP sold that onto Dexus in 2023. It's an independent asset stream for those companies. They can trade, and then they have the arrangement with us, so I just wanted to correct the record for that purpose.
Thank you very much. Thank you to you all for your participation. You are free to depart.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text:
Thank you for the opportunity to make a short opening statement. As this committee is aware, TEQSA commenced its compliance assessment of the Australian National University on 27 June 2025 after it received a range of serious concerns about ANU's governance, culture and leadership. On 2 September 2026, TEQSA concluded its compliance assessment when our commissioners made a decision to impose four conditions on the registration of the ANU. A short form of these findings and the full text of the conditions are published on the TEQSA website, and we will table a copy of that document, which is already public.

I note from previous hearings that the commission wishes to understand as fully as possible the findings of TEQSA's compliance assessment and the basis for the conditions imposed. I also acknowledge the committee's cooperation in not seeking document production when it could have undermined the live compliance assessment previously.

TEQSA recognises the significant public interest in its decisions and carefully considered its options for publishing further details about its findings and reasons. This included whether the statement of reasons provided to the ANU could be published either in full or with redactions, whether a longer description of TEQSA's findings and reasons could be published and whether any other material which was before TEQSA commissioners, and which informed their decision, should be published. There's a substantial amount of personal information, which was before the TEQSA commissioners and which is reflected in the reasons. This includes a wide range of information or opinions about current and former council members, executives, employees, contractors and students. Some of this information was explicitly obtained on the basis that it was confidential or that the individual's consent would be sought prior to further disclosure. Further, the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency Act of 2011, the TEQSA Act, does not authorise the publication of personal information by TEQSA. This led TEQSA to the view that it could not publish the reasons in an unredacted form. It was not practical or realistic to seek consent from the range of individuals whose personal information appears in the reasons. The volume of personal information also meant that it was not practical or realistic to prepare a redacted form of reasons or a longer description of TEQSA's reasons, which fairly reflects those reasons. Disclosure of much of the information could cause real harm either to individuals or to the ANU'S own live processes, which are ongoing. However, I note and accept that statutory privacy or confidentiality requirements are not of themselves a sufficient basis to refuse to provide information to the committee. In anticipation that the committee would require TEQSA to provide a copy of its reasons, TEQSA has prepared a redacted form of the reasons which, while containing some personal information, redacts information that, if published, would prejudice the ongoing processes at the ANU to address the issues in TEQSA's reasons, or would involve unreasonable harm to individuals' safety, wellbeing or reputation. TEQSA has kept redactions to a minimum and avoided the redaction of information unless this kind of harm would be likely to arise. I also note that it's a matter for this committee to consider whether it's appropriate to publish material received in evidence and whether to afford a right of reply to those identified in evidence before this committee. I respectfully ask that the committee agrees to receive TEQSA's statements of reasons with minimal redactions on that basis.

As I've noted previously, Ms Briggs provided me with a report on 7 April 2026, as well as further amendments to her report on 20 April 2026, 21 April 2026 and 12 May 2026. I carefully considered the relevance and weight of Ms Briggs's report when determining how to brief commissioners on the compliance assessment. I also carefully considered the nature of procedural fairness TEQSA would be required to afford, based on the nature of material which was provided or which could be provided to the commissioners. In doing so, I noted that those interviewed by Ms Briggs provided information on the basis that the information they provided was confidential and would not be released without their consent. Having considered these matters, I determined not to provide the commissioners with Ms Briggs's report. I concluded that the principal value of Ms Briggs's report to TEQSA was her identification of issues requiring further investigation by TEQSA and records of discussion between Ms Briggs and other individuals, including current and former ANU officials. Further, if Ms Briggs's report is disclosed in whole or part, it could cause unreasonable harm to the safety, wellbeing or reputation of individuals who are identified or identifiable in the report. As such, I consider it would not be reasonable or appropriate to publicly disclose Ms Briggs's report.

Nonetheless, Ms Briggs's report informed significant further lines of inquiry, which are reflected in TEQSA's reasons. Subsequent to Ms Briggs's inquiries, which led to her report, TEQSA pursued a range of significant lines of inquiry, which are reflected in its statement of reasons. As TEQSA's reasons for its decision are being made available to the committee, I trust that the committee has an appropriate basis to consider TEQSA's decision-making and regulatory action. We are happy to provide those redacted reasons to the committee today.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: My questions really come to powers. I didn't have the benefit of being at the last estimates, in relation to this debate around powers, but I've certainly been following some of the commentary. As I understand it—and just correct me if I'm wrong in terms of my summary of where we got to in the last estimates—TEQSA intervened in relation to the governance of ANU to initially delay a selection process for a new chancellor. Is that correct?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: TEQSA did not impose a delay on the ANU. We spoke to the ANU, through the chancellor and with the council, about the risks that would be posed to a selection process were it to proceed while there were live and serious governance issues that were subject to a compliance assessment. In the first instance, the ANU Council absolutely agreed to delay that process.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text:
I could go through a shopping list of points in this regard, and I suspect we're going to have the same toing and froing. There is a point in time in engagement between a regulator and the entity that's being regulated or in a contractual relationship or any other legal relationship where the characterisation of a voluntary agreement—or someone conceding that they're going to do something when they're requested to—changes its character from being voluntary, as it would usually be known, to being a decision that's made under duress from a legal point of view. Or its coercion, or some sort of unlawful conduct, where the party that's being asked to do something feels as if they're over a barrel.

I can remember an unfair dismissal case I once had decades ago, where the commissioner resigned, but he was given a gun and told to do the honourable thing, right? Those are the sorts of examples where something which has initially been said to be voluntary isn't really voluntary, and, if it were subject to a legal examination, it could well be struck out as being something that was an abuse of power and beyond power. So my blunt question is: did TEQSA act unlawfully when it intervened in the ANU Chancellor selection process in the way it did?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text:
No, and I will make a couple of relevant comments. First of all, the impetus for moving to discussion about a voluntary undertaking, was that the ANU Council was concerned that, with the passage of time, there was increasingly little opportunity to run a selection process for the chancellor before the scheduled end of then-chancellor Bishop's term in December, and they had anticipated that a period of 12 months would be needed to run that process. We entered discussions with the ANU around whether it was possible to meet that need as they saw it, to move forward with the selection process but with sufficient guardrails in place, to deal with the risks that would arise in terms of trust and confidence or any subsequent findings in relation to governance issues and problems.

May I also say, though, that I think an important characteristic of the process is that, after those discussions, when the ANU Council was considering whether to enter into or to offer the voluntary undertaking, there was a period of quite some days when I understand there were many briefings of council members. There were opportunities for council members to talk amongst themselves, to meet with the then pro-chancellor, before, ultimately, conducting a voting process. I think the fact that they held that and that the document they were considering did not predetermine council nominees that would be part of that process aligns with a voluntary undertaking to meet a set of circumstances, rather than a coercive circumstance.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

Where he failed to explore the issues was what happens when those things fail, and that's a different set of circumstances, which do require involvement from the regulator.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Thanks again for all the work you've done at the ANU or for issues related to the ANU, and thanks for the comments in your opening statement relating to personal information contained in your final report and the inability to publish that in full. Obviously, events at ANU over the recent years—I think it's fair to say—have caused an enormous amount of harm to staff and students and its reputation. There's a lot of repair work underway and a lot more to do. There's a feeling in the community that there's been a lack of accountability for the harm that's been caused. How would you respond to that, especially in regards to senior leadership?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

The conditions that we have put in place are designed to strengthen and remedy the governance failings. What we have done in those is to call out some of the specific concerns about trust and confidence within the community to require that ways of consulting with the community and engaging more directly with the community and council are regularised and become part of normal practice, and to really expect that there needs to be comprehensive strengthening of governance. That doesn't really go to the question, I think, that you're putting, though, about consequences for individuals, but it is the entity—which is the council of the institution—that is the focus of TEQSA's regulatory powers. I would note, though, that TEQSA, at all times, has also had an eye to whether the ANU was using its internal processes and any relevant external referrals to deal with matters that, while not within our remit, were relevant for them to deal with in relation to these matters.
