agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Are you able to provide detail around the findings beyond the conditions that TEQSA has provided to ANU's council executive and what assurances it can provide that the identified shortcomings will actually be addressed?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: If I can answer in two parts, before you came in, I explained that we are tabling for the committee's consideration minimally redacted reasons for decision, which I think tell the entirety of the narrative from TEQSA's point of view about the issues of concern, the reasons for taking the action that we have. From that, it should be apparent to you why the conditions are quite extensive, because it sets out the nature, the depth and the breadth of the governance problems that we found. We understand the interest of the committee in being able to see that and we think that is reflected in the conditions.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Sorry—maybe I clumsily worded that. Did you provide the unredacted report, including the Briggs report, to the council and the executive for them to see what—

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: The council have the full unredacted reasons for decision. In fact, it's at the request of the ANU that we've redacted some of that information, because they still have live ongoing internal processes in relation to some of those matters. So we've ensured that, in the redactions, we've mitigated the risk that any of that could be prejudiced. In relation to the Briggs report, I've made sure that Chancellor de Brouwer has been really comprehensively briefed in relation to the findings of Ms Briggs, which of course was the early part of the matter and went to culture. He has also spoken with Ms Briggs.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: But they haven't seen the actual Briggs report.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: No, and that was not something that the commission relied upon in the decision.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Will that stay with TEQSA? What happens to the Briggs report?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: It will.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I've just got a couple of questions about the 'antisemitism' definition. It seems like there's been some confusion about the TEQSA guidelines, which I understand were released in final form today, where universities need to adopt a definition of 'antisemitism' by 1 Jan 2027 under amendments to the Higher Education Standards Framework. Do I read that correctly? Is that what is required by 1 Jan 2027—that every university has to have a definition?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: That's correct.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I just want to be clear. TEQSA's guidelines give two examples but don't require universities to adopt any particular definition of antisemitism.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: That's correct. The standards that were made by the minister require universities to have a definition but don't prescribe which of the commonly used and commonly adopted definitions must be adopted. That, I think, is consistent with the work that's already been done by some universities in this space, and the fact that they are all autonomous institutions.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: So it's mandatory for universities to have a definition of 'antisemitism', but it's up to the university as to what that is?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: That's correct. TEQSA has provided exemplars, which are the Universities Australia definition and the IHRA definition. The UA definition in particular, because it was developed for Australian higher education contexts and with consideration of the need for it to work in conjunction with their obligations for academic freedom, was felt by many in the consultation feedback that it was more easily implemented than the IHRA definition in a context where scholarship might still require debate around some of those issues.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: So the definition just needs to be compatible with academic freedom and freedom of expression?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: There are already obligations under the standards that are relevant to academic freedom, freedom of speech, and student and staff wellbeing. In effect, adopting the definition is only the first step. It needs to be one that can be has enough specificity and clarity to be used to set expectations about conduct and behaviour, about what aspects of scholarship are acceptable and what cross the line into antisemitism, and that it can also be applied in activities such as education, induction, assessment criteria, complaints and grievance processes. There's a level of clarity that needs to be applied from the definition to conduct and implementation in real life.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Just to augment: TEQSA doesn't create the standards. We regulate against the standards that are determined by the minister. If there is no specification of a particular definition in the standards, it's not TEQSA's role to go beyond that, but it's certainly our role to support the providers in implementing.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Thank you very much, Commissioner and Dr Russell, and to your team. That's all I have for now. I'll put a few questions on notice about another matter.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Senator Scarr.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Dr Russell, we're coming to the end of our time; if you want to take something on notice, please feel free. Does TEQSA accept that section 17 of the act governing the Australian National University explicitly prohibits council from delegating its powers with respect to the appointment of the chancellor, the pro-chancellor or the vice-chancellor?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I don't have the benefit of having the ANU Act in front of me. However, the appointment was still a matter for council to make. The process was conducted with council participation. A recommendation was made to council. I understand there were interviews or discussions with candidates by council. But the final matter of that decision was not for TEQSA; it was for council, and I understand that it was made by council in the usual way.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I'm not sure there's much usual about this process. I refer to my earlier comments around what is truly voluntary. What specific sections of the legislation giving powers to TEQSA did TEQSA act under?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I believe Dr Russell, at the last estimates, explained that the agency didn't use statutory powers in relation to the agreement of a voluntary undertaking with the ANU. However, the agency's functions in section 134 of the TEQSA Act contemplate that it may perform compliance assessments and other activities that are consistent with the process to agree to the voluntary undertaking.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: So it's a combination of what you refer to as contemplated powers or actions under section 134 and the supposed voluntary response of the university that you're relying upon. In that context, I am bemused as to why you didn't get external legal advice, especially given the eminent jurists who were giving very strong opinions with respect to this matter. What's to stop TEQSA from using this cobbling together of contemplated actions under section 134 and so-called voluntary processes against another university?

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I can't recall the time relationship between the publication of those references to eminent advice. I recall that the ANU Council appointed Dr Marshall as the acting pro-chancellor, and I recall that, under the ANU Act, it is the specified role of the pro-chancellor to run the chancellor selection process. That's expressly not a matter for the chancellor; it is a matter for the person in that role. I would characterise all that interaction as being very actively conducted, led and consulted upon, from everything we could see, with the ANU Council. You are free to ask Dr Marshall, but he has expressed to me that he was at all times comfortable with that.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I understand your view, but I'm bemused you didn't go externally and get some very eminent opinions.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: We weren't contemplating imposing a condition because we were expecting, and did receive, a voluntary undertaking.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Okay. I may have further questions on notice, thanks.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Thank you, Dr Russell. I believe that does conclude our questions. Apologies there was a bit of confusion from your opening statement.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: I'm very sorry. It's difficult to make the relationship of all the documents clear.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: No, it's all good. We might just take some time to review that and review the document you've asked us to table.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: We're mindful of the concerns you raise.

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Thank you.
witness_organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency

agency: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
text: Thank you to you and to your officers. You're free to depart—quickly, if possible—because I'm now calling the Australian Research Council to the table.
Welcome. I have on my list that I'm also welcoming Professor Shergold, who's clearly not at the table.
Yes. Unfortunately, his car broke down on the way to Canberra, so he's now—
What! I've heard some excuses, but—
somewhere in the bush in a rented car and hasn't made it. He sends his deepest apologies. He was looking forward to being here.
Well, we hope he's okay—
He's okay.
and getting help. Professor Roessner, do you have an opening statement?
No, we don't.
Great. Senator O'Sullivan, you have until 10 o'clock.

Thank you very much. I appreciate the late hour and you hanging around. Sorry that we've been a little delayed in getting to you. I do only have a small number of questions, so I think we should finish on time in any case. I want to ask about grant GA590009. Do you want some time to look that up, or can I continue?
We might have to look it up, because we won't have all the grants. We'll see if we can find the details of it, but, if you have a description of the title, that would assist.

Sure. The title is 'Coffee lifeworlds in a changing climate'. I'll read the description of it, which might give you some time, as well, to look it up. Under this grant there's $1.17 million awarded to the University of Sydney for this project called 'Coffee lifeworlds in a changing climate'. It says:

This project aims to uncover how multispecies approaches offer new ways of intervening in the relations between agriculture, sustainability, climate justice and resilience at a time of intensifying ecological degradation and vulnerability.

Why should taxpayers pay $1.17 million for this when government spending is destroying our economy by driving up inflation?
This would normally be a question for Professor Shergold, the chair of the board, who has—
Get him on the phone! Does his phone still work in his car, or is the whole thing—

the responsibility to oversee our rigorous peer review assessment process, because the board makes, ultimately, decisions on funding outcomes. He would definitely ensure you that the ARC has in place a very rigorous peer review assessment process, taking consideration from expert reviewers from the academic world, as well as our college expert members who are a subcommittee of the board. Grants are assessed based on their research excellence, national benefit, feasibility et cetera. There are very clear assessment criteria that are assessed against, and that leads to a funding recommendation.

Are you saying, though, that you're not in a position now to give me justification for that expenditure and why this particular project received money to 'uncover how multispecies approaches offer new ways of intervening in the relations between agriculture, sustainability, climate justice' and the like?

We would not be able to have insight of the 6,000 grants we're holding individually. That's why we're running a rigorous expert assessment review. A number of experts have assessed this project in much detail and have assessed it as excellent research worth funding.
Can I ask about grant GA589824. This is $1.33 million to the University of Technology Sydney for a study of homicidal corporations. Why are we spending money on homicidal corporations?
It seems like a loaded term!

I will reflect back on Professor Shergold previous comments on similar projects. The ARC is established with the board, and one of the big premises of the board is to ensure we run a rigorous peer review process that relies on eminent experts to provide advice on what is a worthy project. We have 5,700-plus grants on file. It would be hard for us to go through each and every detail of why they're funded. What the board relies on in making its decisions is excellent research based on peer review. What I would add though is that with the revitalised National Competitive Grants Program that was announced by the government earlier this year one of the things that the ARC is looking at is how we better incorporate the national interest into the research that we're doing.

We're going to do that in two ways. In the assessment model, we're introducing a 'why, how, who' model. The 'why' becomes important—understanding why we are investing in this—to help our peer reviewers and our applicants to outline why this is in the national interest when we've got $1 billion of Australian government funding that's being allocated. The second part that we're doing as well is that we're broadening the pool of experts to include community groups, industry end-users and other users of research so that when the board is looking at the process as a whole it's going to be based in peer review. That's a principle that is world renowned for identifying projects.

We always hear about Wi-Fi and a whole range of other projects. It's why these great ideas come to fruition. What the board often does is make sure that the review process that we have in place identifies excellence, and the new National Competitive Grants Program is going to target that more on the national interest as we go forward.
When a decision is made to award the grant to the applicant, do you not record a statement as to why the decision was made by ARC to award that grant?

The ARC does not make the decision. The board makes the decision. The process is that every application is sent to a number of expert reviewers, who are experts in the field. They're called detailed assessors. They return an assessment report and a scoring, and then we have the college of experts. Two of those members also take care of each of the proposals, assess them and rank them, resulting in a ranked list of proposals. If there are 2,000 applications, you have a ranked list. The top ranked ones normally are considered highly competitive and are not further discussed, and there's a middle band of many more proposals than we can fund because of financials.

The size of the pot is much smaller than what we could fund. Then there's a selection advisory panel, which is comprised of members of the college of experts in their disciplinary fields. There are five disciplinary panels who look at those proposals that are competitive where there are too many to be funded and select the best of those. That's the current process. Going forward, we are developing new assessment models.

What I find unsatisfactory is not being able to come to Senate estimates, ask questions and have specific advice as to why a grant was awarded. What's stopping this process from being able to interrogate the validity of a grant and have a grant justified back to the taxpayers through us, as elected members?
It is because the experts have already assessed one assessment criterion—
Yes—I want to understand why the experts agreed to fund homicidal corporations and how many homicidal corporations there are in Australia.
Well, the expert determined that this was a valuable experiment or project—
Yes. And, again, I'm trying to understand their reasons.
Are they experts on homicidal corporations?
You'll have to read the research to find out, Senator!

Yes, you'll have to read the whole proposal! Based on a title, you cannot define whether this is valuable research. There are 10 pages that describe the project. There are another 20 or so pages on each of the CVs and track records of each of the investigators or partners involved. But the whole proposal is very long, and I suspect that they determined it based on the selection criteria—which are investigator capability, project quality and innovation, benefit and feasibility.

But you have abstracts for long academic papers. So just to take on Senator O'Sullivan's point, why can't you come along with a spreadsheet that's got each grant? He asks a question about a grant. You click on the project, or whatever it is—proposal—and you can at least give a one-paragraph or two-sentence 'This is important because of X.'
Yes. Also we normally see only the 100-word summary. There is no capacity for us to read—
So why can't we have the benefit of that here?
You can see the 100-word summary. That's public information.
Yes, that's what I was asking: what's the justification for GA589824?
Why can't you look it up now and read the 100 words?
You can.
There are a couple of factors. There's—
We're really interested in the homicidal corporations!
Perhaps the website link could be provided to the senators, if that would be—
We can take some of this on notice.
In the last ones we described where all the outcomes are listed, you can read the 100-word summary and the 150-word—
That's a summary of the project—
Yes.

And I've read one of them out. So I've got the link already, thanks. But I'm trying to understand: there's got to be a justification that the board has made for awarding that. You're saying that there are experts. I get that. There's plenty that they're rejecting. They probably get a lot more applications than they're able to award—

The board trusts the process in order to make the final funding decision, which is a recommendation by the selection advisory committee, those experts who spend a week in our offices to discuss each of those applications to say which ones will be funded and which ones will not be.
Who are they accountable to?

Maybe I could try to answer in a slightly different way. The rationale for why the government is investing in research is that there's a range of benefits. There are economic benefits, there's social—
Yes, I understand all that.

When it comes to a particular project, one of the things we are working with the academic community on is how to better articulate their projects. When you outline some titles, there might be a better way to engage with the public on what the national interest is and why we're investing. The new process that we're developing as part of the revitalised National Community Grants Program is getting to that. Senator Scarr talked about how sometimes you have a detailed abstract but then you have a plain-English 'Why is this important?' and 'Why should the public care?' And the board understands what you're raising, Senator, and I think going forward trying to really articulate the value of the investment that is there. But the premise of the peer-review process—and this is around the world; this is not just Australia but all the funding agencies that invest in basic and early-stage research—is that we rely on the expertise of the academic community in those disciplines to advise boards or decision-makers on why it is a worthy investment. What we're doing under the new NCGP is improve that so we can articulate that in our—
And then ultimately—
This will be your last question.

last question—the final sort of check of accountability is this process here. It's a significant sum of money, and our job is to hold it to account. I've got a constituent in Western Australia who sends me these things all the time: 'Why are we funding this? Why are we funding that?' So they're expecting me to come in here and ask these sorts of questions about why we are funding a study of homicidal corporations.

Maybe an example: Richard Robson, who just got the Nobel Prize last year, in 1987 got the first grant from our predecessor. It would not be funded today, because it was so blue-sky, and who would care about models of chemistry molecules?
No, no, no, it's a little bit different from a homicidal corporation. I won't say anything else!
That's a different discipline.

And this is the point: I want to make sure—my interest here is so that we can fund more of that, so we can fund more wi-fi projects, so we can fund more cochlear and all the things we're doing and Over-the-Horizon radar and all of that.
But that might lead to the incorrect policy—

Senators, I think we're descending here from a question-and-answer session to a conversation that perhaps we can extend to the tea trolley outside. At this point we're going to move to my closing statement. That concludes today's hearing. Thank you to all our witnesses who have appeared before us today, and to Hansard and broadcasting for their assistance and of course the wonderful support we get from our secretariat and I believe the secretariats we've co-opted in to help us over the last couple of days—thank you, too. I remind senators that the committee has agreed that any written questions on notice should be lodged with the secretariat by Thursday 5 November 2026.
